Its observations and ordered completion markers do not, by themselves, establish that every manuscript tool works, stored edits reach the reviewer, or a saturated progress stream cannot lose request replies. Keep those required behaviors covered by real public-API integration tests and source review. Passing a marker check does not waive them.

§5.1 The idea in plain words

Chapter 2 built a renderer that turned the event log into history.md. It watched the stream and produced a view: an observer. The reader has already built one and can now name it.

A deaf loop processes one request at a time. The model sends back a tool call, the engine runs the tool, and nothing else can happen until the tool finishes. A user typing a hint while a three-second build runs gets no acknowledgment. A second agent waiting for its turn gets nothing at all. The engine is a for-loop, and a for-loop has no ears.

The fix is three pieces that work together.

An observer is a one-way window. The Agent notifies observers when something happens: a state transition, a completed response, a streaming chunk. Observers cannot call back into the engine. They watch and react. A logger is an observer. A GUI is an observer. A parent managing a child agent is an observer. What matters is that the framework defines the interface, observers implement it, and nothing inside the framework knows what the observers do. A GUI, a gateway, and a sub-agent supervisor all plug in here without any of them changing a line of framework code.

A mailbox is a one-way door. The Agent accepts messages through a queue: prompts, hints, tool completions, interrupts. Post does not wait for execution or a receiver. The queue is a slice guarded by a mutex with a channel to signal “something arrived.” Prompts, hints, and tool completions enter through the same door because the loop that processes them needs to see them in order. A hint that arrives while a tool is running goes into the queue after the prompt that started the turn and before the tool completion that ends it. The ordering is the whole point. A separate queue per message type destroys it.

An actor loop drains the mailbox. The Agent runs its actor on its own goroutine. It blocks on the mailbox’s signal channel until something arrives, drains the queue, and processes each message in order. After processing, it notifies observers. The loop is the smallest possible concurrency primitive: one goroutine, one queue, one notify step. It replaces the synchronous for-loop from Chapter 4 with something that can hear. The mailbox synchronizes delivery; the job subsystem synchronizes worker state. Neither gives workers permission to mutate the conversation.

These three pieces are independent additions to the star topology from Chapter 4. The observer interface and public mailbox input types go into internal/common/; private worker messages stay with their owner. The mailbox implementation goes into a new spoke or an existing one. The Agent-owned actor replaces the engine’s synchronous ask while preserving the public blocking API. Internal orchestration helpers are retired, not retained as a second execution path.

§5.2 The framework that imported its own GUI

CodeRhapsody built the GUI before it had a framework seam. The React frontend connected to a Go server, the Go server imported the framework, and the framework reached back into the server for test scaffolding. test_support.go built a real GUI server for the twenty-three tests that needed a UI attached. The import graph formed a cycle, and the cycle hid inside convenience: nobody noticed because every test passed.

The dependency surfaced as a question: can the framework run without the GUI? No. It compiled without it, but tests could not run. Untangling it took five commits across two days. The load-bearing commit was titled “Test scaffolding takes a UIObserver, not a GUI server.”

The fix was not deletion. The GUI was demoted to an observer. Instead of the framework importing the GUI, the framework broadcasts events, and the GUI subscribes to them. The import arrow reversed direction. After the fix, the framework does not know the GUI exists, the GUI is one of several observers, and tests run without building a server.

The guard that enforces this boundary exempts test files and ratchets them downward, on the principle that a guard that fails today guards nothing. Twenty-three tests needed a GUI server. Now thirteen do, and the ratchet prevents the number from climbing back. The boundary found problems, it did not create them: two encapsulation reaches appeared as compile errors the moment the internal/ wall went up, one where a tool file grew a method on a job type and another where the engine called an unexported function on a job.

The fix’s shape is this chapter’s thesis. The GUI went from a component the framework knows about to an observer the framework broadcasts at. The first-edition facade measured who actually used its framework: two-thirds of the API surface serves tool authoring, five percent serves agent lifecycle. Design the observer seam for the ninety-five percent of the world that is not the engine.

§5.3 The outbound seam

An observer receives events. It does not ask for them, it does not call back into the engine, and it does not block. Those three constraints are the interface:

type Observer interface {
    Observe(Observation)
}

Observe takes one argument. The argument is a sealed interface: the framework defines every type that implements it, and external code cannot add new ones. Three types carry the information:

type PartDelta struct {          // streaming chunk
    PartID uint64 `json:"part_id"`
    Chunk  string `json:"chunk"`
}

A PartDelta arrives for every streaming chunk the vendor sends. PartID identifies which part is being streamed so that an observer can assemble the complete response without confusing concurrent parts. Chunk is a string because it is text. A []byte JSON field would base64-encode it, adding about a third to the byte count before JSON overhead.

The streaming rule: do not model streaming as a mode. Model non-streaming as a stream of length one. A non-streaming vendor emits one delta plus the finalizer. Observers that care about liveness render deltas; observers that do not ignore them and act on finalizers. Adding streaming later therefore adds no new event kinds.

Tool results are the proof the rule is right: they are observable but never stream, which needs no special case. They are always length one.

Deltas are transient. They are never appended to the durable log; finalized content and other conversation facts are recorded. The log is the state. The stream is the experience. Replaying the log must produce the same context as the live run, minus the animation. The replay-is-live check tests exactly this: replay the prefix just before the last request_sent and compare the rendered request byte for byte with the captured request. The marker records delivery and consumes pending ephemera, so including it would reconstruct the state after that request was sent.

type PartFinal struct {          // completed part
    Seq    uint64   `json:"seq"`
    PartID uint64   `json:"part_id"`
    Part   Part     `json:"part"`
}

A PartFinal arrives when a part is complete: the full neutral part, including text, a tool call or a tool result, with its sequence number and display identity. A text-only field loses the call arguments and correlation that an observer needs. Durable replay uses the event log, which also contains prompts, hints and request boundaries; the lossy observation stream cannot replace it.

type StateChanged struct {       // turn-state transition
    From   string `json:"from"`
    To     string `json:"to"`
}

A StateChanged fires on every transition: Idle to InputPending, InputPending to InFlight, InFlight to ToolsPending, any terminal state back to Idle. The GUI uses this to show a spinner. An application uses this to display progress; request completion tells it when a particular submitted turn finished. The grader uses this to verify the observer seam works.

The observation types carry no agent identity. For a single agent, that is all you need. For a multi-agent framework, the coordinator tags agent identity externally when it routes observations. The type is cheap because external tagging is just a wrapper.

The observer is told, never asked. The Agent calls Observe after every action: after recording a response, after transitioning state, after a tool completes. Observers receive future events from the same code path that updates the context. Attaching late does not replay earlier observations; history remains the separate source for past facts.

Why Observe must not block

A blocking observer recreates the deafness. The Agent calls Observe on the actor goroutine. If Observe takes a lock, writes to a slow network, or waits for a response, the actor goroutine stalls. The mailbox fills up. Hints arrive and wait. The queue that was supposed to fix the problem becomes the problem.

If an observer needs to do slow work, it copies the observation and posts it to its own queue. The observer’s goroutine drains its own queue. The actor never waits for that slow work.

§5.4 The inbound seam

The agent is deaf, but the obvious explanation is wrong. It is not that the tool runs inline. The tool already runs on its own goroutine since Chapter 4. It is that the conversation loop parks in a select awaiting the job report, and that is the same loop that would drain inbound events. The drainer is parked. Hints arrive and sit in a channel that nobody reads until the tool finishes.

The fix: deliver tool completions INTO the queue instead of awaiting them in a select. The mailbox carries everything the Agent can hear:

type Inbound interface{ inbound() }

type UserMessage   struct{ Text string }
type Hint          struct{ Text string }
type Interrupt struct{}

One queue carries public input and private worker messages. The small mailbox sketch below uses any for those internal messages; public Post accepts only the public input vocabulary. The implementation is a mutex-guarded slice with a buffered channel of capacity one as the signal:

type Box struct {
    mu    sync.Mutex
    queue []any
    Wake  chan struct{}
}

func (b *Box) Post(msg any) {
    b.mu.Lock()
    b.queue = append(b.queue, msg)
    b.mu.Unlock()
    select {
    case b.Wake <- struct{}{}:
    default:
    }
}

func (b *Box) Drain() []any {
    b.mu.Lock()
    q := b.queue
    b.queue = nil
    b.mu.Unlock()
    return q
}

Post does not wait for a receiver. Its brief mutex protects enqueueing; it is not a lock-free guarantee. If the channel is full, the signal is already pending and the loop will drain the queue. Drain returns everything and clears the queue. The mutex protects the slice; the channel is just a wake signal. The queue preserves arrival order and nothing else.

Why one queue

A prompt, a hint, a tool completion, and an interrupt arrive through the same door because the order they arrived in is the order they matter in. A hint that arrived during a tool call matters now. A tool completion that arrived after an interrupt still contains real output. Its former turn is over; its job may still be alive.

Separate queues destroy this ordering. If prompts and hints go to different channels, a select chooses between them, and Go’s select is pseudo-random when both are ready. The hint might be processed before the prompt that it was meant to modify, or after the tool that it was meant to interrupt. A single FIFO preserves arrival order, and arrival order is causal order.

Tool completions enter the mailbox

This is the change that breaks the deafness. In Chapter 4, the Agent dispatcher waits for the job report. The wait has a limit, but the same conversation loop cannot process human input while it is parked.

In Chapter 5, workers execute the tool and wait for its report. They post their outcomes to the mailbox. The Agent is back at its mailbox drain loop, free to process hints and interrupts while the tool runs. The tool result arrives as a message, not a return value, and the actor processes it in queue order alongside everything else.

§5.5 The actor loop

The actor is the Agent’s conversation goroutine with a mailbox. It blocks on the signal channel, drains the queue, and processes each message. After processing, it notifies observers.

func (r *runtime) run() {
    for {
        <-r.owner.box.Wake
        for _, message := range r.owner.box.Drain() {
            switch m := message.(type) {
            case common.UserMessage:
                r.input(m.Text)
            case common.Hint:
                r.input(m.Text)
            case response:
                r.receive(m)
            case report:
                // Record the real result, including reports from older turns.
                r.recordReport(m)
            case common.Interrupt:
                r.interrupt(common.ErrInterrupted)
                // Keep draining: interruption does not end the actor.
            }
        }
    }
}

This is schematic: runtime belongs to the Agent, and recordReport stands for its report-handling branch. The excerpt omits request replies, shutdown, error handling and round limits. Notifications follow successful reduction, so observers see stored facts. The shape remains drain, switch, notify; method names are not the exercise contract.

Starting a turn records the prompt as a MessageReceived event, renders the context and records the request boundary before handing HTTP to a worker. That worker returns response facts through the mailbox. A synchronous HTTP call on the actor would merely move the deafness from tools to the network. Tool calls enter ToolsPending; dispatch remains serial within their batch, with each wait performed outside the actor. When no further calls or pending hints remain, the turn can finish.

Applying a hint records the hint as a HintReceived event and attaches it to the pending context. The next vendor request will include it. A hint arriving during HTTP cannot rewrite bytes already sent; record the request boundary before releasing the transport worker. The hint does not start a new turn and does not change the turn state.

Recording a result records the tool result as a ToolReturned event, checks whether all outstanding calls have results, and if so, sends the accumulated results back to the vendor for the next round.

interrupt ends the active turn and cancels its in-flight model request. The Agent remains usable, and other jobs continue. Pair outstanding calls honestly: a wait was interrupted, not necessarily its job. Refuse calls that were never dispatched. A later real report must not become a duplicate vendor result or finish a newer turn. The accepted implementation retains it as job_report, with the bytes still in the job output file.

Ask, rebuilt

The synchronous Ask API from Chapter 4 still works; the accepted public method also takes a caller context. It delegates to the agent’s owned actor:

func (a *agent) Ask(ctx context.Context, text string) (string, error) {
    reply := a.Submit(ctx, text)
    select {
    case result := <-reply:
        return result.Text, result.Err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return "", ctx.Err()
    }
}

Submit creates a one-element buffered reply channel, posts the request, and returns that channel. Ask waits for its reply, caller cancellation, or actor shutdown. The actor continues processing its mailbox. The buffer lets the actor finish even if the caller has cancelled. The actor returns that request’s text and error, not shared last-text state. When persistence is configured, save before replying; a failed save is a failed completion, not durable success. The accepted library’s empty LogPath leaves persistence with its embedding caller. Notify observers of the same outcome without making observation delivery a prerequisite for returning to the caller.

The excerpt shows the request-specific reply; production also handles shutdown without losing an already completed reply. Starting the actor is lazy and idempotent. Repeated callers use the same Agent-owned mailbox consumer; an additional public Actor wrapper is unnecessary. Shutdown stops new work, cancels in-flight model requests, stops managed processes, joins workers, records their outcomes and saves. An arbitrary Go tool may not be cancellable: shutdown must wait for it, not discard its real result and pretend it stopped. Repeated shutdown is safe; later requests return a distinguishable stopped error.

Delete Engine.Ask and any sibling orchestration loop after migrating their callers, including legacy CLI prompt formats and embedding programs. Keep one-request rendering and transport in Engine and reduction/persistence in History. The Agent actor orders multi-round orchestration, turn setup, runtime context mutation and save-before-reply. Workers send facts through the mailbox; they do not append directly to live History. The synchronous API survives; the duplicate implementation does not.

The same ownership rule applies to the tool-round limit. A positive N permits N dispatched tool batches in one human turn. Zero selects the named default of 200, not infinity. Read the effective setting once at turn start; chapter 8’s persisted setting must feed this same policy. After the Nth batch, allow the model to consume its results and finish. If it asks for another batch, execute none of it, record explicit not-executed results for every call and return a distinguishable limit error. Do not leave dangling calls or edit signed assistant content. A later instruction can start a new turn.

Where is the concurrency?

One actor goroutine owns the engine. A tool execution worker runs the handler; a separate job-report worker waits for completion, the callback deadline or an output pattern. These must be separate: a blocked handler must not prevent the model from receiving a running-job report. A callback is not cancellation. Both workers belong to the shutdown join.

Workers return results and context effects through the mailbox rather than mutating the engine. The job subsystem synchronizes process state, output and completion; the actor owns the conversation. Count ownership boundaries, not a fixed number of goroutines.

The minimalism is deliberate. Every lock is a place where two goroutines disagree about what is happening. Two goroutines can disagree in testable ways. Ten goroutines with a shared map disagree in ways that show up in production at 3 AM on a Saturday.

CodeRhapsody’s Chapter 4 grader exposed five real concurrency bugs in 120 parallel test runs. The root cause of every one was a parent holding stale facts about a child: reading a field on one goroutine while the actor goroutine wrote it. The fix each time was the same: move the read to the actor goroutine, or make the mailbox the only path between them. Two goroutines with one lock is not a style preference. It is what survived the race detector.

That historical two-goroutine fix established the ownership boundary. The job-report worker preserves it while allowing callbacks before a tool returns. The goal is still minimal concurrency, with one execution owner and explicit messages across every boundary.

§5.6 The Wait primitive

This chapter does not introduce agent state. It exposes it. The reader has had a state machine since Chapter 2: TurnState with Idle, InputPending, InFlight, ToolsPending. This chapter adds Interrupted, deliberately as a state rather than a flag, because the interrupted turn must not resume dispatch when a late result arrives. Replay reduces recorded facts; it does not execute tools. The state machine is a fact. The observer seam makes it visible. Wait makes it waitable.

func (a *agent) Wait(ctx context.Context,
    pred func(Observation) bool) (Observation, error)

Wait blocks until an observation satisfies pred or the context cancels. The current actor consumes a bounded observation channel; it is not a subscription replaying every event to every waiter.

Blocking send uses the request-scoped completion described above, not Wait for a shared idle transition.

Wait for agent, join, and wake-any can use observations to watch agent state. But an orchestration decision that requires completion cannot rest on a lossy progress stream. Track the relevant request completions reliably, then publish the resulting progress. A shared idle event cannot acknowledge a particular prompt, and a slow observer must not stall the actor just to prevent a dropped progress notification.

The original check named wake-once verified observations and turn-ended records from distinct Agents. It did not measure wakeup count or simultaneous completion. The Edition 2 label is multi-agent-observations. This application coordinates stages sequentially; reliable request completion tells it when to pass a result to the next Agent. No grouped-results API is required.

§5.7 Hints and interrupts

A hint is the same event as a prompt, distinguished by turn state. A message that arrives while the turn is idle starts a new turn. A message that arrives while the turn is in flight or tools-pending is a hint. Classification belongs to the Agent conversation owner using the current reduced state, not the stdin reader whose view can already be stale. Blocking Ask/Submit calls deliberately queue separate requests instead of becoming hints.

The HintReceived event type exists for exactly this reason: without it, the reducer cannot distinguish “a new prompt arrived” from “a hint arrived during an active turn.” Both carry text. The difference is when they arrived relative to the turn, and the turn state is the reducer’s business.

Bill’s ruling on callbacks is absolute: a callback added to break a Go dependency cycle is a red flag. The mailbox breaks no cycles. It is the mechanism by which concurrent events enter a sequential loop, not a workaround for a dependency the compiler rejected. The Agent owns the conversation goroutine, queue and notification step. If you find yourself adding function-pointer fields to break a compile error, the dependency is real, and the fix is to move the interface to the hub.

An Interrupt ends the active turn, not the actor’s lifetime. The actor continues draining its mailbox and recording results. A Go handler may still complete after the interrupt; its real output is not garbage. An explicit job kill has different semantics: it suppresses late output for that killed job. Shutdown must stop managed processes, join workers and save their outcomes rather than silently applying kill semantics to every non-cancellable Go function.

The stdin protocol

The CLI reads stdin on its own goroutine and posts to the agent’s mailbox. The protocol is JSON lines:

{"kind":"prompt","text":"Write a haiku about refactoring"}
{"kind":"hint","text":"Use a metaphor about gardens"}
{"kind":"interrupt"}

Backward compatibility with the Chapter 1 format:

{"user":"Write a haiku about refactoring"}

A message with a "user" key and no "kind" key is treated as a separate request through the blocking adapter. This preserves the older protocol’s request/reply behavior. Explicit live prompt or hint messages use current turn state; they can become hints while the Agent is busy.

§5.8 Managing multiple agents

A single-agent framework is a special case. The same engine, the same mailbox, the same observer seam scales to N agents with one addition: a coordinator that tracks which agents exist and routes observations.

// Ensemble already owns the peer Agents; it is not a second coordinator root.
type AgentObservation struct {
    Agent       Agent
    Observation Observation
}

func (e *Ensemble) WaitAny(ctx context.Context,
    pred func(AgentObservation) bool) (AgentObservation, error)

Each Agent has its own mailbox and execution loop. It reports observations through its Ensemble parent, which supplies the source identity in an envelope. WaitAny consumes one matching observation from that merged progress stream. It does not gather a group of request results. The application retains each request’s own completion for decisions that must not be lost.

A Go program constructing three agents and passing messages between them is not an agent spawning children through its own tool surface. Multi-agent requires nothing beyond a framework, a prompt, and tools. This exercise is just Go. The distinction matters because a sub-agent chapter adds a tool surface for spawning; this chapter proves it is not necessary.

A framework that manages agents is a parent. The observation stream is how the parent watches its children. A future agent supervisor can use progress from this seam alongside reliable completion. Its spawning and waiting contract is not defined by this exercise. The alternative is reading the child’s history file. One supervision call built that way returned 307,984 bytes, roughly 13% of a context window, because it had no volume contract. The observer seam, delivering events as they happen, returned 3,447 bytes for the same purpose.

The third agent is the proof. If adding it requires a single change inside the framework package, the seam is incomplete.

§5.9 Media capabilities

Accepting images does not imply accepting audio. Accepting audio does not imply accepting video. A renderer that silently drops an unsupported part is the Chapter 1 mistake: the model does not see what the programmer sent, and neither one knows.

ModelFeatures declares what a model accepts:

type Media uint8
const (
    MediaImage    Media = 1 << iota
    MediaAudio
    MediaVideo
    MediaDocument
)

type ModelFeatures struct {
    Media Media
}

LookupModel(model) (ModelFeatures, bool) has no default row. An unknown model returns false. If a blob needs rendering, the renderer refuses rather than guessing its support; text alone is still allowed. For an unsupported audio attachment, the diagnostic names both facts:

error: model "claude-3-haiku-20240307" does not support audio;
       cannot render BlobPart with Ref{Kind:RefPath, Locator:"recording.mp3"}

The error names the model and the media type. The programmer reads the error and knows what to change. A silent drop would do nothing, and the programmer would debug the prompt for an hour before discovering the audio was never sent.

The blob part uses the Ref already carried by the event log:

type RefKind uint8
const (
    RefPath   RefKind = iota + 1
    RefURI
    RefHandle
)

type Ref struct {
    Kind    RefKind `json:"kind"`
    Locator string  `json:"locator"`
}

Three locator kinds cover the three ways content arrives: a local file path, a remote URI, and a handle to a job’s output. The Ref carries through redaction: when a BlobPart is superseded, its Ref survives in the RedactedPart, so the address survives. This does not guarantee that an external file or job output remains available forever. Local-path rendering reads the actual file bytes into the vendor attachment; preserving a locator alone is not media support. URI and handle attachment rendering remain deferred.

§5.10 Exercise: Author, Editor, Reviewer

Build ch06/main.go in a separate Go module importing the public core, as the Chapter 4 consumer did. Three agents, three roles:

The author receives a topic and writes a first draft. Its tools are write_draft (stores text) and word_count (returns the count).

The editor receives the author’s draft and improves it. Its tools are read_draft (retrieves text) and edit_draft (replaces text).

The reviewer receives the editor’s draft and approves or rejects it. Its tool is review (returns accept or reject with notes).

The accepted example uses string text arguments for write_draft and edit_draft, empty objects for word_count and read_draft, and string decision (accept or reject) plus notes for review. Its word count counts whitespace-separated words in the stored manuscript. These are small application-level choices to document in the tool schemas, not new framework builtins. The stored draft is shared application data; synchronize access because a tool worker can outlive the turn that launched it.

The slow-tool fixture also calls think with this argument object:

{"seconds":3,"thought":"composing draft"}

It waits the numeric number of seconds and returns the thought. Register it only on the author in this application; it is not an Ensemble builtin or a substitute for the actual manuscript tools.

The workflow is sequential: author writes, editor edits, reviewer reviews. The application advances through reliable Ask or Submit completions. Post delivers live hints; Wait watches progress. Each agent uses the same vendor (the fake from Chapter 2) with a different system prompt. The workflow is hardcoded Go. Every new collaboration pattern is a new Go program. That is the limit this chapter reaches; agent-created collaboration remains later work. The framework works; the rigidity is in the glue code, not in the framework itself.

Three agents prove the cost was paid once. The first agent might work because the framework was tested with it. The second might work because the code was debugged for two. The third works because the framework is general. If adding the reviewer required a single line inside the framework package, the seam is wrong.

The binary reads JSON events on stdin, writes observations as JSON lines on stdout, and logs to the path in CH06_LOG. The grader drives the fake vendor to script specific responses for each agent.

The reference workflow is in solutions/ch05/ch06/. Keep the historical ch06 application directory and CH06_LOG name for compatibility. Build that module separately. The local provider fake supplies the ordinary Anthropic adapter environment (LLM_VENDOR=anthropic, a model, a dummy LLM_API_KEY, and its loopback LLM_BASE_URL), not a new vendor enum. The grader starts the application without arguments in a disposable directory. It sends a prompt, a hint addressed to the author during think, then EOF:

{"kind":"prompt","text":"Write about the ocean"}
{"kind":"hint","text":"make it vivid","agent":"author"}

Emit observations with the observation discriminator and external agent tag. The kinds are state_changed, part_delta and part_final; their payload fields are shown above. A hint acknowledgment is a delta whose chunk begins hint:. After each actual request completes, the application emits its completion record and stage marker:

{"observation":"turn_ended","agent":"author"}
{"pipeline":"author_done"}

Use the corresponding editor/reviewer names for their stages. These extra records belong to the application protocol, not new sealed core observation types. Log them and the observations to CH06_LOG; keep each Agent’s durable conversation history separately so one Agent’s sequence numbers do not become another’s. EOF waits for the submitted workflow before shutdown.

§5.11 What this chapter does not build

Streaming observations arrive as PartDelta, but the vendor seam from Chapter 2 does not stream yet. It returns a complete response in one block. The PartDelta type exists so that when streaming lands, observers get incremental updates without an interface change.

The Ref type supports RefURI and RefHandle alongside RefPath, but the renderers only handle RefPath so far. A vendor that accepts a URL instead of inlined bytes needs the URI form; a tool whose output is too large for inline needs the handle form. Both are future extensions to the renderer, not to the Ref type.

Sub-agent spawning and its supervision contract remain future work. Today the Go application constructs peer Agents and passes results between them. These seams provide useful foundations without claiming that a lossy Wait supplies every future join contract. You now have a hint channel and a terminal to type into. Streaming and the GUI still lie ahead.

Taking it for a spin

Run the exercise against the fake vendor and watch the observations stream on stdout. Three agents have their own state transitions. The following abridged shape is illustrative, not a captured provider transcript:

{"observation":"state_changed","agent":"author","from":"idle","to":"input_pending"}
{"observation":"state_changed","agent":"author","from":"input_pending","to":"in_flight"}
{"observation":"part_delta","agent":"author","part_id":1,"chunk":"A draft about the ocean."}
{"observation":"part_final","agent":"author","seq":3,"part_id":1,"part":{"type":"text","text":"A draft about the ocean."}}
{"observation":"turn_ended","agent":"author"}
{"pipeline":"author_done"}

The editor and reviewer produce their own tagged progress and completion records after their requests finish. The non-streaming response produces a whole-part delta and finalizer; there are no live token chunks yet.

The observation stream is the display story; request replies carry completion. The framework tells you what happened, in order, and you decide what it means. A logger writes it to a file. A GUI renders it as a chat. The application displays progress and uses the separate request reply to decide when to send the next prompt. The observer seam carries all three without knowing about any of them.

Now try it with a real vendor. Build your own core from its module root:

go build -o /tmp/ch5agent .

Use the credential procedure from Chapter 0: configure the intended child’s LLM_VENDOR, discovered LLM_MODEL, and LLM_API_KEY without printing keys or putting them in command arguments. Use a scratch working directory for jobs. CH02_LOG selects the core event log; the separate workflow uses CH06_LOG. Start the actual human interface:

CH02_LOG=/tmp/ch5-chat.jsonl /tmp/ch5agent chat

Type ordinary text. Ask for a bounded job such as a shell sleep followed by printing a marker. While it runs, type a hint. The hint acknowledgment should arrive before the tool finishes. Type /interrupt, then a new question. The new turn should answer while the older job continues. Inspect its retained output afterward. Ctrl-C also interrupts the current turn; Ctrl-D ends the session and runs shutdown. An interrupt is not a way to quit the Agent.

The accepted implementation did this on October 9 with claude-haiku-5-5. A 12-second shell job was still running when the CLI acknowledged Hint: remember the marker COMET. at 22:45:22.121672 UTC. Interrupt followed at 22:45:22.172780. The new turn answered COMET at 22:45:23.081200; the job’s real report arrived at 22:45:34.088930 with REAL_LATE_RESULT. The interface was usable roughly eleven seconds before the old work finished. That is the point of keeping the actor alive.

The retained CLI transcript and event log preserve one correction: the initial implementation emitted job_finished with status running when the shell handler returned after launch. The final guard emits that event only for a terminal job snapshot. The real late output in the demonstration was correct; the record was kept and no paid run was repeated for the metadata repair.

Build the three-role application from its own module root:

go build -o /tmp/ch5workflow .

Run it from a scratch directory with the same provider setup, then supply one topic as JSON. All three roles use the same vendor and different prompts:

CH06_LOG=/tmp/ch5-workflow.jsonl /tmp/ch5workflow
{"kind":"prompt","text":"Write about the ocean at dawn"}

EOF waits for this workflow. An interruption of a role returns that request’s error rather than advancing with an incomplete draft. The historical example module remains named ch06; the book’s new chapter number does not rename its source or evidence paths.

The October 9 Gemini run used gemini-3.8-flash for all three roles. The author called write_draft, word_count, and think. Asked for 60 words, it first stored 59, saw the actual count, added the word night, rewrote the draft and counted 60. The editor called read_draft and edit_draft; the reviewer called review and accepted the edited draft. The reviewer received the stored edited text, not merely a claim that an editor had run. The full tagged observations and three separate Agent logs remain in the workflow evidence.

Media received its own, different demonstration. A separate public-API client sent a local 96×96 red PNG to gpt-5.4-mini, which answered red. The same renderer refused an audio part with model "gpt-5.4-mini" does not support audio media. These media receipts show actual image consumption and a local refusal; audio, video and PDF positive cases were checked deterministically at the rendering boundary, not presented as additional live model runs.

Retained run Input tokens Output tokens
Anthropic human CLI 4,431 177
Gemini author 5,695 1,157
Gemini editor 1,310 591
Gemini reviewer 663 324
OpenAI image client 63 4

All recorded cache-read and cache-write counts were zero. This was one feature-specific demonstration per vendor, not every feature on every vendor. Original grading remained 80/100 FAIL: inherited logger-shape parity and a text-only unknown-model refusal probe failed. Independent review accepted those documented exceptions; neither was evidence that unsupported media had been silently dropped.

One review mistake also belongs in the lesson. The initial reviewer demanded grouped completion from the misleading one-wakeup paragraph, and the student agreed before stopping at the undefined contract. Bill withdrew that requirement. A real correction remained: changing Gemini’s mimeType key survived a test that only looked for bytes somewhere in the request. The repaired test decoded the actual attachment fields and caught both wrong MIME and wrong data keys. A mutation can reveal a weak test; an agreeable reviewer cannot settle missing scope. The chapter record preserves both corrections and the original results.

The agent was deaf. Now it listens.

Chapter 6: Streaming, or the Same Answer in Pieces

Ask the Chapter 5 agent something hard and the cursor stops. Twenty seconds, or ninety. Behind the curtain a model is reasoning, writing, deciding to call a tool, spelling out arguments one token at a time. You get none of it, then all of it at once.

Every vendor has been willing to send that along as it is produced for years. The agent never asked. Chapter 5 built an observer seam with PartDelta observations, but a whole response still arrived before its length-one deltas. This chapter makes those observations arrive while the response is being read.

The result is not beautiful. Reasoning, reply, and half-finished tool arguments land on one terminal in three colours with no layout. The mess is the point: once you can watch the agent think, you will want somewhere better to watch it. Chapter 7 builds that. This chapter earns it.

TL;DR

Streaming changes how a response is delivered, not what it is. Everything below follows from that one sentence.

The seam

The first-edition incidents and measurements below remain historical. The interfaces shown here follow the accepted Ensemble implementation.

Parse changes signature. It gains no sibling.

// internal/common/stream.go
type Parser interface {
    Parse(resp *http.Response, cb StreamCallbacks) error
}

No ParseStream. Non-streaming is a stream of length one, so one method covers both modes. Render still renders the context through its owning Engine; configuration comes from the Agent parent. The accepted signature is Render(*Context) ([]byte, error). Transport builds the URL and headers separately. Streaming changes those existing request decisions.

The notifications

StreamCallbacks lives in internal/common, alongside Parser. These are response notifications, not copied configuration, sibling services or substitutes for parent interfaces. They run synchronously; their consumers queue slow work. The parser remains attached to its Engine and can reach its Agent and Ensemble.

// internal/common/stream.go
type StreamCallbacks struct {
    // One incremental chunk. partID identifies the PART, not the chunk.
    OnDelta func(partID uint64, kind DeltaKind, chunk string)

    // Each finalized event, in order, for the event log.
    OnEvent func(Event)

    // Each completed part, carrying THE SAME partID its deltas carried.
    OnPartFinal func(partID uint64, part Part)

    // Each frame payload: for SSE, one event's data bytes.
    OnFrame func(eventType string, data []byte)
}
callback wired by to
OnDelta Agent actor mailbox message, then observer
OnPartFinal Agent actor parser ID retained until stored-part publication
OnEvent Engine finalized facts returned to the actor for recording
OnFrame Engine sanitized root-owned API trace

A caller wanting request-scoped notifications can pass them to AskWatching; it uses the same actor as Ask. The accepted CLI attaches an ordinary observer and queues its display work. Neither path starts a second orchestration loop.

The taxonomy

type DeltaKind uint8

const (
    DeltaThinking DeltaKind = iota + 1 // wire: "thinking"
    DeltaText                          // wire: "text"
    DeltaToolCall                      // wire: "tool_call"
)

An enum, not a string, because every consumer switches on every case: the terminal picks an ANSI colour, a GUI picks a CSS class. Constants start at iota + 1 so the zero value is invalid, and MarshalJSON refuses an unset kind rather than emitting a plausible default. Serialized:

{"observation":"part_delta","part_id":3,"kind":"text","chunk":"Hello"}

PartDelta retains an optional agent label for clients combining streams. The actual Ensemble routing still supplies the source Agent in its observation envelope. A display label does not replace that ownership relationship.

The capability

type Stream uint8

const (
    StreamText Stream = 1 << iota
    StreamThinking
    StreamToolArgs
)

const StreamAll = StreamText | StreamThinking | StreamToolArgs

A bitmask on ModelFeatures, not a bool, because vendors ship this capability in pieces. Config gains one field, DisableStreaming bool. Effective behaviour is the AND of caller and table:

func StreamingFor(cfg Config) Stream {
    if cfg.DisableStreaming {
        return 0
    }
    features, ok := LookupModel(cfg.Model)
    if !ok {
        return 0
    }
    return features.Stream
}

An unknown model gets no streaming, and that is not an error, which is the deliberate opposite of what the same table does for media. Section 6.7 is why.

The reader

One shared reader takes an io.Reader and yields (eventType string, data []byte) pairs. The original internal/llm/sse.go measured 111 lines with 14 tests. Those are historical measurements, not target counts; the accepted implementation keeps its smaller reader with translation in internal/engine/sse.go.

The request

vendor asks for streaming with parser’s oddity
Anthropic "stream": true in the body dispatch on content_block_delta, then on text_delta / thinking_delta / input_json_delta
OpenAI "stream": true plus "stream_options": {"include_usage": true} without include_usage, final usage is absent; absence is not measured zero
Gemini :streamGenerateContent?alt=sse endpoint each frame is a whole response object with no block indices; continuation is inferred

What does not change

The event log. A ResponseEnded event still carries the complete response as ResponseData{Parts, From, Usage}, the context still replays from finalized events, and replay still equals live. Deltas are ephemeral: they reach observers and are never recorded. Sanitized frame payloads go to the root-owned api.log trace as they arrive.

The part id rule

Within one response, a part id identifies exactly one part. Two parts never share an id, one part never uses two ids, and an id never crosses kinds.

The parser chooses IDs from vendor indices or its local continuation mapping. They can restart with each response, so a turn containing a tool call can go around the loop twice and reuse them. The key a consumer needs is therefore (response, part id), not part id alone.

The parser supplies the id on every delta and reports the matching final identity; the actor publishes the stored PartFinal. The caller never reconstructs an ID from final position, because real wire formats can defeat that guess. Section 6.4 has the receipt.

The exercise

ch07/main.go: one agent, one observer, a report on the shape of the stream including time to first delta. CH07_NO_STREAM=1 runs the identical script with streaming disabled.

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 6 path/to/core

The local streaming fixture uses a declared model, by default the historical claude-sonnet-5 row shared by the references. -stream-model MODEL selects another implemented streaming-capable Anthropic row; it is a grader input, not provider discovery. A separate deliberately unlisted model tests plain fallback without teaching a special capability for a fake.

-stream-exercise DIR selects the separately built shape module; otherwise the grader finds ch07 inside or beside the core directory. Earlier consumer, workflow and media-model flags still apply to inherited parity. The core’s incremental JSON observations and the external application’s aggregate report serve different checks; neither substitutes for the other.

check points what it tests
stream-deltas 20 Asking for the stream produces one: many deltas per turn, not one per part
deltas-match-final 20 Text deltas grouped by response and part id concatenate exactly to that part; at least one part arrived in several deltas
thinking-streamed 15 Reasoning arrives as DeltaThinking, correlated by part id, never leaking into the reply
tool-params-streamed 15 A tool call’s name and arguments arrive as DeltaToolCall, correlated by part id
delivery-not-content 10 Streaming off: same final content and usage, different delta count; unknown-model fallback and the separate shape report remain usable
ch5-parity 20 Every Chapter 5 check still passes
total 100

6.1 The idea in plain words

An HTTP response is a stream of bytes. io.ReadAll is a choice to ignore that, convenient enough that it stops looking like a choice.

Non-streaming does not mean the vendor produces the answer atomically. The model emits tokens one at a time either way; the server holds them until the last one is written. The latency a user feels is the cost of thinking plus a decision to say nothing while it happens.

Three things change. The HTTP client hands the open response to the parser instead of reading the body. The parser takes a live stream and calls back per chunk. The Agent actor receives those chunks through its mailbox and fires observations instead of buffering the whole response behind a blank terminal. Each worker message carries its turn identity, so stale progress after an interrupt cannot contaminate the new turn.

One thing pointedly does not change: the record. At end of turn the event log holds what it held before, and rebuilding context from it yields the same bytes. Recording deltas as additional conversation content would duplicate finalized parts or force replay to assemble them. Keeping display fragments out of the durable log preserves the existing replay contract.

Hence the sentence that makes the seam small. Non-streaming is streaming with a length of one. A response in one piece is the same kind of thing as a response in forty pieces. No code downstream of the observer asks whether something was streamed; it receives deltas and the only question is how many. Which buys one Parse instead of two, one path per vendor instead of two, and a grader that runs the identical exercise both ways and demands identical content byte for byte.

6.2 Server-sent events, and the reader that survives them

Streaming from an LLM vendor uses plain HTTP. The response body is framed in server-sent events, a text format older than all of this.

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type":"content_block_delta","index":0,"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":"Hello"}}

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type":"content_block_delta","index":0,"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":" world"}}

Lines of field: value; a blank line ends an event. Those rules carry every streamed token you have ever watched appear in a chat window.

Each vendor parser could scan for data: itself in six lines, and those six lines pass every happy-path test. Then:

case what a naive scanner does
multi-line data: field keeps the first line only, truncating content with no error
comment line, starting : treats a keepalive as an event with an empty payload to unmarshal
CRLF fails to recognize the separator because the line still contains \r
data: [DONE] tries to unmarshal a sentinel, erroring on a stream that completed
unterminated final event drops the last chunk, which usually holds the stop reason

None is hard. All share a shape: a framing imprecision that produces plausible output and fails later, somewhere with no mention of SSE in the stack trace.

The first edition collected these cases in one reader with 14 tests. Keep the framing function small; line and test counts are consequences. Vendor-specific work starts after framing is resolved, with an event type and a slice of JSON in hand. The same “fakes first” pattern from Chapter 3 in different clothes: the framing is deterministic, ugly, and testable without touching the network or spending a token.

6.3 One Parse, not two

The obvious design keeps Parse(status int, body []byte) and adds ParseStream. Nothing existing breaks and each method is simpler than a method doing both.

Three vendors times two methods is six implementations. Each vendor’s pair must agree exactly about what a tool call is, what a thinking block is, which stop reasons map to which events, and how usage is counted. Nothing in the type system enforces that, and nothing in the test suite does unless somebody keeps writing a test that runs both and compares. Fixes land in the streaming path because that is the path in production, and the other drifts until somebody disables streaming to debug something and finds the framework behaves differently in the mode they picked to have fewer variables.

One entry point keeps the modes together; shared final construction prevents the semantic drift:

Parse(resp *http.Response, cb StreamCallbacks) error

On SSE, Parse reads frames and calls OnDelta per chunk. On a plain JSON body it reads the body whole and calls OnDelta once per part with that part’s entire content. Both routes then run the same semantic decoder to build events and call OnEvent and OnPartFinal. The accepted stream readers accumulate provider messages before using that decoder, preserving one place for canonical arguments, provenance, opaque replay material and usage.

The non-streaming route could skip OnDelta entirely, since nothing is incremental. It fires anyway, because “length one” has to be true in code and not only in prose. Were it silent, every observer would need a second rendering path fed from finalized events, and the seam would have bought nothing except a longer interface.

The seam still has exactly two methods, Render and Parse, which is what the vendor-independence claim has rested on since Chapter 2. Adding a third to ship a feature would concede that the seam was shaped around the features that existed when it was drawn, which is the thing a seam exists to deny.

6.4 Part ids: who is allowed to name a part

A stream delivers forty chunks belonging to a paragraph of reasoning, a reply, and a tool call’s arguments. A GUI appends each chunk into the right widget, then replaces that widget’s content with the finalized part. It needs to know which chunks belong together. A part id is nothing more than that.

The first-edition brief originally minted a fresh id per chunk with an atomic.AddUint64. Forty unique ids tell a consumer that forty things happened and nothing about which were the same thing. The field would exist, be populated, look reasonable in a log, and carry no information.

So ids are per part. The question is who assigns them.

The instinct is the caller, leaving the parser a pure translation layer, with the obvious formula being the part’s position in the finished response. That formula is wrong on the wire, and OpenAI is the proof: it streams a tool call’s arguments before it is knowable whether a text part will occupy index zero. When the first tool-argument chunk arrives the response is unfinished, positions are undefined, and any id the caller computes is a guess a later chunk can falsify.

The code that chose an id is the only code that can be trusted to repeat it.

Anthropic can retain block indices. The accepted OpenAI parser reserves zero for text and maps tool index i to i+1, avoiding a collision when a tool arrives first. Gemini must infer continuation locally. Zero is a valid ID; insisting that all IDs are positive tests a different contract.

The parser chose it, so the parser owns both ends: it supplies the id on every OnDelta and reports OnPartFinal carrying the same id. Finals carry the parser-chosen ID, not a position recomputed from the finished list. The id is thereby freed from meaning “where”, and only ever means “the same part as that other one”, which is the sole property a consumer can rely on.

These parser-local IDs have a consequence worth stating before Chapter 7 trips over it: the ids may restart with each response. A turn that calls a tool goes around the loop at least twice; if part id 0 is reused in the second response, it names a different part from part id 0 in the first. Uniqueness holds within a response, not within a turn. The grader for this chapter had to learn the same lesson, and its harness now tracks response boundaries rather than assuming ids are unique across a turn.

So a consumer keying widgets needs (response, part id). The current state_changed transition to in_flight lets the grader separate live responses. That transient boundary does not itself give a reconnecting GUI a persistent response identity. Keep that distinction in view when Chapter 7 reaches for the seam.

OnPartFinal exists for this. It looks redundant beside OnEvent, since finalized parts are inside the events, but the events do not carry the ids the deltas used, and reconstructing that mapping from outside is the same guess that fails on the wire.

Ordering matters too. Parse reports a completed event before its part finals. The HTTP worker collects those facts and IDs; it does not mutate History. The actor records the response, then publishes PartFinal using the stored parts and the parser’s IDs. A request watcher receives its final notification there too. An observer re-rendering on finalization reads a log that already contains it. Reversed, every consumer gets an intermittent view of a log one event behind.

deltas-match-final grades this the hard way. A check that concatenated every text delta in a turn and compared against the final message would pass on a submission whose ids were noise, including the fresh-id-per-chunk submission this section rules out. So the check groups by id first, requires each group to concatenate exactly to its own part, and requires at least one part to have arrived in several deltas. Grouping by id is the real check; concatenation afterward is arithmetic.

Text and readable thinking fragments reconstruct their corresponding content. Tool arguments need one additional distinction: the transient JSON fragments are displayed as received, while the complete tool part retains canonical JSON. Whitespace can differ without losing an argument. Compare the decoded complete argument value when testing that boundary, and never execute fragments.

6.5 Three vendors, three dialects

The framing is shared. The meaning is not, and the differences are listed in the TL;DR table above. Two deserve a closer look.

OpenAI’s stream_options.include_usage is not decoration. Omit it and a streamed response contains no usage object at all, just an absent field, so a careless accumulator can record zeros for every streamed turn. The answers are correct, the tools run, the log is well formed, and careless cost tracking reads zero forever. Missing accounting must still be treated as missing, rather than converted into measured zero. A silent success that is wrong, one JSON field deep.

Gemini sends response-shaped frames containing new content, rather than Anthropic-style named delta events. Text can still arrive incrementally. There are no equivalent block indices, so continuation is inferred from position and the shape of what arrived before. Preserve the thought flag and trailing signatures, including signatures on ordinary text; a signature-only frame must not disappear just because it has no new visible words.

The seam does not make vendors identical. It makes their differences local: all three oddities live inside one vendor’s Parse, and none escapes the translation implementation into the actor, observer, event log or terminal. Locality is the whole claim, and it is smaller than “vendors are interchangeable”, which was never true.

6.6 When a capability table pays for itself

Gemini’s row has StreamToolArgs clear.

"gemini-3.8-flash": {
    Media:  MediaImage | MediaAudio | MediaVideo | MediaDocument,
    Stream: StreamText | StreamThinking,
},

In the retained implementation and observations, function parameters arrive as complete objects there. The parser handles that dialect locally; the actor and terminal need no vendor-specific workaround. The table says the bit is off, StreamingFor returns a mask without it, and the parser emits the complete tool object as one display chunk. It does not manufacture fragments that the wire never sent. Behaviour degrades exactly as far as the capability is missing and stops there.

The following are historical capability rows retained in this implementation, not a current provider-availability or crossover-readiness claim:

model family text thinking tool arguments
claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5 yes yes yes
gpt-6-astra, gpt-5.6-sol yes no yes
gemini-3.8-flash, gemini-3.1-pro-preview yes yes no

Three families, three combinations, no two the same shape. A single Streaming bool would force two of those rows to choose between losing text streaming and inventing tool-argument chunks that never arrived. The bitmask is the minimum structure the observed facts require.

The table will go stale; vendors ship these bits on their own schedule. An updated row can enable a capability the translator already supports. A new wire shape still needs parser work and evidence; changing a bit cannot create a decoder. The table gives the reader a clear place to start.

6.7 Guessing about delivery is not guessing about content

Given a model name it has never seen, StreamingFor shrugs: no error, no refusal, a non-streaming request, turn proceeds. Asked whether the same unknown model accepts an image, the same table produces a loud refusal, which Chapter 5 spent real effort keeping. Two lookups, two opposite answers on a miss. An inconsistency like that is either a bug or a principle.

A guess about content can corrupt the conversation. A guess about delivery cannot.

Silently drop an image because a model cannot see and the request may still succeed. The model answers confidently about a picture it never received, and nothing downstream can recover the missing input. Fall back to plain delivery and the same scripted response arrives, same text and parts, in fewer pieces. The cost of that conservative choice is a slower first token, not a missing image. Separate live generations can differ; deterministic parity compares the same scripted content in both delivery modes.

The practical half matters as much. Model names are an open set: this framework’s own tests already use gpt-5-2025-08-07, fake-model, and several -fake suffixes no honest table would claim to know. A framework that refuses to send any request until its table has heard of your model is one whose first patch in every deployment removes that check. Refusing to guess is right; refusing to work is not. The line is drawn per capability, which is why the two lookups disagree.

The negative boolean

DisableStreaming bool

Stream bool is the better name and the wrong field, because in Go the zero value picks your default. Stream bool makes a hand-built Config{} mean streaming off, the opposite of the intended default, recoverable only inside a constructor other people are free not to call. In a framework whose premise is that other people construct these structs, a default holding only when someone uses the front door is not a default. When the zero value and the good name point in opposite directions, the zero value wins: the compiler enforces it and the name does not.

6.8 Three record-keepers

The event log is unchanged. Deltas fire at observers and are never recorded; a ResponseEnded event carries the full text as before, and replay-is-live still holds.

api.log records wire payloads separately. In the first-edition story, the preceding engine logged the response JSON after reading the body, and under streaming there is no moment when the body exists as a blob, because the parser consumes it as it arrives. Left alone, the response half of the API log would have gone dark the day streaming shipped, silently, which is the worst way for a debugging facility to fail. OnFrame carries each raw frame out as it arrives and the engine writes it, so the trace retains payloads in order in both modes. This is not a byte-for-byte HTTP transcript: SSE framing/comments and authentication headers are not the payloads delivered by OnFrame.

The wiring follows ownership. Parser methods belong to Engine and reach its Agent parent; Engine reaches Agent.Ensemble() for logging. Ensemble owns and serializes the trace writer. Notification callbacks carry parser output, not logger services smuggled around this chain. The accepted Engine redacts a reflected configured key before logging a frame or forwarding OnFrame, and keeps authentication headers and credential-bearing URLs out of the trace.

Observers get deltas as they arrive, PartFinal on completion, and events through the normal path. A widget streams chunks in for immediate reading, then re-renders from the authoritative part. The fast path may be approximate because the slow path corrects it, and the correction is safe because the part id links each streamed approximation to the authoritative version that replaces it.

6.9 The terminal, and the flush that makes it real

content stream style
reply text stdout plain
thinking stderr dim
tool call arguments stderr yellow

So agent chat < prompts.txt > answer.txt yields exactly what the assistant said and nothing else, while a human sees all three interleaved. One binary serves the pipeline and the person with no flag, because the stream split already encodes the difference between output and commentary. Colour is chosen by isTerminal(stderr), so redirected output is never salted with escape codes.

With a buffered writer, the line that decides whether any of this is visible:

case common.DeltaText:
    clear()
    fmt.Fprint(out, chunk)
    // Flush per chunk. Without it the buffer holds the whole
    // answer and releases it in one lump at the end, which looks
    // exactly like streaming having no effect.
    out.Flush()

A buffered writer does its job perfectly and destroys the feature. Every delta delivered correctly, every chunk written correctly, and the user sees a blank terminal then the whole answer at once, indistinguishable from never having implemented streaming. No error, no warning, no failing test unless somebody wrote one about timing. A pipeline can be correct at every stage and useless end to end when the property that matters, here “arrives incrementally”, belongs to no single stage.

The accepted CLI instead writes each chunk directly to os.Stdout, an unbuffered file. Either approach must deliver bytes before the response ends. Its observer queues display work without dropping reply chunks or waiting on a slow terminal; after the Agent joins producers, the display drains before its summary. Finals add separators, not a second copy of the streamed reply.

The initial student streaming CLI had another quiet routing defect. It treated any chunk beginning hint: as a human-hint acknowledgment and moved it to stderr. A real parser/actor/CLI test sent hint:early and then late; stdout contained only late. The final implementation marks actual acknowledgments with PartDelta.Hint and routes by origin, leaving assistant prose untouched. A display prefix is not a protocol discriminator.

The corrected test withholds the rest of the HTTP response until stdout contains hint:early, then requires the complete hint:earlylate reply. That proves flushing while work remains, rather than merely observing several reads after the provider has finished. Restoring the prefix heuristic fails this same test; removing the actor’s origin marker fails the acknowledgment check. The observation vocabulary still has the same three content kinds.

The output is a mess: dim reasoning, plain reply, yellow half-formed JSON, all at once, wrapping at terminal width. Development tooling, honest about it.

6.10 The exercise

ch07/main.go is a separate public-library module. It builds one agent, attaches one observer, and reports the shape of the stream rather than its content: deltas per kind, parts they group into, and time to first delta. Total turn latency barely moves, because the model takes as long as it takes; what changes is how long the human stares at a blank terminal before the first word appears.

CH07_NO_STREAM=1 runs the identical script with DisableStreaming on.

The reference application is in solutions/ch06/ch07/. Keep the historical ch07 directory and environment names. The core’s no-argument JSON protocol receives this prompt, followed by EOF:

{"kind":"prompt","text":"what does the configuration say?"}

Its delta records use observation:"part_delta", part_id, kind and chunk. Finals use observation:"part_final" and the matching ID. The existing exercise envelope exposes top-level text or tool names; the neutral part retains full content, including tool args. The grader also accepts complete arguments in the envelope. Tool-result finals are distinct from model-response finals and must not be folded into the streamed response. A final assistant record carries the completed answer.

EN_DISABLE_STREAMING=1 controls the core CLI, while CH07_NO_STREAM=1 controls the separate exercise. Do not silently depend on one name while testing the other. The original grader launched only the core, despite the chapter asking for an external exercise; the revised grader builds and runs both through the actual public library.

The external observer can count in memory and print a summary after reliable request completion. It need not print individual deltas. Its JSON record uses observation:"stream_stats", with per-kind deltas, finalized parts, first_delta_ms, and the final assistant text (or a separate answer record). The accepted example also reports elapsed_ms, effective streaming and usage. The grader checks all three delta counts, a nonnegative first_delta_ms, and answer delivery. Review the observer’s timing and finalized part counting in source; the summary alone does not prove those measurements or that a human terminal flushed before completion. The gated CLI regression described above supplies the flush evidence.

The original deterministic fixture produced this shape, not a promise about how many chunks a live provider will choose:

measurement streaming on streaming off
text deltas 36, across 2 parts 2
thinking deltas 27, none leaking into the reply 1 per part
tool call deltas 19 1 per part
final reply text identical identical
finalized parts identical identical

Thirty-six pieces or two pieces. Same answer. delivery-not-content grades this rather than leaving it as a remark, because the claim carries the chapter: it is why one Parse suffices, why the event log needed no changes, why replay still equals live, and why no observer needs to ask whether a response arrived in one piece or forty.

The mutant that states the thesis

In the first-edition audit, no-stream-flag removed the request field asking for streaming and nothing else. Final text identical, parts identical, event log identical byte for byte, and the grader says:

saw 2 text deltas, want at least 8

Nothing about the content changed. Only the shape of its arrival did.

Two predictions from that audit were wrong, and both are worth keeping. The first per-chunk-part-ids mutant used a package-level counter; it failed its intended check and also historical ch6-parity, by tripping original Chapter 5’s no-mutable-globals. Two failures for one deleted behaviour means the audit stops telling you which check does which job, so the mutant was rewritten to derive the id from the chunk. Catching it required logging each failing check’s details, not only its id: which checks failed says a mutant is wrong, why says whether it is wrong for the intended reason.

Second, no-thinking-deltas does not cascade into deltas-match-final, contrary to prediction, because that check walks text parts and ignores the reasoning stream. Recording that division of labour here keeps it from looking accidental when a reader sees the two checks side by side.

6.11 What this chapter does not build

No re-rendering. The terminal appends and never redraws a finalized part, though PartFinal provides everything needed. Doing it well needs cursor control, wrapping, and terminal width, which is Chapter 7’s problem wearing a different hat.

No acting on partial tool arguments. Streaming tool arguments is for display only; the arguments are incomplete JSON until the part finalizes. Starting early, opening the file as soon as the path appears, is how an agent runs a tool call with half its arguments. Deltas render, finalized parts execute.

No observer backpressure. Observers are told, never asked, and Observe must not block. A slow observer stalling the actor is a deaf agent by another route, which Chapter 5 was about. An observer that cannot keep up drops optional progress or buffers without holding up the actor. A terminal promising the full reply must preserve its bytes; lossy observation queues are not reliable request completion.

Taking it for a spin

Build your own CLI from the core module root, and run it from a scratch workspace with the provider environment configured as in Chapter 0. Discover an available streaming-capable model; keep the key in the intended child’s environment without printing it or putting it in a command argument.

go build -o /tmp/ch6agent .
/tmp/ch6agent chat

Type an ordinary prompt:

write a short story about a lighthouse keeper who collects fog

For a model exposing readable reasoning, it appears dim on stderr. The story arrives on stdout as the provider delivers it. Ask for a tool and the name and argument fragments appear on stderr, yellow on a terminal. The tool still waits for complete arguments. Provider behavior determines whether those arguments arrive incrementally or as a single object.

The core’s explicit opt-out is EN_DISABLE_STREAMING=1:

EN_DISABLE_STREAMING=1 /tmp/ch6agent chat

The separate shape exercise uses CH07_NO_STREAM=1. Build it from its own module root and run the same prompt in separate scratch directories:

go build -o /tmp/ch6shape .
/tmp/ch6shape "Return only the numbers 1 through 20 separated by spaces."
CH07_NO_STREAM=1 /tmp/ch6shape "Return only the numbers 1 through 20 separated by spaces."

In your own code the equivalent is one field: DisableStreaming on the Agent’s config. The delivered parts should remain intact in either mode. Two independent live generations need not choose the same words; the fake makes equivalence exact by returning the same scripted content both ways.

The retained October 9 live shape pair used gpt-4o-mini and did return the same numbered text in both modes. It reported 40 text deltas versus one, one finalized text part each, and first-delta times of 1,059 ms versus 1,149 ms. Total times were 1,350 ms and 1,150 ms. Each request used 733 input and 40 output tokens. Streaming improved the first visible delivery in that small pair; it did not make the total run faster. The exact reports remain in enabled and disabled evidence.

The human CLI demonstrations were less tidy, and more useful:

Historical run Visible story delivery What the retained record establishes
claude-sonnet-4-6 62 stdout reads, first 2.6112 s, last 5.5389 s Separate reasoning, streamed arguments, successful echo STREAM_PROBE; two human turns and one busy hint.
gpt-4o-mini 61 stdout reads, first 1.8427 s, last 2.5454 s Three turns; the model chose nonexistent shell print, received exit 127, and accurately recalled the failure.
Initial gemini-2.5-flash Four stdout reads, first 1.6210 s, last 1.6541 s Three turns, thought summaries, whole tool arguments and successful output recall; this model selection failed Bill’s instruction.

These are OS read counts, not token counts. The initial evidence summary records 5,991/261, 3,419/160 and 5,826/248 input/output tokens respectively, with zero recorded cache counts. The raw event and API logs remain alongside it.

The Anthropic launcher initially labeled its last input a third turn because it watched file modification times. A log rewrite changed the timestamp more than once; the launcher sent that input while the second turn was active. The durable log proved a hint instead. That useful hint was kept, along with the mistaken capture label and its correction. A changed file is not a reliable request-completion signal.

The Gemini choice needed a different correction. Bill had required Gemini 3.0 Flash or newer and specifically requested 3.8 Flash for hints. The student selected 2.5 from discovery; the handoff and first review missed the restriction. A working older model did not satisfy it. One bounded run on the actual gemini-3.8-flash CLI supplied the missing evidence; no production change or other-provider repeat was needed.

That run made a real command create waiting.marker, wait for release.marker, then print RELEASED. After seeing the waiting marker at 5.1767 s, the launcher sent a busy hint changing a red-lighthouse paragraph to blue and requiring HINT_38_APPLIED. It observed the actual stderr acknowledgment at 5.1780 s, then released the command at 5.1787 s. The next provider request contained both the successful tool result and the hint. Its answer began HINT_38_APPLIED and described a blue lighthouse. Tool and CLI both exited zero.

The corrected Gemini record contains two requests and eleven response frames, including six nonempty reply chunks, two thinking chunks and one tool-call frame. Three nonempty stdout reads spanned only 1.1 ms, so this run proves correct incremental writes and hint delivery, not perceptibly paced typing. The gated CLI test supplies the stronger before-completion flush evidence. Usage was 1,241/181 followed by 1,486/755 input/output, including 130 and 649 thinking tokens in those output counts. No cache counts were recorded.

Afterwards, page through api.log from a streamed run: frame payloads in order, including terminators and opaque signatures, with the configured key redacted and authentication headers excluded. The accepted CLI writes it in the working directory; CH07_AGENT_LOG selects its durable event log. The public shape application uses api.log and ch07-agent.jsonl. Those are different records serving different questions, and keeping both modes visible is the purpose of OnFrame.

Original student grading remained 0/100 FAIL. Its five streaming checks selected unknown fake-model while demanding streaming; the implementation correctly chose plain delivery. Inherited parity failed the documented earlier exceptions. The original legacy reference scored 90/100 FAIL, with its supposedly disabled run still streaming. Those results remain historical; the chapter record separates fixture mistakes, real CLI corrections and the approved-model live evidence.

What Chapter 7 does with this

The terminal is now honest and ugly: three kinds of content distinguished by colour, across two file descriptors, in a display that cannot redraw.

The display vocabulary is in place, with response identity still to resolve. Chunks carry a kind, so a consumer can route them. Chunks carry a part id, so a consumer can group them into one widget. Parts finalize with the same id, so a consumer can replace streamed approximations with the authoritative version. Clients attach observers without importing GUI behavior into the core. Persistent widget identity and connection lifetime belong to the GUI chapter.

A GUI’s requirements list, written as a seam before anyone wrote a line of the GUI. Chapter 7 cashes it in.

Chapter 7: Everything Is an Artifact

The terminal from Chapter 6 is honest and ugly: three streams in three colours, wrapping at terminal width, no memory of what scrolled past. A tool the human cannot comfortably watch is a tool the human cannot steer, and steering is the entire safety argument. This chapter builds one reusable component, wires it to the agent through a WebSocket, and the agent never learns the GUI exists.

TL;DR

The agent writes observations. The GUI reads them. The core has no GUI import, dependency or display configuration. Chapter 5’s public observation and input seams connect the two. GUI and WebSocket implementation live in a separate optional Go module; the application constructs one Ensemble and one Agent for both terminal and browser.

The observer, extended

Two tool-boundary observation types, plus turn-end display progress:

// Shared vocabulary in internal/common; public aliases expose it to clients.
// Keep observation names distinct from mailbox reports and stored events.

// ToolDispatched reports the boundary before handler execution.
type ToolDispatched struct {
    // CallID correlates execution with its requested call.
    CallID string          `json:"call_id"`
    // Name identifies the selected tool.
    Name   string          `json:"name"`
    // Input preserves raw arguments without interpreting them.
    Input  json.RawMessage `json:"input"`
}

// ToolFinished reports a wait result, including late reports after interrupt.
type ToolFinished struct {
    // CallID identifies the call that returned this result.
    CallID  string  `json:"call_id"`
    // Result is bounded text; full job output remains recoverable.
    Result  string  `json:"result"`
    // IsError distinguishes failed tool output.
    IsError bool    `json:"is_error"`
}

// TurnEnded is progress, not a reliable request acknowledgement.
type TurnEnded struct {
    // Text is the final reply, excluding intermediate tool narration.
    Text  string `json:"text"`
    // Error is a safe diagnostic for a failed or interrupted turn.
    Error string `json:"error,omitempty"`
}

func (ToolDispatched) observation() {}
func (ToolFinished) observation()   {}
func (TurnEnded) observation()      {}

ToolDispatched fires before execution. ToolFinished reports the returned tool wait result; a job can still be running after that wait. Preserve later real job reports. Together with PartDelta, PartFinal and StateChanged, these observations show the turn’s progress. Ensemble identifies the source Agent when notifying clients; tools do not acquire a copied Agent identity or a GUI parent. Reliable request replies remain separate from display progress.

The wire

A WebSocket server subscribes through Ensemble’s public identified observer interface and fans out JSON to connected clients. Durable content comes from the Agent’s history; transient deltas and state observations complete the view. These are examples of individual envelopes, not one complete conversation:

{"type":"part_delta","part_id":3,"kind":"text","chunk":"Hello"}
