§10.2 The Save File

Four fields: config, as_of, context, log. Use the existing Context and Event types; a second persistence-specific conversation model would need a second set of rules for the same history.

Context is the snapshot: exactly what the renderer reads. Log is the audit trail. AsOf joins them. It is the Seq of the last event already folded into the snapshot, and it is the field everything else in the chapter hangs on. Without it, a loader holding a snapshot and a log cannot tell which events the snapshot already contains, so it has two choices and both are wrong: apply the whole log and duplicate every turn, or apply none of it and lose whatever came after the snapshot.

Config records vendor, model, system prompt, and tool declarations. It is a record only. The running agent’s own configuration wins on load, so a save made with one model resumes under whatever model the user starts with today. A save that pinned its model would turn every model retirement into a pile of unloadable files. API keys and base URLs are excluded from this metadata, so the save is portable across machines and endpoints without carrying transport credentials.

There is a small distinction between configured and effective instructions. The student’s first save code copied Config.SystemPrompt. An ordinary Agent without a skill left that field empty, while Engine supplied a nonempty default to the actual request. The conversation resumed correctly and the metadata lied. The grader’s supplied primary skill hid the problem because that path had already filled in the configured text.

The correction asks Engine for the effective instruction through its existing owner interface. Saving and all three renderers now use the same decision. An intentionally empty primary body must remain empty; blindly filling every empty string with the default would fix one case by breaking the other. The regression compares saved system_prompt with the captured HTTP field, then checks an empty primary separately. Restoring either defect fails its corresponding assertion. No new paid run was needed to verify this correction.

The save does not reconstruct a running job, a handler closure or the skills registry’s loaded/pending state. The new Agent supplies its current tools and primary skill; its restored conversation may contain earlier tool results and manuals. Serialized declarations describe what was available when saved. They do not install executable capability on restart.

§10.3 Snapshot Plus Tail

Loading has one loop. This excerpt belongs in the history implementation, where validate and apply are the existing event validator and reducer; SaveFile itself stays shared vocabulary in common:

func restoreContext(sf common.SaveFile) (*common.Context, error) {
    ctx, after := sf.Context, sf.AsOf
    if ctx == nil {
        ctx, after = &common.Context{Turn: "idle"}, 0
    }
    for _, e := range sf.Log {
        if err := validate(e); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("restore: event %d: %w", e.Seq, err)
        }
        if e.Seq <= after {
            continue
        }
        apply(ctx, e)
    }
    return ctx, nil
}

With a snapshot, install it and apply only the tail: events whose Seq is strictly greater than AsOf. Without one, start from an empty context and apply everything. The same loop serves both, which leaves one replay path to get right instead of two.

Decode into a fresh save value and validate its configuration, snapshot state and increasing log sequence numbers before installing the restored history. The excerpt shows the fold, not that surrounding validation and installation. An invalid later event must not leave the live Agent half-restored. The accepted loader stages the candidate context and log, then replaces the owned state only after all checks succeed.

The tail looks unnecessary. A normal save from a complete history has AsOf equal to the last Seq in its log, so the tail is empty and a loader that skips it passes every test built from its own output. The tail matters the moment a snapshot and a log come from different moments: a snapshot kept from an earlier save, with a newer log written after it. That is the shape a crash leaves behind, once the log is written event by event and the snapshot only now and then. The grader builds that shape on purpose, splicing an old snapshot onto a newer log to distinguish a correct loader from one that ignores its anchor. This chapter still saves on normal exit. Journaling events during execution and recovering from a process crash arrive in Chapter 14; the tail fixture does not claim that machinery exists yet.

The <= is the other half. An event at or below the anchor is already inside the snapshot. Applying it again gives the conversation a duplicate turn, and the model answers a question it has already answered.

Take the snapshot and its anchor together. If one is copied before an append and the other afterward, the file can claim to contain a fact its context has never seen. History already owns those values; its existing lock can protect the pair without a new persistence coordinator. Load before submitting work; save after shutdown has joined the jobs that can still append final facts.

§10.4 Replay Equals Snapshot

The chapter’s central claim fits in one sentence. For a save whose log is complete, loading it as written and loading it with context set to null must produce byte-identical vendor requests for the next prompt under the same runtime configuration.

The first load takes the snapshot path. The second takes the rebuild path, replaying every event from nothing. If the reducer is a pure function of the events, the two paths land on the same context and the renderer turns that context into the same bytes. If they differ, inspect the restoration and reduction first, then the renderer’s ordering and configuration. Both paths must use the same model, declarations and settings for the comparison to isolate persistence.

The grader compares vendor requests. A request is the only thing the model ever sees, and it is a format every student’s agent already produces, so the grader can compare two of them without knowing anything about how a particular solution stores its context. Two contexts that differ in some field the renderer never reads are the same conversation. Two requests that differ by one byte are not.

Byte-identical requests do not require byte-identical save files. Indentation and object-key formatting on disk are yours; the renderer already determines the bytes compared here. A canonical disk format, checksums or an origin certificate would solve a different problem and add nothing to this test.

The precondition is real. A save with a trimmed log (§10.5) has nothing to rebuild from, so nulling its context leaves an empty agent. A run that starts fresh and retains its log can write a complete history. After loading a deliberately trimmed save, however, the agent can retain only the events it was given and the ones it creates next. A new save cannot recover discarded facts. Keep the snapshot in that case; do not call nulling it a replay-equivalence test.

§10.5 The LLM Never Sees the Log

The renderer reads the context. The context holds dialogue entries, the entries hold parts, and at no point does the renderer consult the log. A save with "log": [] and a non-null context is therefore complete: it loads, it resumes, and the next request carries the full conversation.

This is what makes the log trimmable later without touching behavior. It also creates one small trap. Numbering must continue after the loaded events, and a save with an empty log knows its anchor and nothing else. The next Seq is one past the larger of AsOf and the last event in the log; neither alone is enough.

For example, a snapshot anchored at 7 with an empty log must assign 8 to the next event. The resulting save has anchor 8 and one retained event, not an eight-event log. Sequence identity and array length measure different things.

§10.6 Default Load, and Refusing a Bad File

The first design had a --load flag. Bill’s review of it was one line: “Let’s load by default without a flag.” The agent now loads ./save.json at startup if it exists and writes it when stdin closes. --save PATH names a different file for both directions and leaves loading on. That is the command’s choice, so a project directory remembers its own conversation. The library itself resolves its default under the owning Agent’s data directory; two Agents with different directories must not share one process-wide save. An explicit path belongs to Agent configuration too. In the current GUI command, preferences remain at cr/settings.json; the save does not need to move beside them or take over their persistence.

Loading by default makes one failure mode dangerous. If save.json exists but cannot be read, the agent exits with an error and leaves the file untouched. Starting fresh instead looks friendlier and is worse: the fresh session saves on exit and overwrites the history the user came back for. A refusal costs one confusing startup. A silent reset costs the conversation.

Install save-on-exit only after load succeeds. An unconditional deferred save placed above Load would overwrite the bad file while returning the right error. Check the bytes after refusal and verify that no HTTP request was sent; an error message alone leaves the destructive half of that bug invisible.

For a successful exit, the accepted implementation writes a temporary file in the destination directory, closes it, then renames it over the selected path. Encoding, close and rename failures propagate to the caller. This avoids truncating the old save before the replacement is complete; it makes no promise of power-loss durability. A database or write-ahead journal is unnecessary for the normal-exit exercise.

§10.7 Taking It for a Spin

Run the agent in an empty directory, ask it to remember a word, and close stdin with Ctrl-D after the answer. save.json appears. Run it again in the same directory and ask for the word. The second process never saw the first one’s turn; it answers from a context restored out of a file. Build from the core module, then launch from your scratch directory with provider configuration already in the child environment:

go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch10 .
/tmp/ensemble-ch10 chat

For the override case, use /tmp/ensemble-ch10 --save chosen.json chat on both starts. It should create and resume chosen.json without also creating the default save.json. Test the optional GUI command’s stdin EOF too; a browser that appears restored does not establish that the application saved when its terminal closed.

Then break copies on purpose. Preserve the complete first save, and make each variant independently from it. Delete "log" down to [] and the agent still remembers, because the log was never on the rendering path. In another copy, set "context" to null and it still remembers, because the full log rebuilds the same context. Do not make that second edit to the already trimmed copy. Truncate a third copy to half its bytes and the agent refuses to start, which is the correct answer.

The first-edition reference also shipped a verify subcommand that rebuilt from the log and printed MATCH or MISMATCH against the saved snapshot. It remains an optional debugging aid outside the contract; the accepted Edition 2 solution does not need it. The grader never trusts an agent’s opinion of its own determinism; it compares the requests.

The retained October 10, 2026 sessions used claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-4o-mini and gemini-3.8-flash, reusing the same day’s model discovery from the Skills exercise. Each first process received:

Remember the secret word cobalt-juniper. Reply briefly; do not use tools.

Each second process was asked for the word without supplying it again, and each answered cobalt-juniper. The Claude session also resumed independently from the snapshot-only and log-only variants, with the same answer. Those eight model-response processes exited normally without a timeout. The ninth process, given the truncated save, exited 1 before any HTTP request and left the damaged bytes unchanged. The Claude, OpenAI and Gemini receipts retain the actual inputs, replies and captured conversation payloads. These are historical model choices, not an account inventory for your next run.

Remembering the word demonstrates useful restoration, but it cannot establish byte identity. A model might answer correctly despite duplicated history or a dropped tool result. The deterministic source checks use all three real renderers with recorded tool identities, opaque material, a redaction and pending ephemera. Snapshot, full replay, older-snapshot-plus-tail and snapshot-only variants produce the same rendered request. Appending afterward verifies the next sequence and the next save’s anchor as separate obligations.

The original full grader was interrupted and unscored during inherited parity. Its separately invoked Persistence phases scored 70/85 on the initial submission. The shape check stopped at the undefined think declaration, before checking later sequence and anchor predicates; those predicates cannot be called original-grader passes. Independent final-source inspection and focused tests verified the valid shape obligations after the effective-prompt correction. The original review preserves that distinction and the live receipts’ earlier source provenance. The Edition 2 grader report records revised results separately.

Chapter 11: MCP: The Extension Protocol

Every tool the agent has used so far was compiled into the binary. Adding a new one means writing Go, rebuilding, and restarting. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a JSON-RPC 2.0 wire protocol for connecting an agent to external tool servers: processes, browsers, remote services. This chapter builds the client, the transport layer, and a course extension: ephemeral tools that the engine calls automatically, injecting their output into the context window without declaring them to the LLM.

A browser snapshot makes the distinction useful. The model needs to know which tab is selected before deciding what to click. Asking it to remember to request a snapshot adds a tool round and leaves correctness dependent on its memory. Automatic context puts the observation where the decision needs it. The tool still does real work, and the request must wait for that work to finish.

TL;DR

The client sends initialize, receives capabilities, sends notifications/initialized, then calls tools/list to discover what the server offers. Admit discovered tools through the owning skill’s grants. Ordinary admitted tools use the existing model declarations and job dispatch; hidden automatic tools supply completed round or turn context. The bidirectional channel also carries reverse requests to enabled Agent tools.

The exercise implements the historical wire version 2024-11-05. Its reverse tools/call, ephemeral field and $/cancelRequest notification are course contracts. This chapter does not claim compatibility with every current MCP server or present those extensions as current standard requirements.

Extend Chapter 10 with replaceable transports, request correlation, actual job cancellation, hidden automatic context, browser tunneling and skill-owned server startup/shutdown. Keep the common interfaces, real parent relationships and optional GUI module. The exercise and check table below cover the same capabilities through their appropriate clients; --mcp-pipe is a dedicated protocol service, with no implicit model turn. From the repository root, grade with go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 11 path/to/core.

Transport

One interface, multiple implementations:

// MCPTransport carries whole messages independently of GUI framing.
// Close must unblock both directions; one receiver and concurrent senders use it.
type MCPTransport interface {
    // Send writes one complete JSON-RPC message.
    Send(msg json.RawMessage) error
    // Recv reads one complete JSON-RPC message.
    Recv() (json.RawMessage, error)
    // Close releases the boundary and wakes blocked I/O.
    Close() error
}

Pipe: an in-process connected pair, for testing the actual client and codec. Stdio: spawns a subprocess, JSON-RPC over its stdin/stdout. Raw: wraps an io.Reader and io.Writer; the --mcp-pipe flag uses this. WebSocket: tunnels JSON-RPC through the GUI server to the browser.

The interface belongs in internal/common, with a public alias for external clients. Raw, pipe and subprocess behavior belongs in the MCP package. WebSocket framing belongs in the separate GUI module, so a headless consumer does not acquire a browser dependency merely to call an external tool.

Agent owns the MCP manager; the manager owns its clients. A client reaches admission, jobs and diagnostics through manager → Agent → Ensemble. The GUI transport keeps its actual server parent. The composition root establishes those relationships. A reader and writer are boundary resources, and need no invented domain parent or bag of sibling services.

Serialize whole outgoing messages: a reverse reply can arrive while another goroutine sends a request. Closing a transport must wake blocked I/O. For a subprocess that includes closing its pipes, stopping its process group and reaping the child; closing only the Go wrapper leaves a server running after its skill has gone away.

Codec

The codec handles JSON-RPC correlation: outgoing requests get incrementing integer IDs, responses are matched by ID and delivered to the blocked caller. A background goroutine reads the transport and dispatches: responses go to pending callers, incoming requests go to reverse tool handling.

One client can own the transport, ID counter, pending-reply map and reader. The accepted implementation keeps correlation there; a separately exported Codec would add an ownership layer with no other user. The mechanism matters more than the extra object.

Keep the reader free while executing a reverse call. That tool might itself call the peer, whose reply needs the same reader. Running the handler on the reader goroutine would let both sides wait forever for a message already on the wire. Concurrent requests also need an out-of-order reply test: two correct answers delivered to the wrong callers are two failures.

MCP Client

The client initializes, discovers tools, calls them and closes its transport. Its owner supplies reverse dispatch through the existing Agent interface. The public embedding API exposes Agent.MCP().Connect(ctx, name, transport); ensemble.NewMCPTransport(reader, writer, closer) adapts streams, and ensemble.MCPPipe() returns a connected pair. With skills enabled, the peer’s name must match a declared server. Connect performs initialization and discovery before making the peer’s tools available.

tools/call sends params with a string name and object arguments. Text results arrive in ordered content blocks. Preserve a tool’s isError result as a failed tool outcome; a JSON-RPC error is a protocol failure. Neither should be turned into a successful empty string.

MCP tool calls go through the same job infrastructure as run_command. If the job is killed, its context is cancelled and the client sends $/cancelRequest with the request ID to the server. A callback deadline only returns control and a job handle. Interrupt ends the current turn while the job continues; shutdown stops the owned work and closes peers. One context cannot represent all four lifetimes.

Ephemeral Tools

A discovered tool may carry an ephemeral field: "round" or "turn". Ephemeral tools never appear in the tool declarations sent to the LLM. The model cannot call them. The engine calls them automatically:

  • round: called before every RequestSent. The GUI snapshot arrives fresh each round.
  • turn: called once when a new turn starts, for data that can stay fixed through that turn. A later turn gets a fresh call.

Results are combined and attached through the existing event/reducer path into Context.Ephemera, the pending field consumed by the next request. The log retains the arrival for replay; stale snapshots do not accumulate in dialogue. Gather outside the actor so reverse requests, interruption and job facts can still be processed. Send the gathered content back with its turn identity and attach it only if that turn remains active.

Ephemeral errors are logged but not fatal. A GUI snapshot failure should not abort a turn.

The first student implementation used an ordinary job wait for this gathering. An independent peer delayed its turn snapshot by 3.4 seconds. At three seconds, the callback returned a running notice with Use wait_for_job, and the provider request carried that notice where the snapshot should have been. The once-per-turn flag had already been set. When the actual result arrived, it was too late to serve as that turn’s automatic context.

A hidden tool has no model-directed caller to follow up on its handle. Its collector needs the completed content, or an actual failure, before releasing the provider request. The correction carries the handler’s completed result through a buffered reply while preserving the ordinary callback path. Enlarging the three-second timeout would merely select a slower peer for the next failure.

Interruption still lets the collector abandon the old turn without killing the job. The regression holds the old peer reply, interrupts, completes a new turn, then releases the old result. Its output remains available through the job, and none of that stale context enters the new turn. A separate slow-peer check holds both round and turn responses past the callback deadline and verifies that no provider request goes out early. These tests exercise the real jobs, actor, reducer and renderer, with only the external peers replaced.

Bridge

The bridge is the seam between MCP’s type system and the agent’s. It converts discovered names, descriptions and input schemas into ordinary tool definitions. The engine can then dispatch an admitted remote tool through the same path as a compiled one. Inside the accepted manager’s Tools method, the handler captures the client and that iteration’s tool information:

tool := common.ToolDefinition{
    ToolDeclaration: common.ToolDeclaration{
        Name: info.Name, Description: info.Description, Schema: info.Schema,
    },
    Ephemeral: info.Ephemeral,
    Run: func(call common.ToolContext, args json.RawMessage) (string, error) {
        return c.call(call.Job().Context(), info.Name, args)
    },
}

The job supplies the context. Substituting context.Background() here severs explicit kill from the outstanding RPC even though the handler looks correct on every successful short call. The original example made that mistake.

Discovery describes what a peer offers; a skill determines what this Agent admits from that peer. Apply that grant before exposing definitions, then apply the Agent’s enabled-tool policy at declaration and dispatch. Another loaded skill naming the same tool must not widen this server’s grant. Automatic tools remain absent from model declarations and unavailable to guessed ordinary calls. The accepted registry also prevents an external definition from shadowing a compiled capability with the same name.

Reverse Calls

The MCP channel is bidirectional. When the server sends a tools/call request, the client’s reverse handler invokes the Agent’s enabled-tool dispatch. The result goes back with the request’s ID. A browser, a Python script or a remote service can call read_file, run_command, or another enabled ordinary tool, subject to the Agent’s trust and skill boundaries.

Treat admitting such a peer as granting access to those capabilities. A server’s own offered-tool filter limits what it exports; it is not a filesystem sandbox for reverse calls. Only connect a peer you trust with the enabled Agent tools. Confinement arrives later. Unknown, disabled and hidden automatic names must still fail when guessed over this channel.

Reverse execution uses real jobs and retains their facts. It does not fabricate a model-authored tool call in conversation just because the caller used the same method name. Its reply may legitimately be an ordinary running-job notice; the automatic collector described above has a different completion requirement.

WebSocket Tunneling

The browser cannot open a port or spawn a subprocess. The GUI server already carries prompt, hint, interrupt, and settings messages. MCP adds one more type: jsonrpc. The server routes {"type":"jsonrpc","payload":{...}} messages between the Go MCP client and the browser’s MCP server over /ws. Replies use the same envelope and retain the JSON-RPC ID. Give each peer reliable delivery through its connection’s serialized writer; a lossy progress broadcast cannot carry an awaited RPC response. The current implementation uses one active browser MCP target, while other tabs retain ordinary chat and settings access.

On the browser side, mcp.js handles these frames and implements the chapter’s initialize, tools/list and tools/call methods. It registers four tools:

  • gui_snapshot (ephemeral/round): walks the visible DOM and returns a Markdown summary: pane layout, interactive elements with CSS selectors, artifact previews. Capped at 4096 UTF-8 bytes. The cap is reported rather than silent: the summary states how many characters it elided and how many artifacts it omitted, and it reports the state attributes of every control it lists. An observer that truncates in silence will tell you a screen looks fine when it never saw it, and a control whose state it cannot read is a control it will guess about.
  • gui_click(selector): dispatches a click event on the matched element.
  • gui_input(selector, text): sets the value and dispatches input/change events.
  • tts_queue (ephemeral/round): returns pending TTS utterances as JSON: text, state, timing.

The agent receives a textual observation of the visible GUI, updated every round. It can click buttons and fill text fields, then inspect the changed state on the next request. The speech queue reveals what the application is trying to say and whether an utterance has started. It cannot tell whether a human heard intelligible audio; that still requires listening.

SKILL.md Integration

Skills declare MCP servers in their frontmatter. For example, save this as skills/browser-tools/SKILL.md and list browser-tools in your primary skill’s loadable-skills field:

---
name: browser-tools
description: Inspect and operate the visible browser interface.
type: loadable
tools: gui_snapshot gui_click gui_input tts_queue
mcp_servers:
  - name: browser-debug
    transport: websocket
---
Use the current snapshot's selectors to operate visible controls.
Check the next snapshot before claiming the interface changed.

A separate code-search skill can declare this fragment, provided scripts/search_server.py implements the server and offers search_code:

tools: search_code
mcp_servers:
  - name: code-search
    transport: stdio
    command: python3
    args: ["scripts/search_server.py"]

Loading a skill starts its MCP servers and discovers their tools. The transport field determines the wire: stdio spawns a subprocess, websocket tunnels through the GUI. Browser discovery requires both a declared skill and a connected browser; an already-open browser can serve a later skill load. The tools grant must include automatic tools as well as ordinary ones.

Arguments are a JSON-style string array, passed literally without shell expansion. Relative script paths resolve from the Agent’s workspace. Keep provider credentials with the model client; the accepted subprocess launcher passes only basic OS environment values to an external server. The limited frontmatter parser handles these declared fields without becoming a general YAML implementation.

Unloading stops that skill’s external servers and removes their executable tools immediately. Chapter 9’s compiled tools and retained instruction text still follow pending removal. Those lifetimes differ because a retained manual does not require keeping a subprocess alive. Compaction is still a later feature; this chapter adds no new way to erase the retained manual.

Exercise

Extend the accepted Chapter 10 agent. Implement the transport/client/bridge, automatic round and turn tools, reverse calls, browser tools/tunnel and skill server lifecycle above. Preserve prior behavior through the same Agent runtime. Build from the core module with go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch11 .. Begin with a protocol peer connected to that executable:

/tmp/ensemble-ch11 --mcp-pipe

The flag dedicates stdin/stdout to one JSON-RPC 2.0 object per newline. The client initiates the handshake; replies preserve integer request IDs. Keep diagnostics off stdout. This service mode does not start a conversation, so successful initialization alone cannot prove model-driven tool execution.

Then use normal chat with a skill-declared stdio peer. Inspect the actual provider declarations and correlated results, including an ordinary tool error. Verify that round content refreshes before each request, turn content runs once per new turn, automatic names stay hidden and a failed automatic call is logged without aborting the turn. Check reverse execution with an enabled file read and refusals for unavailable names. Exercise the separate GUI’s real tunnel in both directions.

Check Points Observable
mcp-handshake 15 initialize, initialized notification and discovery sequence
tool-discovery 15 actual discovered schemas and admitted model-visible tools
mcp-tool-call 15 forwarded arguments and correlated real result/error content
ephemeral-round 20 hidden round/turn context, refresh timing and nonfatal errors
reverse-call 15 enabled tool execution and unknown-tool refusal
ws-tunnel 10 JSON-RPC through the actual separate GUI connection
ch10-parity 10 Chapter 10 through its appropriate clients 
go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 11 path/to/core

Omit the final path to grade solutions/ch11. Existing -gui DIR, -gui-model and inherited fixture options remain available. Keep focused source tests for ownership, out-of-order correlation, slow automatic completion, callback versus kill/interrupt, per-server grants and subprocess unload/reaping. The numeric checks do not establish all those properties. Browser DOM and native speech need an actual browser in addition to a faithful JSON-RPC peer.

Taking It for a Spin

Give the agent an external capability small enough to inspect. In a fresh scratch directory, write a word of your choice into marker.txt, then save this server as peer.py. It implements the historical course wire and records its call counts locally so the model’s account can be checked:

import json
import pathlib
import sys

counts = {}
tools = [
    ("read_marker", "Read the exact marker file text", ""),
    ("environment_snapshot", "Current live snapshot", "round"),
    ("session_brief", "Session configuration", "turn"),
]
for line in sys.stdin:
    message = json.loads(line)
    if "id" not in message:
        continue
    method = message.get("method")
    if method == "initialize":
        result = {"protocolVersion": "2024-11-05", "capabilities": {"tools": {}}}
    elif method == "tools/list":
        result = {"tools": [
            {"name": name, "description": description, "ephemeral": mode,
             "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}}
            for name, description, mode in tools
        ]}
    elif method == "tools/call":
        name = message["params"]["name"]
        counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + 1
        pathlib.Path("peer-counts.json").write_text(json.dumps(counts))
        if name == "read_marker":
            text = pathlib.Path("marker.txt").read_text()
        elif name == "environment_snapshot":
            text = f"Snapshot number {counts[name]}"
        else:
            text = "Use read_marker to inspect the local marker."
        result = {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": text}]}
    else:
        continue
    print(json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": message["id"],
                      "result": result}), flush=True)

This little demonstration peer serves only the listed tools. It is not a general server implementation or a cancellation test. Save the following primary skill in skills/base/SKILL.md:

---
name: base
description: Read a local marker through the demonstration MCP peer.
type: primary
tools: read_marker environment_snapshot session_brief
mcp_servers:
  - name: local-observer
    transport: stdio
    command: python3
    args: ["-u", "peer.py"]
---
Read the marker through read_marker when requested.
Automatic snapshot data describes the current round.

Build in your core module, then launch from that scratch directory. Set the usual LLM_VENDOR, available LLM_MODEL and LLM_API_KEY in the child environment without putting the key in a command line or transcript:

go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch11 .
EN_SKILLS_DIR=./skills EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base /tmp/ensemble-ch11 chat

Enter:

Use read_marker exactly once. Report the exact marker and current automatic snapshot number in one sentence. Do no other work.

After the answer, close stdin. Compare the reported marker with marker.txt and inspect peer-counts.json. The ordinary call reads the file; the round tool updates automatically before the initial request and before the request carrying that result. The turn tool runs once. A model may take extra rounds, so check the actual requests and counts rather than treating an expected count as proof of what happened.

The retained October 10, 2026 sessions used this pattern with claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-4o-mini and gemini-3.8-flash. Each successful run made one marker read, two round snapshots and one turn snapshot, and each final answer reported the correct marker and snapshot number 2. The Claude, OpenAI and Gemini receipts retain the actual inputs, replies and requests. These are historical model choices; select an available model when you run the exercise. The published peer and skill make that pattern reproducible without claiming they are byte-for-byte copies of the original launcher’s generated files.

The first Claude attempt produced no answer. Its process exited zero while stderr reported invalid streamed Anthropic content. The inherited streaming parser had replaced valid initial {} arguments with an empty accumulated input_json_delta. Keeping the initial input when no JSON bytes arrived fixed the call. One bounded repeat succeeded and captured a valid tool-use start block followed by partial_json: "". The initial attempt had retained requests but not response frames; only the repeat supplies that wire receipt. A regression using the captured stream reproduces the parser failure when the defect is restored.

The browser has separate evidence. Fifteen checks ran actual Chrome through the Go tunnel and Agent with a local provider fake. A tool click selected the Settings tab; tool input changed the font value and computed size. Later snapshots exposed the selected state, and a native utterance appeared with queue and start timing. A large snapshot stayed within the byte cap while disclosing elided characters and omitted artifacts. The browser receipt preserves these observations. The font assertion proves applied and effective state; it never reads the settings file. Disk persistence has its separate Chapter 8 restart check. Nor do those browser checks turn the live CLI sessions into live-provider browser demonstrations.

Check the actual result when testing the bridge. One deliberately broken argument-forwarding implementation initially passed because the assertion searched the whole provider request. It found the marker in the earlier tool call’s arguments even though the result was wrong. Restricting the assertion to the correlated result blocks exposed the defect. A request contains both what the model asked for and what the tool returned. Match the assertion to the fact it needs to establish.

The original full grader was interrupted and unscored, with exit 143. A separate unchanged current-chapter probe scored 80/90 on interim source; recursive parity was unrun. Its tool-call and ephemeral credits did not execute those behaviors, and its WebSocket check searched fixed filenames rather than running a tunnel. Independent integration, browser and live evidence established the valid obligations, including the later slow-peer correction. The original review preserves those limits and source versions; the Edition 2 grader report records revised results separately. A handshake opens the channel. The useful test follows a call through it and reads what came back.

Chapter 12: The Agent Sees Itself

A coding agent that cannot see its own GUI is debugging blind. Reading the source tells it what a button should do. Watching the running interface tells it what the button did. Chapter 11 supplied the browser tools and MCP transport; this chapter makes that view available at startup through one skill, then points it at the interface the agent is using.

The wiring is short and mostly mechanical. What follows it is less tidy: an observer that froze what it watched, a debugger whose escape hatch was unreachable, and a settings repair that made the server correct while leaving the screen wrong. Giving an agent eyes is useful partly because it exposes how much the programmer had been assuming.

TL;DR

Extend Chapter 11 with --gui-debug and --skills-dir PATH in both the headless command and the optional GUI application. The first selects the reachable gui-debug skill during Agent construction; the second overrides EN_SKILLS_DIR. With debug enabled and no directory selected, use ./skills. When a directory is selected and EN_PRIMARY_SKILL is empty, these applications select ensemble as primary. Keep explicit skill kinds and tool grants.

Startup uses the existing skill/MCP lifecycle. Assemble the primary and startup manuals before freezing the system prompt. Ordinary later load_skill calls still return instructions through history. Discover the peer’s tools, admit only the skill’s grants, hide automatic tools from model declarations, and refresh completed DOM and speech-queue content before every round. A click or input must affect the next snapshot.

Unloading gui-debug immediately removes its external tools and automatic context and closes its peers. A guessed tool name cannot bypass removal. Compiled grants and instruction text remain pending removal under Chapter 9’s existing rules; this chapter adds no compaction. Preserve human typing and speech pacing without treating programmatic input as a human pause cause. Explicit unpause in any tab still unpauses the whole Agent.

Build on the existing owners and common interfaces. Agent owns its skill registry and MCP manager; the optional GUI owns browser connections and framing. No new callback bundle, dispatcher or driver application is needed.

The skill

Here are the supplied files, including the primary that makes the optional skill reachable. Put this in skills/ensemble/SKILL.md:

---
name: ensemble
type: primary
description: A concise coding assistant with optional browser inspection
tools: read_file write_file edit_file list_directory search_files run_command
loadable-skills: gui-debug
---
You are a coding assistant. Use the available tools to inspect facts before
claiming results. Available skills: $SKILLS.

And this in skills/gui-debug/SKILL.md:

---
name: gui-debug
type: loadable
description: Inspect and operate the connected browser
depends: ensemble
tools: gui_snapshot tts_queue gui_click gui_input
mcp_servers:
  - name: browser-debug
    transport: websocket
---
The current browser snapshot and speech queue arrive automatically before each
round. Use gui_click with a visible CSS selector and gui_input with selector and
text. Observe the next snapshot to confirm the effect. Hidden or omitted state
is not evidence of success: report what you can actually observe.

The kind, dependency and grants do different jobs. type: loadable makes this an optional skill; the primary’s loadable-skills makes it reachable; depends ensures the base is present; tools admits the named capabilities. Discovery alone grants nothing. An MCP peer advertising another tool does not authorize the model to use it. Reverse calls still pass through the Agent’s enabled-tool dispatch.

The browser entry uses the WebSocket tunnel from Chapter 11. For a deterministic check, replace only that server entry with a stdio peer’s command and arguments, retaining the skill kind and grants. The existing Chapter 11 Python peer illustrates that external boundary. A subprocess and a browser use the same discovery and dispatch path; only transport creation differs. The historical wire version and course extensions retain Chapter 11’s scope.

Skill-based MCP lifecycle

Loading a skill with mcp_servers asks the Agent’s MCP manager to start its peers. It opens the transport, initializes the client, discovers the tools, and retains the connections for cleanup. The manager exposes only admitted tools through the Agent’s existing declarations and dispatcher. Jobs still own running calls and their output; a callback delay is no new server lifetime.

This wiring already exists. The registry reaches Agent.MCP() through its actual parent interface. The composition root constructs and attaches the Agent’s children before loading skills. The command selects configuration and calls that root; it does not become a collection of closures holding sibling services together. The optional GUI supplies its public transport without importing GUI code into the core.

At startup the application sets AgentSpec.StartupSkills to []string{"gui-debug"}. The constructor loads the primary, activates the optional startup skill through the same admission path, and assembles both manuals before the prompt freezes. There is no model-authored call to answer yet, so inventing a load_skill result would invent conversation history. The accepted implementation records application-origin activation at sequence zero instead.

Once construction finishes, the distinction matters: a later load_skill returns its manual as a tool result and leaves the system prompt alone. Likewise, unloading a startup skill cannot rewrite the frozen prompt. Describe the immediate effect accurately: its MCP tools disappear, automatic browser context stops, and its clients close. For stdio that includes terminating and reaping the peer while the Agent can continue. Instruction removal remains pending; an old manual is not evidence of a live connection.

The four browser tools

These are the tools from Chapter 11’s browser peer:

Tool Automatic timing Observable result
gui_snapshot Each round Markdown DOM: panes, selectors, semantic control state and artifact previews
tts_queue Each round JSON array of pending speech utterances with state and timing
gui_click Model call Clicks the visible element named by selector
gui_input Model call Sets the element named by selector to text, then sends input/change events

The two automatic tools remain absent from model declarations. Their completed output appears in ephemeral context, replaced on the next round. The model sees what changed without repeatedly asking for another screenshot. Preserve Chapter 11’s wait for completed automatic content; a three-second running notice cannot describe a DOM.

The callable tools return ok on success in the supplied browser. That confirms the handler ran. The next snapshot establishes whether Settings opened or a field acquired its new value. A test that searches the whole request for the desired text may find only the earlier call arguments. Read the result associated with that call and the actual state in the refreshed snapshot.

Exercise

Add the startup selection and directory override to both clients, reusing the existing skill lifecycle. Supply the two complete manuals above. Preserve fresh automatic context, actual click/input behavior, immediate external-tool removal, peer cleanup, and the human-input cause distinction described below.

From your core solution directory, build the headless executable:

go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch12 .

With a stdio peer declared in the selected skill directory and the existing LLM_VENDOR, LLM_MODEL, LLM_BASE_URL and LLM_API_KEY configured, its protocol invocation is:

/tmp/ensemble-ch12 --gui-debug --skills-dir ./skills

Stdin uses the existing newline-delimited input; the flag supplies no implicit prompt:

{"kind":"prompt","text":"Inspect the browser state, click a visible control, and report the change from the next snapshot."}

EOF drains the submitted work and ends the session. For human terminal conversation, append chat. A headless process can talk to an external stdio peer; to reach the actual browser, build and run the separate GUI as shown below.

The revised grader runs both actual clients with valid skills and a stateful external stdio peer. It checks startup instructions, directory override, fresh snapshot and TTS data, forwarded click/input arguments and results, then unloads the skill and attempts another browser call. That call must fail, the automatic context must be gone, and the peer must have stopped while the Agent remains alive. The independent browser evidence covers native speech, semantic DOM state and the real tunnel; a stdio fake cannot prove those browser properties.

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 12

The default is solutions/ch12; supply your core solution directory as the positional argument and use the existing -gui option if its separate GUI module is elsewhere. The original grader remains historical: it returned 0/100 after an untyped fixture prevented startup, while its parity detector required particular method names. That run observed neither successful browser behavior nor the later real speech/input defect. Valid runtime obligations need their own evidence.

What the wiring found

The plumbing above is small because the preceding chapters already own the difficult lifetimes. A skill declares an MCP server. The registry connects when the skill loads and disconnects when it unloads. A browser tab exposes four tools over a WebSocket that was already there. The interesting part is what arrives the first time an agent can see a screen it did not render and press a button nobody told it about.

The first-edition experiment ran on September 19 and 20, 2026. Its driver and transport arrived on the first day; four code repairs and three documentation commits followed the next afternoon. The retained experience report supplies the account below. The ninety-eight-second outcome is that report’s measurement, not a new run of this edition.

The asymmetry is useful. Once a failure was visible, the repair was often small. The experiment exposed faults that source development and passing graders had missed, but it did not find every fault without help. The report specifically attributes a truncation observation to the human supervisor and the unsafe rendering path to subsequent source inspection. Those are valuable findings too; their origins matter when assessing the observer.

The user that cannot read the source

The historical driver was a separate small binary. It connects to the same hub the browser connects to, discovers its tools through MCP, and registers exactly one tool of its own, file_report, so it has somewhere to put conclusions. It is built on NewBareAgent, which is an agent with no builtin tools at all. No read_file, no run_command, no editor. Its interaction tools arrived through discovery. That experimental driver also gained submission and waiting helpers; those are history, not extra tools assigned by this four-tool exercise.

Its system prompt states the constraint directly:

You CANNOT read files, edit code, or run commands. You can only
interact through the GUI, exactly as a human user would.

That restriction is the entire value of the driver. An agent with filesystem access will answer a question about the interface by reading the source, which tells you what the interface was meant to do. An observer restricted to the GUI has to answer from the screen, which tells you what the interface actually does. The gap between those two answers is where the bugs live.

The human observer

The protocol around these runs matters as much as the tooling, because it is what makes the results mean anything.

Bill Cox supervised the experiment, reading the reasoning as it streamed. The method was to let the driver inspect the interface before supplying a diagnosis. Watching it walk past a defect is useful evidence about the view it has; immediately pointing out the defect would erase that evidence.

He did direct, and the distinction is worth drawing precisely. Direction covered what to test next, which binary to rebuild, and once, usefully, the observation that a stale server was still holding port 8084 while the freshly built binary bound to nothing and served no one. That is operational guidance, and withholding it would have wasted an hour proving nothing. Findings were different. The retained report also records a screenshot observation about truncation supplied by the human. That finding cannot be counted as an unaided discovery merely because the subsequent repair was automated.

The reason to run it that way is that a supervisor who volunteers the answer cannot tell the difference between a tool that works and a tool that agrees. A supplied hint can make a successful report look like an independent discovery unless the assistance is recorded. To learn whether the snapshot is sufficient for a finding, let the observer attempt it before supplying the missing answer.

This is the same discipline the book asks of a reader supervising an agent on live code, applied to the machinery itself. Keep the human assistance with the result so the next reader can tell which capability was exercised.

The observer that froze what it watched

The first runs never reached a task at all. The driver typed its prompt and the coding agent stopped responding, permanently, before any work began.

The cause was a feature working exactly as designed. Chapter 7 pauses the engine while the user is typing, so that an agent does not barrel ahead while a human is halfway through composing a hint. The feature exists for a particular working style: Bill Cox reads the agent’s reasoning as it streams and sends corrections mid-turn, which makes the pause the difference between a hint that lands and a hint that arrives after the decision it was meant to change. The first-edition implementation watched the input field:

// The original handler. WebSocket readiness guards elided for clarity.
let userTyping = false;
input.addEventListener('input', () => {
    const typing = input.value.trim().length > 0;
    if (typing && !userTyping) {
        userTyping = true;
        ws.send(JSON.stringify({type: 'pause'}));
    } else if (!typing && userTyping) {
        userTyping = false;
        ws.send(JSON.stringify({type: 'unpause'}));
    }
});

Read that as a human and it is correct. Text appears, the agent waits. The field empties, the agent resumes.

Read it as a program driving the field and it is a trap with no exit. gui_input sets the value and dispatches an input event, which is what makes it indistinguishable from typing, and that indistinguishability is the entire point of the tool. So the pause fires. Then gui_submit sends the prompt and clears the field by assigning to value, and assigning to value in JavaScript fires no event at all. The branch that sends unpause is reachable only by a path the driver cannot take. One keystroke in, the engine is paused, and nothing in the system will ever unpause it.

The historical repair expressed two intentions. A flag marks input as programmatic so the pause handler ignores it, and submission sends an explicit unpause rather than relying on an event that will not arrive:

if (window._mcpProgrammaticInput) return;

The general shape of this is older than software. An instrument that shares a channel with the thing it measures will perturb it, and the perturbation is worst where the system was tuned to human timing. Pause on typing, debounce on scroll, idle timeouts, animations that wait for a settle: each one encodes an assumption about how fast and how continuously a person acts. An automated driver violates all of them at once, and it does so silently, because from the GUI’s perspective nothing unusual occurred. A user started typing and never stopped.

The second pause, after the fix

The second-edition student reproduced the self-input freeze in a real browser. Marking MCP input as programmatic fixed the immediate listener: a model could fill the field and click Send with speech disabled. Independent review then turned native speech on. The utterance finished, the programmatically filled field still contained MCP submitted, and the Agent remained paused.

The missed path was pace(). On speech transitions it looked at the field’s contents again, forgetting how the text got there. The input listener knew the event was programmatic; the later speech callback silently promoted that same text to human typing. Ignoring one event could not repair a second reader of the same mistaken signal.

Keep the cause, rather than reconstructing it from the value. The browser MCP handler sends a marked event after setting the control:

element.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("input", {
  bubbles: true, detail: { mcp: true }
}));
element.dispatchEvent(new Event("change", { bubbles: true }));

The ordinary input listener preserves the actual cause:

input.addEventListener("input", event => {
  humanTyping = !event.detail?.mcp && input.value.length > 0;
  pace();
});

Speech and typing then combine as speaking || humanTyping. Successful submission clears humanTyping explicitly after clearing the field. Human whitespace still counts as typing; programmatic text does not acquire a human origin merely because a speech callback ran later.

Pause remains Agent-wide. A browser sends automatic pause/unpause commands when its local causes change. If another tab explicitly unpauses, an unchanged local cause cannot immediately veto that command. The corrected native-browser check covers speech ending with programmatic text still present, genuine whitespace typing holding pause, explicit unpause from another tab, and a subsequent actual MCP submission. It also waits for the concluding speech to finish. The earlier passing check with speech disabled proved less than its author thought.

Those checks used native speech start/end events, with a local provider fake driving the actual Agent and browser. They establish the measured pause transitions, not subjective listening quality. The second tab closed after the global-unpause control; the retained earlier two-tab speech stall has no established cause and is not a general claim about concurrent speech reliability.

A debugger that would not start

The first historical task given to the driver was small on purpose: ask the coding agent for Tower of Hanoi, then watch it debug the result. The agent wrote the program, ran it, and produced fifteen moves. Then it started dlv and stopped forever.

Chapter 4 predicted this in print. Section 4.8 is titled “Your agent drives a debugger,” and it warns that a dispatcher which waits for process exit will hang on an interactive program, because “the dispatcher would wait for an exit that never comes, and on pipes dlv refuses to start at all.” The chapter named the trap. The reference implementation walked into it anyway.

The mechanism was a single synchronous read. toolRunCommand read the PTY inside the tool function, so the function could not return until the process closed its output. For go build that is correct and invisible. For a debugger sitting at a prompt it is fatal, and it is fatal in a way that disables the exact feature meant to rescue it: ai_callback_pattern is matched inside Wait, and Wait runs after the tool function returns. The escape hatch was behind the door it was supposed to open.

The first-edition repair changed the lifetime: the tool function returned once the process was running, and a reader goroutine owned the PTY until exit. Its DeferFinish field told that dispatcher the job would finish itself. The following historical excerpt shows the handoff; it is not an API to add to the current implementation:

// The reader goroutine copies output from the PTY to the job until the
// terminal closes, then reaps the process and finishes the job. It runs
// independently of the dispatcher, so an interactive process that never
// exits (dlv, python) does not block the model from getting a handle.
job := c.Job
c.DeferFinish = true
go func() {
    buf := make([]byte, 32*1024)
    for {
        n, rerr := f.Read(buf)
        if n > 0 {
            _, _ = job.Write(bytes.ReplaceAll(buf[:n], []byte("\r\n"), []byte("\n")))
        }
        if rerr != nil {
            break
        }
    }
    _ = f.Close()
    werr := cmd.Wait()
    // ... exit code extraction elided ...
    job.Finish("", nil)
}()

Two dispatchers

The experience report records the next surprise: the debugger worked, but the older Chapter 4 checks returned zero.

The failure signature pointed in the wrong direction. Tool output came back as the empty string, and the capture file on disk held zero bytes. That reads as a broken output path, and an hour can be spent there. The actual fault was lifetime again. There were two tool dispatchers in that first-edition codebase: Engine.Execute, which serves chapters 3 and 4 through the older Ask path, and Actor.dispatchTool, which serves chapter 6 onward. Only the second had been taught about DeferFinish. The first still called job.Finish the instant the tool function returned, and Finish closes the capture file. The reader goroutine was writing correctly the whole time, into a file that had already been closed underneath it.

The diagnostic detour is worth recording, because it cost more than the bug. Debug prints added to Actor.dispatchTool never appeared in the output, and the first explanation reached for was a stale build cache. It was not stale. The prints were in a function the failing tests never called. Silent debug output is evidence of the wrong code path at least as often as it is evidence of a bad build, and the cheaper check is to confirm which function runs before rebuilding anything.

Ninety-eight seconds

With both dispatchers corrected, the report records an end-to-end rerun. The driver typed the prompt into the real text field and submitted it. This time the coding agent wrote a three-disk hanoi.go, ran its seven moves, then opened dlv and worked through a full session: set a breakpoint on move, continue, print disk, quit. The reported debugger exit was zero and elapsed time ninety-eight seconds. The earlier hung run had used four disks and fifteen moves; those are different runs.

That historical run explains why the capability is worth building. Chapter 4 of this edition already establishes the independent job lifetime; keep it when adding browser access. An agent that can drive a debugger can inspect a running program’s state rather than reasoning about what the state ought to be, and an agent that can drive a GUI can do the same for an interface.

The bug that only appears after you fix the bug

The next task sent the driver into the settings panel with instructions to try values a careful user would not. It set temperature to negative five, and the server accepted it.

That is the obvious bug, and the fix is ordinary: a clamp function, called both when a settings patch arrives and when settings load from disk, so a hand edited file cannot bypass validation either. The original chapter also reports a targeted check with clamp disabled; that historical claim is separate from this edition’s settings evidence.

The second bug appeared only because the driver was asked to repeat its own test after the fix landed. The server now clamped correctly, and the GUI still displayed negative five. Server state and screen state disagreed, and the screen is what a user believes.

The cause was a single struct doing two incompatible jobs. Settings was used both as a sparse patch, where an absent field means “leave this alone,” and as a full state broadcast, where every field should be present. Those two roles want opposite JSON encodings. With omitempty on every field, a value clamped to zero vanished from the broadcast entirely, and the client guard reads:

if (s.temperature !== undefined) { /* update the input */ }

An absent field is indistinguishable from an unchanged field, so the stale value stayed on screen. The same flaw meant TTSEnabled: false could never be transmitted, because false is empty. Turning speech off was unrepresentable on the wire.

The deleted code had confessed. SettingsStore.Apply carried this comment:

// Since omitempty skips false, we handle this via the raw patch.
// For simplicity, always apply.

Someone met this bug, understood it precisely enough to describe it in one sentence, and routed around it instead of removing it. The method had no callers outside tests.

There was a real choice about how far to take the repair. The cautious option preserves the existing wire format and introduces a second type for broadcasts, leaving the patch struct untouched, which costs nothing today and leaves two nearly identical structs for the next reader to confuse. The maintainer settled it in one line: the format has no external consumers, so make the code clean. The repair therefore dropped omitempty from every field, so a broadcast always carries complete state, and deleted Apply outright, leaving one merge path with defined semantics.

A zero missing from a full snapshot would still be the defect. The corrected broadcast must carry temperature: 0 and tts_enabled: false explicitly. A clamped value on disk, the value applied by the server, and the value shown by the client are separate observations. Chapter 8 now follows all three instead of treating a settings-file inspection as proof of the screen.

The settings panel that does not exist

The strongest finding came from a test that failed in an unusual way.

Asked to exercise the sidebar tabs, the driver reported that clicking “Artifacts” opened the Settings panel. The report was specific, confident, and false. There was no Settings tab in that version of the markup. The data-tab and data-panel attributes map correctly, chats to chats and artifacts to artifacts, and clicking either one does what it says.

The report was fiction, and the reason it was fiction is the finding. Tab state lived only in a CSS class. gui_snapshot built its element labels from textContent, aria-label and placeholder, and read no state attributes at all, so the driver could see that two tabs existed and could not see which one was selected. It had also reached for an ambiguous selector, button:nth-of-type(2), because the buttons carried nothing better to aim at. Asked what happened after the click, it had no way to observe the answer, and it produced a plausible one.

In this run, the driver filled missing state with a confident guess. The observation supports fixing the missing state; it does not establish that every model must guess whenever information is absent.

The repair was to put state where a machine can read it. The hamburger and the tabs now carry aria-expanded and aria-selected, synchronized on every click, with the initial value derived from the live CSS class rather than hardcoded, because the markup default had already drifted from the rendered default. gui_snapshot now reports those attributes alongside each control.

Rerunning the identical test produced a correct before and after table, and in the one place where the driver lacked information, it wrote “not observable” instead of inventing a panel. Same model, same prompt, same GUI. The only change was that the interface stopped hiding its state.

This is the accessibility argument in a form that a developer who has never used a screen reader can feel directly. Semantic state attributes are usually presented as a courtesy extended to users with assistive technology. They are also the difference between an automated observer that reports what happened and one that reports something reasonable. This observer produced wrong data where the interface supplied no selected state, and delivered it with the same confidence as the truth.

What an interface owes an observer

Two smaller findings came out of the same pass, and both generalize.

Source inspection found an injection hole. artifact-scroll.js built the tool card header by interpolating the tool name and its serialized arguments into innerHTML. Tool arguments can carry text from outside the agent. They contain filenames, URLs, and the contents of files just read, which is to say text an attacker can influence. Twenty lines further down, the result path rendered with textContent and was safe. One file, both patterns, and the vulnerable one sat on the path that renders attacker-adjacent text. The book spends a chapter on prompt injection arriving through the model. This was the same threat arriving through the renderer.

The truncation investigation followed the human screenshot observation, and the initial notes about it were backwards. The working document asserted that the driver saw the full DOM while the human saw a trimmed version. Measurement found four independent caps running the other way: the human view truncated tool input at 500 characters and results at 1000, while the snapshot truncated each artifact at 120 characters and the whole document at 4000. For an individual result preview, the snapshot could show 120 characters where the human view showed 1000. Worse, the snapshot silently dropped every artifact past the tenth with no marker, so it could not distinguish ten artifacts from fifty.

The report corrected its earlier claim after checking the actual caps. The caps were kept, because both views need them, and both were made honest: truncated text is now reachable through a title attribute rather than deleted behind an ellipsis, and the snapshot states how many characters and how many artifacts it withheld.

That is the rule the section converges on. Silent truncation lets an observer report that a screen looks fine without seeing the omitted content. Hidden control state invited the guess in this run. Unsafe HTML interpolation gives attacker-controlled markup an execution path. Runtime observation and source inspection answer different parts of the diagnosis. The unsafe renderer was visible in source; the observer’s confident report showed what the missing state caused during use.

The bugs travel back into the book

The instruction that produced this section came once the fixes were in: update the chapter summaries wherever a bug made it through. Tracing them was the first step, and each defect was matched to the chapter that should have prevented it. Several repairs also exposed an instruction that should have made the obligation explicit.

The original Chapter 4 explained the job model, named the interactive process trap in plain words, and never stated the obligation that follows from it. Chapter 8 built the tool card and showed the rendering without saying which parts of it carry text the agent did not write. Chapter 12 specified gui_snapshot with a 4KB cap and did not require the cap to announce itself. In each case the mechanism was taught correctly and the duty attached to the mechanism was left implicit.

The original Chapter 9 is the sharpest example, because the reasoning that let three bugs through is stated plainly in its opening:

The graded surface is small: four server-side settings checks and a parity gate. Everything else is client code you can see working.

That passage left client behavior to visual inspection. Looking at a screen confirms that a value was accepted. It does not confirm that the value was validated, that the server and the screen agree about it afterward, or that a control’s state can be read by anything other than an eye. Three bugs fit in that gap, and all three shipped.

A missing obligation in the teaching is worth repairing even when an experienced implementer could have inferred it. That does not make every implementation defect inevitable or transfer every mistake to the book. The repair was therefore made in the prose as well as the source. The historical repair made Chapter 4 state that the tool returns when the process is running and the job owns it from there, and gives the failure signature, which reads like broken output capture and is really a closed file. Original Chapter 8 states that tool cards are built with textContent and that capped content stays reachable. Original Chapter 9’s summary gains the three obligations that survive the absence of a grader. Original Chapter 12 requires the snapshot to report what it withheld.

A loop closes here. The agent described in these chapters was built by following these chapters. When it acquired eyes and a way to press buttons, the first thing it did was find places where the chapters were wrong. Some repairs belonged in the GUI and some obligations needed to become explicit in the instructions. The next implementation gets both lessons.

A book that produces a working program gets to be tested by the program it produces. This section is the first time that test came back with findings, and the findings were about the book.

Taking it for a spin

Use the supplied WebSocket skill for the real browser. From the core solution directory, build its separate module:

(cd gui && go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch12-gui ./cmd)

With your provider environment configured, run from that same core directory:

/tmp/ensemble-ch12-gui --gui-dir gui/web/gui --gui-debug --skills-dir ./skills --port 8088

Leave the terminal open and connect to http://localhost:8088 before submitting a prompt. These assets still come from disk, so the explicit --gui-dir matters when launching outside the GUI module. The browser supplies the peer that the startup skill has selected. Use a scratch copy or a fresh selected --save path when you want an independent conversation; Chapter 10’s default load still applies.

Ask the agent to open Settings, change the font size to 20, inspect the next automatic snapshot, then unload gui-debug. Tell it to use browser tools and avoid file or shell access. Observe the actual control and effective page font as well as its report. After unload, inspect the next provider request: browser declarations and automatic context should be absent even though the startup manual remains in the frozen system text.

The retained October 10, 2026 browser sessions used claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-4o-mini and gemini-3.8-flash. These are the models actually exercised, not a claim about today’s catalog. The live record links the captured requests and real Chrome observations.

Claude Haiku and Gemini changed the effective font to 20, received the refreshed snapshot, and unloaded the skill. Claude then incorrectly said the MCP tools remained available until compaction. The old generic unload message encouraged that explanation; the final request already showed the tools gone. The implementation’s message was clarified to separate immediate server removal from pending instruction removal. No paid repeat was needed merely to demonstrate revised wording.

Both GPT-4o mini attempts failed the full task. The first guessed input[type='number'], received a missing-selector error, then unloaded without repairing it. A guided second attempt supplied the observed #font-size selector and explained that it was a select. It changed the setting and unloaded, then tried read_file on path/to/the/snapshot despite the instruction forbidding file access. That nonexistent path failed, and the final response claimed the snapshot could not be inspected. The capture already contained the refreshed state.

The second attempt passed the script’s GUI assertions. It remains a task failure. That distinction is especially useful here: working controls do not guarantee that a model will use them correctly or report their result faithfully. A guided selector is assistance, and a prompt restriction is weaker than the historical blind driver’s actual absence of file tools.

These live runs preceded the final native-speech correction and small manual/message corrections. They establish the recorded interaction and unload behavior on their captured source. The corrected speech path has its separate native-browser evidence; no final-source paid rerun is claimed. Likewise, a visibly effective font change is not a restart-persistence test. Chapter 8 supplies that separate check.

Checking the correction itself

The first-edition chapter ended with a quotation-verification story. It said that “You know the client works because you can see it.” had been invented and appeared nowhere in the original settings chapter. The retained source contains those exact words, split across a newline. They are present even in the revision before this narrative was appended.

A literal one-line search misses a wrapped sentence. That miss establishes a search result, not the sentence’s absence. Read the surrounding paragraph or normalize whitespace before comparing the quotation. The supposed correction needed the same scrutiny as the original claim.

The comparison with the phantom Settings panel remains useful, with a narrower conclusion: check the observable that supports the claim. For a tab, read selected state. For a quotation, compare the actual source text. For a successful tool, inspect its correlated result. A confident diagnosis can survive an inadequate check just as easily as the bug it diagnoses.

Chapter 13: The Channel Nobody Tested

This chapter is for me. Accessibility is an afterthought everywhere, never in the critical path of creating a product. Since I am in control here, your AI coding agent gets decent a11y from the start, if you follow this codebook accurately.

The test has to run over data as close as possible to what a blind or low-vision coder actually receives. So in this chapter we build a virtual blind coder, one that can only hear TTS output, and it has to drive the AI coding agent successfully.

If you care about SWEs with low vision, please do not skip this chapter.

An automated observer can complete a task without depending on the channel under test. The historical GUI experiment in Chapter 12 found real interaction defects, alongside findings supplied by human observation and source inspection. Its DOM-based work did not establish that speech carried the same useful information. The screen could look right while the listener missed the message.

The first-edition speech investigation exposed that gap. This chapter preserves its findings and builds the instrument that was missing: an observer whose only account of the target agent comes through the speech transcript.

TL;DR

Two deliverables. A speech pipeline that turns a stream of arbitrary text fragments into utterances a person can listen to, and a small blind virtual-user client that perceives the target through its speech transcript alone. Chapter 12’s historical driver is not a prerequisite project.

The speech pipeline contract

Text arrives as arbitrary fragments. The GUI receives decoded text deltas, frequently mid-word, and the pipeline owns the job of turning that into speech.

  1. Buffer until a phrase boundary. Never speak a fragment as it arrives. A word split across three chunks is one word.
  2. A sentence-ending period is a boundary. A single newline is not. Prose wraps, and splitting at the wrap breaks the sentence. Treat a lone newline as a space and a blank line as a boundary.
  3. Provide an explicit flush(). End of stream, a tool announcement, and an error each force the buffer to be spoken. Without this, a response ending in a colon is never heard.
  4. Filter for the ear before speaking. Emphasis markers, inline code markers, headings, bullets, and link syntax are removed. A fenced code block is named rather than read.
  5. Resolve fenced blocks against the whole buffer, before splitting. A fence broken into separate lines can never match a fence pattern, and the orphaned markers get spoken aloud.
  6. Expand identifiers. camelCase, snake_case, and HTTPServer are read as separate words. Ordinary words are left alone.
  7. Speak parts that arrive whole. A final delivered to the renderer without preceding deltas is still spoken, and a part that streamed is not spoken twice. Provider nonstream mode alone does not prove that renderer path was exercised.
  8. Speak errors. An error that is displayed and not spoken does not exist for a listener.
  9. Record a transcript. Every filtered utterance entering the channel is recorded with its text and source before audio bypass or the Read aloud setting can suppress sound. Preserve text, thinking, tool-announcement and error origins. Tool results stay automatically silent.

The pause gate

The browser derives its automatic tool-dispatch pause from queued speech and actual human typing:

local_pause_cause = speaking OR human_typing
  1. One derived predicate, not three call sites. Compute the value, compare it against the previous value, and send only on an edge.
  2. A human-entered space counts as typing. Keep Chapter 12’s event provenance; programmatic input cannot become a human cause during a later speech callback.
  3. Automatic release requires both local causes clear. Explicit unpause from any tab still releases the Agent for everyone. Escape cancels speech regardless of input contents; human typing may still hold the local cause.

The blind persona

  1. Deny the DOM. The listener Agent has exactly hear, type, submit, wait, and sleep. No snapshot, click, file, shell or skill-lifecycle tools. Enforce the same boundary at dispatch, including guessed names.
  2. Bypass audio without bypassing processing. The blind peer opens the real GUI in transcript mode. It reads the same filtered entries that would enter the speech queue, without waiting for native synthesis.
  3. Drive the actual client. Typing and submission reach the real target; waiting observes its completion; hearing advances a transcript cursor. End the peer’s whole lifetime on EOF, including a pending sleep. Keep ordinary sleep working while the session is alive.

Yours

Which markdown constructs to filter beyond the required set. What to call a fenced block when you skip it. Whether the transcript is a ring buffer and how large. The wording of a tool announcement. Whether an error preempts the queue or joins the back of it.

Exercise

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 13

13.1 The idea in plain words

A fire alarm inspector who checks the panel will never discover that a speaker in the east stairwell is disconnected. The wiring diagram is correct, the current draw is nominal, the panel reports green. Finding that fault requires somebody to stand in the stairwell during a test and notice the silence.

A DOM observer has a similar blind spot. It can read the text it needs from gui_snapshot, complete a task, and report success without checking what reached speech. The earlier GUI work established useful visual behavior. It supplied no equivalent assurance about missing utterances or awkward phrase boundaries.

The instinct at this point is to give the observer better reporting. Add a tool that returns the speech queue, describe it well, and ask the agent to check it. That helps only if the returned data and the task make the missing behavior observable.
