Chapter 12’s confident phantom-panel report shows the danger of asking for a conclusion without supplying the state needed to support it.

The alternative is to remove the channel the observer has been leaning on. Take away the DOM, leave speech, and give it a task it cannot finish without listening. Now a defect in the speech channel is not a line in a report. It is a task that fails.

The principle generalizes beyond accessibility: test over data as close as possible to what the user actually receives. A DOM snapshot is not what a listener receives. It is a different signal, richer in some ways and poorer in others, and an observer consuming it can miss a failure that matters to someone listening.

13.2 The channel that reported on itself

This investigation started with a suspicion rather than a bug report. Bill, who listens to this agent for hours a day and had no way to audit the channel he was listening to, put it this way:

I’m worried the TTS feedback, available via the MCP tunnel, isn’t evaluated by any agent. It needs work.

The first-edition account records that concern before describing the investigation. Its findings explain why the listener is useful, even though this edition already carries forward several repairs.

In that implementation, four event paths met in the artifact renderer. Streaming deltas went in as they arrived, for both text and thinking. Tool dispatch announced itself. A part arriving complete flushed the buffer. Errors rendered to the screen.

Three of those four had defects. The fourth, error rendering, had no speech call at all: it built a div, set its text, appended it, scrolled, and returned. For a user who works by listening, the one message class that most needs to interrupt was the only class that made no sound.

The agent did have a tool for inspecting speech state. It was called tts_queue, and it read a variable named window._ttsQueue. The reported source inspection found reads of that name but no writer. The tool always fell through to its backup path, which returned either an empty array or a single synthetic entry whose text was the string (speaking).

That tool was declared ephemeral: "round", the MCP mechanism that injects a tool’s output into every round automatically. So the agent had been receiving speech telemetry continuously, and the telemetry had been contentless the entire time.

The older GUI-skill grader checked that this injection worked. It asserts that tts_queue output reaches the request context, which is a claim about the engine rather than about speech. A pipe that carries nothing is still a pipe. The check was green while the channel behind it was dead, which is a useful thing to know about green checks.

The historical pause gate had a related omission. The design specified:

paused = tts_speaking OR user_typing

Only the typing half was ever wired. Every pause and unpause message in the client came from a keystroke handler, and the client contained no reference to speech state at all. The Go side was correct, checking the gate before every tool dispatch. One of the mechanism’s two inputs had simply never been connected.

The speech module advertised pause integration in its opening comment:

// TTS — Text-to-speech for artifacts with Chrome wake-up and pause integration.

The historical source inspection found that comment and no other occurrence of pause in the file.

The repair makes the cause explicit in one place. Chapter 12’s accepted browser already does this, including the distinction between a person composing text and MCP filling the same field:

function pace() {
  const next = speaking || humanTyping;
  if (next !== localPaused) {
    localPaused = next;
    send({ type: next ? "pause" : "unpause" });
  }
}

Speech starting, speech ending, input and successful submission all update their cause and call this function. Comparing against the previous value makes automatic messages edge-triggered: more keystrokes do not create more pause messages while the cause remains true. An actual human space still counts as composing. Programmatic field contents remain programmatic when speech ends.

This is a local decision about when to send a command. The Agent has one pause gate, and an explicit unpause in another tab releases it. An unchanged cause in the first tab cannot immediately reinstate a private veto. The transition rule preserves both the listening pause and that deliberate override.

Escape now cancels speech even with text in the input field:

document.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {
  if (event.key === "Escape") speech.cancel();
});

Cancellation empties the speech queue and unfinished speech buffers. It does not erase the person’s typed text. The cause calculation then decides whether typing still requests a pause. Stopping the voice and releasing the Agent are different actions when the person is still composing.

13.3 A user who can only listen

Removal is the operative word. A prompt asking the listener to avoid the DOM leaves the capability available when the task becomes difficult. Build its Agent with only the five required tools and reject unknown operations at the peer as well. Inspect the consuming Agent’s declarations: a narrow peer attached to an ordinary skill-enabled coding Agent would still leave file and lifecycle capabilities beside it.

The accepted implementation uses a small optional application, gui/cmd/virtual-user, through the public Ensemble API. It creates the Ensemble root and an Agent without builtins or skills, then attaches a raw MCP transport to the browser peer. No second actor loop or core API is needed. The separate GUI module continues to own browser automation; the core remains independent of it.

Tool Arguments Effect
hear {} Returns new transcript entries with their source, advancing the cursor
type {"text":"..."} Replaces the actual chat input
submit {} Submits that input and records which turn to await
wait {} Waits for that submitted turn to end, then returns new transcript entries
sleep {"milliseconds":150} Waits the requested nonnegative finite duration

The peer privately operates the real page, but exposes no arbitrary selector, evaluation, click or snapshot operation to the model. Its process receives only the environment needed to launch the browser, without the model credential. The listener must obtain target information from returned speech entries rather than another view of the same answer.

Speech in this mode produces no audio. Opening the page with ?speech=transcript uses the real renderer and filters, records each utterance, and skips native synthesis. A long reasoning trace can therefore be inspected without waiting for every word to be spoken. This tests the text channel a synthesizer would receive; it does not make the observer capable of judging sound.

Keep navigation outside this exercise. The application owns its running commentary of thinking and response text; keyboard and screen-reader navigation remain separate concerns. One restricted listener is enough to test this channel. That scope decision does not claim that a transcript covers the application’s entire accessibility surface or that all low-vision and blind users need the same interface.

Closing the listener

A small client can still leak a lifetime. The student’s first peer closed its browser on stdin EOF but left a pending Node sleep timer alive. The Go client closed the transport, then waited for the peer before returning. Its model turn could finish while process cleanup continued waiting for a timer that no longer served a session.

The independent probe made the difference visible: idle EOF exited in 125 ms; EOF during a 4000 ms sleep took 3865 ms. The peer did eventually exit, so calling this a permanent hang would misdescribe the measurement. A longer requested sleep would make the same ownership error more expensive.

The correction shared the existing close-browser-and-exit handler between EOF and SIGTERM. On the corrected peer, the same pending-sleep probe exited in 127 ms; its idle control took 126 ms. Normal sleep still works while the session remains open. A separate real-client check covers a pending sleep whose job has returned an ordinary running callback before the model finishes. Ending the owned process ends its timers; no arbitrary sleep ceiling or new cancellation framework is needed. The paired receipts preserve both versions.

13.4 The run that succeeded for the wrong reason

The first-edition investigation gave the blind persona a task expected to fail.

Tool results do not enter the automatic speech channel. Only dispatch is announced, so a listener hears that a command is running and then hears nothing about what it did. The task was to run a command against a path that does not exist and report the exit code, and the prediction, written down before the run, was that the listener would come back empty.

It came back with the correct exit code.

Its retained account prints the explanation: six transcript entries, in this order. These are historical entries, not output produced by the corrected pipeline:

1. "run command"
2. "The command failed with exit code 1:"
3. "`"
4. "ls: /nonexistent-path-xyz: No such file or directory"
5. "`"
6. "This is expected since..."

Utterance 1 is the dispatch announcement. Utterances 2 through 6 are the model’s own prose, describing what happened. No tool result appears anywhere in the transcript. The listener learned the exit code because the model chose to mention it.

The observer reported its transcript accurately and drew the wrong conclusion from it, writing that no gap had been found. That conclusion was reasonable given what it could perceive, which is the whole problem. Without a source label, the words alone cannot show whether the exit code came from tool-result delivery or model narration. A listener receiving the right information cannot tell whether the system delivered it or the model happened to be chatty that turn.

Accessibility resting on a model’s prose habits is discoverability by luck. A terser response, a different system prompt, a model tuned to skip the summary, and the same task can yield silence with no warning and no error.

The scope ruling made the intended channel explicit. Tool results are not spoken automatically, by design: “I listen to your thinking, and that is enough.” Thinking and response text both feed the channel; the exit code arriving through prose is permitted behavior, not proof that raw tool output was spoken. The GUI still lets a person deliberately read an artifact through its speaker button.

That ruling also redirected the instrument. A blind persona that hunts for unspoken tool results is testing a decision rather than a defect. The transcript checks whether thinking and response text arrive completely and in order, with announcements and errors labeled separately. A person must still judge intelligibility.

Utterances 3 and 5 expose another defect: punctuation leaked into the channel.

13.5 A bug found by ear

Two of the historical entries were a single backtick. Punctuation had reached the synthesizer input instead of being removed by the speech filter.

The obvious explanation is streaming. Deltas arrive on arbitrary boundaries, a fenced code block gets split across two chunks, and each half is filtered separately, so neither half contains a complete fence and the markers survive. That explanation is clean, mechanical, and wrong.

A test disproved it. Feeding the entire fenced block as one chunk, with no split anywhere near it, still produced spoken backticks.

The real cause sat one layer earlier. Filtering ran per phrase, and phrases were produced by splitting the buffer on newlines. A fenced block contains newlines by construction, so by the time the filter saw anything, the fence had already been cut into separate lines. A pattern that needs an opening marker and a closing marker to match will never match a line containing exactly one of them. The filter examined three fragments, found no fences, and passed all three through.

The fix resolves fences against the whole buffer before any splitting happens. The filter then sees a complete block and replaces it with a name, and the listener hears “code block” where a wall of syntax used to be.

The account also records the listener’s objection to splitting on newlines. Prose wraps. A sentence broken across two source lines is one sentence, and splitting at the wrap produces two utterances with an unnatural pause between them. Speech engines work a phrase at a time, and every boundary the pipeline invents is a pause the listener hears.

So a lone newline became whitespace and a blank line stayed a boundary. A wrapped sentence is now spoken as one utterance, and paragraphs still separate.

A visual-content check does not establish correct speech segmentation. A DOM snapshot shows text that is present and correct. A screenshot shows a page that renders properly. A grader asserting on rendered content passes. The content is fine. The segmentation of the content is wrong, and segmentation determines where the voice can pause.

13.6 The bug nobody could hear

Listening is a better instrument than looking, for this channel. It is still not sufficient.

A part that arrives complete, with no deltas preceding it, was rendered to the screen and never queued for speech. The handler set the element’s content and called flush(), which empties a buffer that in this path is already empty.

In the historical implementation, disabling provider streaming reached that path. In this implementation, the Engine can synthesize display deltas even for a plain provider response. Switching off HTTP streaming does not prove that the renderer ever received a final without deltas.

The student’s first mutation check demonstrated the trap: removing whole-final speech still passed its nonstream test. The fix was in the test boundary. Preserve actual Agent finals but drop transient deltas at the external WebSocket boundary, then observe the real renderer and transcript. That reaches the missing branch; restoring the defect now loses the utterance. A separate check catches duplicate final speech.

A listener who expects a reply can notice silence. Silence alone cannot tell them which text was omitted or whether the model produced any. Compare the emitted final with the speech transcript as well as inspecting the feed sites; the expectation must come from a boundary outside the failing channel.

The naive repair introduces a worse bug. Queue the final part unconditionally and every streamed response gets spoken twice, once from its deltas and once from its final. The pipeline needs to know whether a given part already streamed.

The renderer already knows whether a card received deltas. The accepted implementation marks card.streamed on a delta and uses that fact when a final arrives:

if (!message.replay && ["text", "thinking"].includes(kind))
  speech.chunk(id, card.streamed ? "" : card.text, true, kind);

An empty final chunk still flushes the saved tail. A final without prior deltas supplies its complete text, and history replay remains silent. The speech buffer holds unfinished text by part identity, with a back-pointer to its owning Speech queue. It cannot join the tail of a thinking part to a response merely because they arrived nearby.

13.7 Why a daily listener was not enough

The first-edition account describes a daily listener who depended on the channel but raised a suspicion rather than a list of its defects. That is a reason to build a better instrument, not a reason to doubt the listener.

Missing errors and missing finals produce no corresponding utterance to inspect. A pause input that never engages may show up only as a tool starting too soon. Empty telemetry needs an independent check that the queue was actually empty. Audible defects can be difficult to attribute too: an odd pause may come from segmentation, network timing or the voice itself. The retained account does not measure how quickly people adapt to these defects, and the chapter need not invent that explanation to show why a second observation point helps.

Preserve the distinction between guidance and evidence during a supervised run. Supplying the task, identifying a stale binary or freeing a port makes the experiment possible. Supplying a missing selector or the expected answer changes what success demonstrates. Chapter 12’s historical corrections are a reminder to record human and source-inspection assistance rather than retroactively calling every finding autonomous.

13.8 What a program cannot verify

A grader for this chapter can check a great deal. Whether a word survives being split across three fragments. Whether a wrapped sentence produces one utterance. Whether any markup marker reaches the channel. Whether a part that arrived whole was spoken, and whether a part that streamed was spoken twice. Whether the pause gate releases only when both of its causes are clear.

Those observations need different boundaries. Filtered text and its source belong in the transcript. Queue progress and pause transitions belong to the real application around it. The executable grading harness drives that application with an external provider and speech synthesizer fake; it does not discover and load arbitrary JavaScript modules or replace the Agent and renderer.

Native browser callbacks supply separate evidence that the actual synthesizer started and ended utterances. Chapter 12’s cause-based pause controls still apply with native speech here, including human whitespace, programmatic input, explicit other-tab unpause and actual subsequent submission. The extra control tab closes before the single-tab speech sequence; this does not settle the earlier unexplained two-tab queue stall.

What those checks do not establish is how any of it sounds.

Pronunciation needs a listener. Whether HTTP Server is clearer than an unexpanded identifier is a judgment about ears. Prosody and comfort at a chosen rate vary with the listener and voice. A browser’s accepted rate value is not a measured words-per-minute rate, and this chapter has no retained measurement supporting the original fixed browser-speed ceiling or dedicated-engine comparison.

The boundary deserves to be stated plainly in the chapter that builds the instrument. These checks verify that the intended text reaches the speech channel at the intended boundaries and that measured state transitions occur. A human decides whether the result is worth listening to.

13.9 Exercise, graded

Build both deliverables: the speech pipeline on the existing GUI path and the restricted public listener application. Keep filtering with the unfinished-text buffer and its actual Speech owner. Reuse the native queue, renderer identities, Agent and MCP transport. A separate transcript algorithm that produces the right fixture text while the GUI still speaks broken fragments does not satisfy the exercise.

Provide an executable tts-harness.sh at the core solution root, or scripts/tts-harness.sh. A normal invocation receives a prompt as its first argument, optionally followed by --type-during-turn TEXT. The grading process supplies:

Input Meaning
LLM_BASE_URL The local external provider to exercise
WORKSPACE The prepared workspace; file fixtures use absolute paths rather than assuming this changes the GUI process directory
TTS_LOG Destination for observed JSON-lines speech and gate records
STREAMING=off Request plain provider delivery; otherwise stream

The supplied implementation’s root script launches gui/tts-harness.mjs. It uses the real GUI, Agent, provider parser, renderer and speech pipeline in a browser. Only the external provider and asynchronous synthesizer are fakes. Install the GUI module’s optional Node dependencies and a usable Chromium browser before running it. No paid provider is needed for grading.

The optional description invocation is:

./tts-harness.sh --describe

The supplied harness returns:

{"read_file_tool":"read_file","read_file_arg":"path","supports_type_during_turn":true,"supports_streaming_off":true,"log_format":"jsonl"}

This describes public capabilities; it does not prescribe a JavaScript class or module filename. The actual prompt run writes JSON lines to TTS_LOG, with numeric ms and seq, kind: "utterance" and the actual filtered text, plus its source. Gate records use kind: "pause" or kind: "resume" with the observed cause, including typing where applicable. Record real events; do not construct the expected sequence independently of the running page. Finish and clean up owned children on every path. The grader bounds a harness run at 90 seconds and can terminate its process group.

From the repository root:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 13

The default is solutions/ch13; a positional argument selects your core directory and the existing -gui option selects its optional GUI module if necessary. The revised rubric preserves the actual original grader’s weights, which differed from its printed chapter table:

Check Points Observation
tts-discrimination 20 Successful file results stay automatically silent; distinct model answers are spoken
tts-filters-markup 20 Required markup is removed and a fence is named
tts-buffers-fragments 10 Words survive fragment boundaries
tts-speaks-unstreamed 15 Plain provider output is spoken exactly once
tts-gate-both-causes 10 Typing pause and subsequent release are observed in order
tts-speaks-errors 10 The actual error reaches speech
tts-boundaries 5 Wrap, paragraph and trailing-tail boundaries remain meaningful
tts-expands-identifiers 5 Identifiers expand; ordinary capitalization survives
Corrected Chapter 12 parity 5 Prior obligations remain intact

The transcript grader does not independently establish every clause in the TL;DR. The final-only renderer branch needs its direct delivery check because a nonstream provider can still produce synthetic deltas. The numeric gate check observes ordered typing pause and release; those edges alone do not prove human whitespace or both orders of overlapping speech and typing. Keep the actual browser controls for those causes. The actual listener’s five-tool boundary, dispatch refusal, hearing cursor, submission and pending-sleep shutdown need their public-client/browser evidence. Native audio and human listening remain separate again. Keep those obligations visible rather than claiming a numeric speech score proves them all.

The original student run scored 95/100 FAIL: all new speech checks passed 95/95 and inherited parity failed 0/5 on the invalid earlier skill fixture. That build preceded the finished blind client and later cleanup correction. Its score is historical evidence, not a final-source pass.

A stronger check later exposed a gap inside that speech score. The old fixture requested notes.txt, but the harness launched the GUI in a different directory from its prepared workspace. The actual file read failed. Silence could not prove suppression of file contents that had never arrived. Using the planted file’s absolute path exercises the existing reader successfully; compare that correlated result with the transcript before claiming that its bytes stayed silent. An absence check needs something real to exclude.

The historical fence investigation ran the example whole and fragmented. Keep that distinction when checking your buffer: an intact fence that fails proves a different cause from a split token. Preserve line structure until filters that need it have run. An early grader review found the same mistake in bullets: flattening a single newline first let the second line’s bullet escape an anchored filter. A normal two-item list is enough to expose it; no new markup language is required.

13.10 Taking it for a spin

Work in a scratch copy of your solution so the target save and listener history do not join an earlier experiment. From the core directory, install the optional driver dependencies and build both actual applications:

(cd gui && npm ci)
(cd gui && npx playwright install chromium)
(cd gui && go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch13-gui ./cmd)
(cd gui && go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch13-listener ./cmd/virtual-user)

The listener supports --browser /path/to/chromium if you already have a browser. Configure the target’s provider through the existing environment. To keep the target focused on prose instead of loading tools, create skills/listener-target/SKILL.md:

---
name: listener-target
type: primary
description: Brief answers for the speech listener exercise
---
Answer briefly in two sentences. No tools are needed.

Start the target GUI from the core directory, leaving its terminal open:

EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=listener-target /tmp/ensemble-ch13-gui \
  --skills-dir ./skills --gui-dir gui/web/gui --port 8088

In another terminal, configure the listener’s own provider environment and run from the same core directory:

/tmp/ensemble-ch13-listener --agent-url http://localhost:8088 \
  --persona blind --peer gui/virtual-user.mjs \
  --task 'Ask the target to explain queueChunk, max_tool_rounds and HTTPServer in two short sentences using inline code markup, and to choose one fruit to mention. Then report exactly the spoken transcript, including its chosen fruit. Use only the five available tools.'

The peer opens a quiet transcript-mode tab itself. Close other talking tabs when isolating this channel. The supported persona here is blind; there is no required sighted mode to invoke for comparison. The listener writes its actual history to virtual-user.jsonl and reports what hear or wait returned. Keep that result beside the target’s speech entries, because the model can add Markdown when quoting a transcript even though no Markdown entered target speech.

The retained October 10, 2026 sessions used claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-4o-mini and gemini-3.8-flash. They are recorded model identities, not current catalog recommendations. All three listener processes exited zero and used the restricted interface to type, submit and receive the target’s real transcript. The live receipts retain their earlier-source provenance.

The filtered entries contain queue Chunk, max tool rounds and HTTP Server, with no inline backticks. Claude’s listener received two response entries, but its target never chose the requested fruit; it said “fruit-sized” instead. The listener reported that omission. GPT-4o mini’s listener heard the chosen apple in three response sentences rather than the requested two. Gemini’s eleven entries include both thinking and response sources, followed by a report of the apple. These are useful channel results with different target-content limits, not three claims that every instruction was followed.

No human listened to judge these runs. Transcript mode bypassed native audio. The separate native-browser checks exercised real speech callbacks and pause, and the later peer-lifetime correction has its own deterministic evidence. Neither was a final-source paid repeat. After checking the words and their sources, turn ordinary audio back on and listen: the question of whether this voice and phrasing are usable for you remains yours to answer.

Chapter 14: The World’s Best Context Engineering, Before Breakfast

This may be the most important chapter in the book.

If you’ve ever started a new chat because your agent seemed confused, well, that’s yesterday’s context engineering. I did it myself, several times, on the day I designed this chapter. As of September 2026, what follows is tomorrow’s. The book is evergreen, so I hope it always has modern advice.

The design had been in my head for a couple of months. On a Tuesday morning I typed it out for about twenty minutes while CodeRhapsody turned it into a design record and checked it against the code. Then I took a shower. The first commit landed at 7:42, before breakfast, and frankly it felt good to get it out.

This is how long-running actors should work: what the actor knows, organized by section at several levels of detail, with the most critical parts kept longest, instead of some lame summary of the first half of the context.

A long session with a coding agent can degrade in a familiar way. The answers get vaguer. The agent re-reads a file it read an hour ago, then forgets a decision made before lunch. A fresh chat helps because a human decides what to carry over. This chapter moves tool-traffic cleanup inside the agent and records every cut as an event, so nothing leaves the window without a record of what removed it.

TL;DR

Tool bytes gain a removal policy. Every entry gets a kind that says which verb removes it. Tool bytes fall off a ladder of recorded redaction events. On a model configured for stubbing, each round trip’s results are stubbed unless the model keeps them. The actor can checkpoint with micro_handoff. Loaded skills survive as entries instead of as tool results. The system prompt stays frozen. The log reaches disk as it grows, so a process crash can recover the journaled work.

The shared entry vocabulary gains four kinds. These definitions belong in internal/common; reduction belongs in History, not on common-package structs:

// EntryKind identifies what removes an entry. Survivors never contain tool parts.
type EntryKind uint8

const (
    KindDialogue EntryKind = iota + 1
    KindHandoff
    KindSkill
    KindTools
)

// MicroHandoffData records the checkpoint text that survives its tool call.
type MicroHandoffData struct {
    Text string `json:"text"`
}

Each context entry carries its kind alongside sequence, actor and parts. Reuse the existing skill body and redaction payloads. Add micro_handoff and tools_changed facts; the latter carries full added declarations and removed names. A tool_decls part holds that delta without becoming a call or result.

  1. Frozen prefix. The system prompt is byte-identical on every request of a session. Only a refreshed Agent changes it. Startup tool declarations stay frozen too on a model that can carry tool changes in the dialog; other models re-declare when tools change, as rule 2 describes.
  2. Tools arrive through the dialog. A skill load, a skill unload, or an MCP connect mid-session emits ToolsChanged, and the reducer turns it into a Tools entry. On a model whose features row sets InlineTools, that entry carries the declarations in the dialog. The tool_decls part is neither a call nor a result, so rule 3 still holds. The renderer places inline declarations after the complete user/tool-result/ephemeral turn. A model without InlineTools folds every delta into the startup set and re-declares, changing the prefix.
  3. Survivors carry no tool parts. A Handoff, Skill or Tools entry never holds a tool call or a tool result, so no tool clearing can touch it.
  4. Skills are entries. The reducer turns SkillLoaded into a Skill entry holding the rendered body. The load_skill tool result is an acknowledgement only. Replay uses the recorded body, without rereading the file. unload_skill removes grants no other active skill supplies and stops its servers, but leaves the Skill entry where it is: deleting old bytes would change the prefix. A later chapter’s verb removes it.
  5. micro_handoff is three records: the tool call, an ordinary result, then a MicroHandoff event. Its reducer waits until the batch’s last result has arrived, so a call made alongside micro_handoff is cleared with it, even if it has not started yet in the serial dispatcher. Then it removes every tool call and tool result part, opaque reasoning and private replay signatures from the context, including signatures attached to visible text. It preserves visible dialogue and the event log, drops entries left empty, and appends one Handoff entry. The text appears in the next request exactly once, and no call is ever left without its result or a result without its call. The tool takes {"text":"..."}.
  6. Keep or stub, per round trip. On a model whose features row sets StubsToolResults, every tool result above the stub threshold is replaced by a stub in the request after the one that carried it, unless the actor’s next message calls keep_tool_results({}), which keeps that whole batch. Called alongside other tools, it keeps the previous batch, not the one it rides in, and its own result is never stubbed. The call survives either way. The stub is an ordinary RedactResult event, so replay reproduces it. Other models get no per-round-trip stubbing; the ladder alone applies.
  7. The ladder records a Seq. With target size T, whole tool traffic has a T/8 budget. Older results become stubs (RedactResult) and their calls stay, for a T/16 budget of calls and stubs. Older tool traffic goes entirely (RedactTool). A band is cut in steps: when it passes twice its budget, one event cuts an old prefix back toward its budget. Cut only completed batches the model has already seen. Each event stores To as a number, never as “the watermark”, so a later settings change cannot rewrite the past.
  8. The reducer is total over known events. A save file that does not parse is still refused (Chapter 10). A familiar event that parses but cannot be applied, such as a malformed payload or a redaction naming an entry already gone, is skipped with a diagnostic and loading continues. Validate before mutation; unknown event types and invalid sequence ordering remain errors.
  9. Crash-safe. Events reach the journal before publication, so a process crash leaves a tail after Chapter 10’s as_of anchor. Recovery loads the snapshot, its tail and the journal. A normal shutdown snapshots. Write the new snapshot before truncating the journal, never truncate past the anchor, and keep one backup of the previous snapshot. Power loss is out of scope; the log is never fsynced.
  10. One knob. The Context Management settings tab sets context_target: T in bytes, 0 for the default of 400,000, clamped to at least 20,000. The stub threshold is T/100 and the bands are rule 7’s, so the default gives 4,000, 50,000 and 25,000. The tab’s other setting, log_retention, is the number of events kept in the saved log, 0 for all. Store settings at the owning Agent’s path and preserve unsent browser edits when a settings snapshot arrives.

The model-feature matrix is part of the exercise:

Row InlineTools StubsToolResults
claude-opus-5-course true true
claude-sonnet-5-course false false
All existing real-model rows false false

The course rows are deterministic fixtures. Keep both new flags false on existing real-model rows. Dialogue and survivors remain outside the tool budgets; this chapter does not yet bound the whole window.

For live Anthropic use, choose an older supported model such as Sonnet-5. Bill reports that 5.5 models do not work with ephemeral context and has excluded them from supported use. Historical 5.5 runs below retain their actual names; they are not reader model choices.

Yours: the on-disk layout of the journal, what a diagnostic says, and the settings tab’s appearance.

Exercise. Start from your Chapter 13 agent. Add context management until the following command, run from the repository root, scores 100/100:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 14

The default core is solutions/ch14; a positional core directory and existing -gui option select another implementation. Section 14.14 gives the actual launch, settings and eight-check contract.

§14.1 In Plain Words

The context window is not storage. The log is storage: Chapter 2 made it append-only, recording what the agent saw or said. The window is a working set rendered from that log, sent again on every request. Every byte has to answer three questions: why is it here, who put it here, and what removes it. A byte that cannot answer the third question stays forever, and a window full of such bytes can crowd out the work a person wanted the agent to remember.

Most of the bytes in Chapter 2’s measured sessions were tool bytes: results were about 42 percent of conversation history by volume, and call arguments another 30 percent. Nearly all of those bytes are needed once. The agent reads a file, decides, edits; after that, the file’s contents are recoverable from disk and the decision lives in what the agent said about it. Hence the chapter’s rule: keep the words, let the bytes go. Dialogue stays. Tool results go first, then the calls that produced them, oldest first.

Some things must never go with them. A loaded skill’s instructions and the note an agent writes to its future self at a checkpoint look like tool traffic today, because they arrive through tools. If they stay tool traffic, the first cleanup deletes the manual and keeps the tools it explains. Anything that must survive becomes its own kind of entry, removed only by its own verb. Survivors are safe by construction.

Every cut is an event in the log with an exact number in it; nothing is re-evaluated later. That is what keeps Chapter 10’s promise: replaying the log reproduces the same window, byte for byte, even after the settings that chose the cuts have changed.

Two laws decide where cuts may happen. The front of the request, the system prompt and, on an inline-capable model, the startup tools, is frozen so a prefix cache can keep serving it. Changing a byte near the front invalidates more of that prefix than changing one near the end. So cuts come in steps, not a trickle: one larger cut now and then invalidates that region less often than a small one every turn.

The redaction levels are Chapter 2’s, the frozen prompt is Chapter 9’s, the snapshot and replay are Chapter 10’s. What was missing is the policy that decides when to use them, and kinds for the entries that must survive.

§14.2 Why Is This Byte Here?

Chapter 2 built the machinery for this chapter before it had a cleanup policy to call it. RedactData has four levels. RedactResult turns a tool result into a stub and keeps the call. RedactTool removes both and keeps the reasoning around them. RedactDialogue and RedactSummary reach into the conversation itself. The first edition left a comment at that boundary:

case RedactDialogue:
        // Prose and reasoning go. Survivors are defined by the compaction
        // policy, which is a later chapter's problem.

This chapter supplies the tool-traffic policy. Dialogue removal remains a later exercise. Context engineering, as the book uses the term, is managing every byte in the context data structure as well as today’s models allow. The management is a policy: for each byte, a reason it is in the window, a record of what put it there, and a verb that takes it out.

Walk a request from a Chapter 13 agent after an hour of work and ask each byte the three questions. The system prompt answers all three: the agent’s constitution, written at startup, removed by nothing. A user prompt answers them. A 9,000-byte file read forty minutes ago answers the first question with “the agent needed it once”, the second with read_file, and the third with silence. Nothing removes it. It rides along on every request until the session ends or a human copies the good parts into a fresh chat.

The fix is that silence. Give the old tool traffic a remover.

§14.3 Two Laws

The vendor’s prompt cache decides where a cut may happen. Under prefix caching, everything after the first changed position loses its match. This describes reuse, not a bill: bytes are not tokens, and the provider must actually grant caching for the stable prefix to save money.

Law 1: the prefix is frozen. The system prompt and, on an inline-capable model, the startup tool declarations are byte-identical on every request of a session. Chapter 9 already made the system prompt a constitution and put dynamic skills in the dialog. It left one leak: a skill that brings tools changed the tool list, and the tool list is the first thing in the request. Loading one skill could invalidate reuse from the tool array onward.

The chapter closes the leak with an event. A skill load, a skill unload, or an MCP server connecting mid-session emits ToolsChanged, a delta of declarations added and names removed. The reducer turns it into a Tools entry at the tail of the context, where it preserves the earlier declaration prefix. On a model whose features row sets InlineTools, the renderer sends that entry as a mid-conversation system message:

{"role": "system",
 "content": [{"type": "tool_addition",
              "tool": {"type": "tool_definition",
                       "definition": {"name": "gui_click",
                                      "description": "Click a matching element",
                                      "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                                                       "properties": {"selector": {"type": "string"}},
                                                       "required": ["selector"]}}}}]}

The course renderer sends the header inline-tools-2026-09-15. A removal uses a tool_removal block containing {"type":"tool_reference","name":"gui_click"} under tool. These dated wire shapes belong to the course fixture; the exercise does not enable them on live models. A model without the feature gets the old behaviour: the renderer folds every delta into the startup set and re-declares, changing the prefix.

The declaration’s position matters as much as its bytes. During the student run, a new MCP declaration followed a tool result, then automatic ephemera added another user message after it. The roles became:

user, assistant, user, system, user

The initial fake accepted that request, and prefix and replay comparisons passed. A faithful placement check rejected it: the contentful system message belongs after the complete user turn. The corrected renderer holds declaration blocks until the assistant boundary or request end, after tool results and automatic context:

user, assistant, user, system

The fix changes only the disposable wire view. The log keeps its chronology, and ephemera remain user content. Equal replay bytes are useful only after the request itself is valid.

The prefix does change on purpose once in a while. New defining instructions require a refreshed Agent. Changing context_target leaves the instructions and already recorded cuts alone.

Law 2: the cost of changing a byte grows with its distance from the end. Everything after the changed position loses its prefix match. Stubbing the result that arrived on the last round trip changes bytes near the tail. Stubbing a result a hundred thousand bytes back invalidates a hundred thousand bytes of later content.

The design record preserves a useful failed prediction: stubbing every tool result one round trip after it arrived would wreck the cache, since the request changes on every trip. The first session run that way, on CodeRhapsody with Opus 5.5 on 2026-09-22, reported a cumulative cache hit rate of 77 percent, after a cold first request that missed on over 100,000 tokens. The prediction had the law backwards: a just-finished result sits at the tail, where less later content loses its prefix match. The cumulative figure also hides the steady state, because that one cold miss is averaged into every later request, which is why a display of cache rate should show the last request beside the total.

Law 2 has a second consequence. A trickle of small cuts deep in the window breaks that prefix match on every turn; one larger cut now and then breaks it once. The agent cuts in steps.

§14.4 What Survives Is Never a Tool Call

The Chapter 13 agent returns a loaded skill’s manual as the result of the tool that loaded it. The first edition wrote it this way:

result += "## Instructions\n\n" + body

The arrangement becomes a bug the moment cleanup can discard that result. Tool results are the first bytes to go. The first time the ladder stubs old results, the manual becomes a one-line stub and the tools it explains stay declared. The agent keeps calling gui_click with no memory of the rules for calling it. A checkpoint note passed as a tool-call argument has the same defect one level later, because RedactTool deletes calls.

The cure is a naming rule, printed in the code as the comment on EntryKind: anything that must outlive tool clearing is its own kind.

Kind Created by Holds
KindDialogue prompts, hints, model output text, reasoning, tool calls and results
KindHandoff MicroHandoff the actor’s checkpoint note
KindSkill SkillLoaded a skill’s body
KindTools ToolsChanged a declaration delta

Tool clearing only ever touches tool parts, and tool parts only ever live in Dialogue entries. The other three kinds hold none, so tool-part clearing cannot remove their contents. Survivors are safe by construction, without a list of exceptions for the ladder to consult. load_skill still returns a result, a one-line acknowledgement that the skill loaded; the body arrives through its own recorded skill_loaded fact.

One timing problem remains even though dispatch is serial. The model can return several calls together; after the first runs, others from the same reply are still outstanding. A micro_handoff issued beside a read_file clears every tool part in the context. If it landed immediately, the read_file result would arrive afterwards with its call already gone, and a result without its call is a request the vendor refuses. So the reducer holds survivors until the batch completes:

// Holding survivors preserves call/result pairing even under serial dispatch:
// another call from this same model reply may still be waiting to start.
func survivor(c *common.Context, entry common.Entry) {
    if !toolsComplete(c.Dialogue) {
        c.Held = append(c.Held, entry)
        return
    }
    land(c, entry)
}

When the last result of the batch arrives, the held entries land in order. The payoff: nothing is outstanding when the handoff clears tool parts, so every call removed takes its result with it, and no result loses its call.

Unloading changes executable capability immediately. The registry drops grants that no other active skill supplies and stops the skill’s external servers. The next recorded declaration delta makes the model’s view agree with dispatch. Its instruction entry remains: removal of old instruction text is a different operation, deferred beyond this chapter. Lifecycle and checkpoint tools stay available, and a shared grant survives while another active skill owns it.

This advances the pending-unload policy from Chapter 9: compiled grants now disappear too. A stale manual cannot make a removed tool callable; guessed names still fail dispatch.

§14.5 The Layout

With four kinds and two laws, the request has one shape:

[ frozen prefix   ]  system prompt; startup tools on inline-capable rows
[ memory region   ]  empty until the agent has memories
[ context         ]  dialogue and survivors, with recorded Seq identities
                     ^ oldest                  newest ^
                     cheap to keep            cheap to change

The order runs from least volatile to most, which is also the order of meaning: who the agent is, then what it knows, then what it is doing. Two independent arguments, one about cache economics and one about reading order, give the same layout, which is a good sign that the layout is right.

A survivor keeps the sequence identity of its recorded fact. If a tool batch is incomplete, the reducer holds it and appends it only after the companion results arrive, even when those results have later sequence numbers. That batch-completion placement preserves call/result pairing. Moving the survivor up next to the prefix would edit bytes far from the end. Reordering is a verb of its own.

The kinds also preserve why an entry belongs in context. The system prompt and a skill body are instruction: the agent is meant to follow them. A tool result is data: the agent reads it and decides. A dialogue entry is conversation. Keeping those apart is why Kind records the origin of an entry instead of guessing it from the text, because text that looks like instructions and arrived as a file’s contents is still a file’s contents.

§14.6 Visible Reasoning Is the Storage Format of the Self

After the ladder runs, what does the agent remember about a file it read an hour ago? Exactly what it said about the file. The result is a stub and the call may be gone. The words the agent wrote in the dialogue remain a readable account through tool clearing. Ordinary tool redaction also preserves opaque provider parts under their replay restrictions. A micro_handoff additionally clears that private replay material and its signatures while keeping visible text. Chapter 2 wrote the rule into the definition of RedactTool: remove calls and results entirely, keep visible reasoning.

So an agent that narrates keeps its past, and an agent that works in silence loses it. Compare two turns that make the same edit:

(silent)   read_file config.go   edit_file config.go

(narrated) The port is set in config.go; reading it.   read_file config.go
           Port is 8092 at line 40, hardcoded. Moving it to settings.
           edit_file config.go

Once both tool bands clear that turn, the silent version may retain no explanation of the edit. The narrated version still says which port, where it was, and why it moved. A system prompt should ask for one sentence of intent before every tool call, and the ladder turns that habit from courtesy into storage.

Narration has a failure mode of its own. An agent rereading its old sentences can trust a figure it wrote down over the file that has since changed, and a figure written from memory carries the same confidence as one copied from the source. The defence is in what the narration records: where a fact lives, the path and line and command, so the agent’s reflex is to re-read the source rather than quote itself.

§14.7 The Ladder

The ladder keeps tool bytes in two bands measured back from the tail, with one number, the target size T, setting both:

    stub threshold = T/100    results band = T/8    calls band = T/16

The Agent reads T from its owned configuration. Its policy measures serialized tool parts, excluding ordinary dialogue and survivor bodies. The newest T/8 bytes of tool traffic stay whole. Older results become stubs by RedactResult, and their calls stay, for the next T/16 bytes. Tool bytes older than both bands go entirely by RedactTool, leaving the dialogue around them. At the default T of 400,000 bytes, the stub threshold is 4,000 bytes, the results band is 50,000 and the calls band 25,000.

Law 2 sets the rhythm. A band is cut when it reaches twice its budget, and one event cuts it back to its budget, so cuts arrive as occasional steps. The two doubled budgets sum to 3T/8. That arithmetic describes the eligible tool bands, not a hard maximum for the whole request. A newly presented large result must survive once, whole batches constrain cut boundaries, and dialogue and survivors have no budget here.

Three rules keep the ladder honest.

  • Every cut is an event. The Agent runs policy before rendering and records redacted facts through its existing append path. History alone changes the projection; Engine renders it. Its To field is a number, a Seq in the log. The watermark is computed once, at the moment of the cut, and never again. Replay applies the recorded number, so lowering T tomorrow cannot reach back and cut yesterday’s session differently.
  • Nothing is cut before the model has seen it. A result goes out whole at least once, however large. The ladder only reaches entries already sent.
  • No call loses its result. The calls-band cut snaps back to a point where every call removed takes its result with it.

The ladder applies to every model, because it needs no judgement from the model. It is also blunt: a 40,000-byte file read that the agent will never look at again stays whole until the band passes it.

§14.8 Keep or Stub

A capable model can do better than the ladder, because it knows which results it is finished with. On a model whose features row sets StubsToolResults, every tool result above the stub threshold becomes a stub in the request after the one that carried it, unless the actor’s next message calls keep_tool_results. The keep takes no arguments and keeps the whole batch.

The keep governs the batch that has already arrived, the one the actor is looking at. Called alongside other tools, it keeps the previous batch, never the one it rides in, since those results do not exist yet when the actor decides. Its own result is never stubbed. The call survives either way, so the agent can see what it asked for and re-run it. The stub is an ordinary RedactResult event, so replay reproduces it without asking the model again.

Law 2 prices this well. The stub replaces bytes that arrived one round trip ago, at the tail, which is the cheapest place in the window to change anything. The 77 percent in §14.3 was measured under this rule: CodeRhapsody, the agent that co-wrote this book, runs it with its own thresholds.

The feature is a column in the model table because deciding which results to discard is a model’s judgement. Whether it chooses well depends on the work it can still do and the rereads it needs. The course Opus row lets the grader exercise keep-or-stub; real rows use the ladder alone.

Open risk. Per-round-trip stubbing may interfere with the model’s thinking: a model reasoning across several round trips has its evidence removed between steps. The retained experiments did not measure that effect on reasoning quality. A useful comparison would hold the task and model fixed, run with stubbing on and off, and assess the work rather than bytes.

§14.9 From compress_context to micro_handoff

The ladder removes bytes the agent is done with. It gives the agent no way to say what it needs in order to keep going. A checkpoint does, and the book’s own lineage tried two designs for it before this one.

CodeRhapsody’s first design was a tool called compress_context: the model chose a range of messages and replaced them with its own summary. Bill described how that went on 2026-09-13:

“compress_context was the old system that you (Claude) did pretty well, picking a range of messages to summarize, but freaking Gemini almost always deleted 80% of messages, starting with message 1, with a terrible summary, lobotomizing the LLM, so we switched to handoffs instead.”

The failure has a shape. The cut ran by position, from message 1, and message 1 is where the user stated the goal. The summary was written by the model that was about to lose the originals, so nothing could check it, and summarized dialogue is in no file the agent can re-read. In those trials, the model was handed a choice it could not undo and kept making it badly.

The handoffs that replaced it, handoff_task, wrote a structured document and started a fresh instance from it with an empty window. That design assumes continuity lives in a note to a stranger. It also added a second path for writing the agent’s durable state, and second paths drift: CodeRhapsody’s handoff path never triggered the memory cascade that its save_memory path did, and the gap sat in its notes as a known bug for months. Ensemble builds neither tool.

micro_handoff keeps the same instance and visible dialogue. The actor writes a note; after the complete tool batch, the reducer removes calls, results, opaque reasoning and private replay signatures, including signatures attached to visible text, then appends the note as a Handoff entry. The event log preserves the original records; this clears the working context. Two lessons from the older designs are built in. The model’s discretion covers tool bytes that can often be regained by re-reading their sources; the dialogue, which cannot, stays. And the note travels with the same conversation, instead of becoming a stranger’s only account of it. micro_handoff is available on every model row.

In the log it is three records: the tool call, an ordinary result that acknowledges it, and a MicroHandoff event carrying the text. The event is what the reducer acts on. The result is an acknowledgement for the same reason load_skill’s is: a tool result is tool traffic, and the note must outlive tool traffic. Replay sees the event and makes the same cut.

What goes in the note decides whether the checkpoint works. The version CodeRhapsody uses asks for fields, and its tool description is blunt about which one matters. Of tried_and_failed, it says: “Highest value per byte in the document: it is the only field that prevents repeating a mistake, and errors are the part of a record most likely to be discarded as noise.” It also says when to call the tool: “at a completed micro-goal, never at a token threshold.” A checkpoint taken mid-task drops the tool result that held the task’s state. The note has to say what the agent worked out and which failed approaches it should avoid repeating.

§14.10 Compaction Is Described, Never Performed

No policy code edits context directly. The policy decides a cut and records it as an event; the reducer applies events; the log keeps them. While the full log is retained, every window the agent has sent can be rebuilt, including windows the current settings would cut differently. The grader’s ladder-is-recorded check does exactly that: it replays a session under a changed T and expects the same requests.

A retained log can contain a known event the current reducer cannot apply: a redaction naming an entry a later handoff removed, a payload a newer version malformed. Previously, one bad event made a whole session unloadable. History now reports and moves on:

func (h *history) replay(e common.Event) {
    if err := validateFor(&h.context, e); err != nil {
        h.parent.Ensemble().Logf("restore: skipped event %d: %v", e.Seq, err)
        return
    }
    apply(&h.context, e)
}

The skip is clean because validation checks an event before it mutates anything, so a rejected event leaves the context exactly as it was. Totality covers known event types. An event type the code has never heard of is still refused at load, loudly, because a log from a newer agent is a different problem than a bad record in a familiar one.

The original design also considered provider-side context editing. Its dated API documentation described a server editing the input while the client kept its full history. That can coexist with a local log, but it moves the decision about what the model reads outside this reducer. Here, the chapter needs a recorded keep decision and reproducible local projection, so the existing event path owns the cut.

§14.11 Keep the Words, Let the Bytes Go

A stub removes bytes from the window. It removes nothing from the log. The ToolReturned event that carried the result stays in the log until log retention truncates it, and in the common case the bytes were never unique anyway: the file is still on disk. Re-read the source when it is needed again; a changed file or a command with side effects may of course give a different result.

The stub carries no address. The reason is a bug in the agent that co-wrote this book. CodeRhapsody’s stubs cite the output file of the command they replace, a path like cr/io/26. When this chapter was designed, its handle counter started again at 1 on every launch, so after a restart cr/io/26 named a different command’s output. The agent that followed the stub read a file, got plausible output, and had no way to tell it was the wrong one. Chapter 12’s rule applies: wrong data is worse than no data. The first edition records the fix: CodeRhapsody’s counter kept counting across restarts. Ensemble’s stubs say the bytes are gone and leave recovery to the tools that produced them.

§14.12 Crash-Safe Persistence

Chapter 10 saved at shutdown. A process that dies mid-session loses everything since the last save, including work whose results have already reached the model.

The current Agent appends each accepted event to a journal beside the save file, <save>.journal, one JSON line per event, as the event happens. Recovery is Chapter 10’s load with one more source: Recover reads the snapshot, applies the tail after its as_of anchor, then applies the journal. A normal shutdown writes a new snapshot and resets the journal. The grader’s crash-recovery check runs a clean session, then runs a second for two turns and kills it with SIGKILL, restarts it, and checks that journaled work survives the restart.

Two orderings are load-bearing, and neither is commutative. The new snapshot is written before the log is truncated: in the other order, a crash between the two steps leaves neither the old events nor the new snapshot. And the log is never truncated past the snapshot’s anchor, because the anchor is where replay starts. log_retention is a saved-history preference; the anchor is a correctness boundary, and the anchor wins. History installs its checkpoint in that order and keeps the previous save at <save>.bak, using the Agent’s selected save path.

Two things are out of scope. The journal is never fsynced, so power loss can take the last few events; “crash” means a process crash. And truncation deletes old ToolReturned events, which are the only on-disk copy of a redacted text result. The snapshot can still restore the current window, but retention may make older windows and raw results unavailable. Zero retention keeps the full saved log; it does not promise bounded disk growth.

§14.13 One Knob

The tool budgets run off one setting. The Context Management tab in the settings panel writes context_target: T in bytes, 0 for the default of 400,000, clamped to at least 20,000. The original budget comment explains its floor: below it, “the stub threshold would fall under the size of a directory listing”. The tab’s other field, log_retention, is the number of events the saved log keeps, 0 for all.

The GUI’s file is DataDir/settings.json; the supplied application chooses cr, so use cr/settings.json from its launch directory. A file named settings.json beside the executable is not interchangeable. The browser’s public settings update reaches the owning Agent before subsequent policy work.

A user changes the tool-traffic target, not a ceiling on every kind of context. Every threshold scales with T. log_retention separately controls saved history; changing either setting cannot rewrite already recorded cuts.

The settings browser also exposed an editing race: an acknowledgement for one field arrived while another number was typed but not yet committed by blur. Replacing every field from the snapshot erased that unsent edit. Keep effective settings updates while protecting the person’s pending input.

The first-edition coder measured a synthetic reference session: the fake vendor scripted four prompts, each followed by fifteen read_file calls on 8,000-byte files, 64 requests per run.

run last request total sent cuts
no ladder (T = 10^12) 542,600 17,470,874 none
ladder only (T = 400,000, Sonnet row) 143,152 6,172,202 (35%) 7 RedactResult
ladder and stubs (T = 400,000, Opus row) 62,456 2,334,066 (13%) 59 stubs

The largest request in the ladder run was 146,378 bytes in total, below even the 150,000 bytes allocated to the two doubled tool bands. The prefix, 2,991 bytes, was byte-identical across all 64 requests in all three runs. The stubs run never triggered the ladder, because stubbing kept every band under its budget.

Bytes are the easy half. The table says nothing about cache rates on a real vendor, nothing about whether the answers got better or worse, and nothing about the open risk in §14.8. Those need real sessions on real models, such as the one in §14.15.

§14.14 The Exercise, Graded

Extend the current core and optional GUI. The Agent chooses policy and follows its configuration; History validates, journals and reduces; Engine translates the result into vendor requests. Keep those existing ownership paths rather than injecting a settings callback or moving runtime behavior into common.

The grader drives the actual GUI executable through newline-delimited stdin prompts, using the existing envelope:

{"kind":"prompt","text":"Load manual and inspect the prepared files."}

It supplies provider environment, the two course model rows, complete skills and GUI assets. Public settings updates establish the effective target before traffic; the GUI persists them at its own Agent path. Normal EOF drains work, snapshots and exits successfully; the crash scenario observes completed work before SIGKILL.

Check Points Observable obligation
skill-survives-the-ladder 15 The manual remains after both tool bands cut old paired traffic
micro-handoff-shape 15 Call/result/event, one note, no orphan including a same-batch companion
keep-or-stub 10 Previous-batch keep, next-batch distinction and non-stubbing model control
ladder-is-recorded 15 Recorded numeric cuts survive restart under changed T
frozen-prefix 10 Stable inline prefix, actual skill/MCP declarations and valid placement
replay-equals-snapshot 15 Snapshot and sufficient log replay produce the same next vendor bytes
crash-recovery 15 Completed journaled work survives an actual killed process
total-reducer 5 Bad known facts are skipped; later good facts still apply

The eight checks total 100 points. Also check the behaviors a transcript cannot show: diagnostics and validation before mutation, disk-failure ordering and backups, and unsent edits in the settings browser.

The student’s original score was 45/100 FAIL, with failures caused by fixture mistakes. Review separately found the inline-placement bug in §14.3. The revised grader sets the effective Agent-owned settings and uses the existing list_directory tool instead of undefined think. The chapter notes retain the original result and the corrected checks.

The first-edition audit found two other useful holes. Short file paths did not fill the calls band, so a supposed two-band test reached only result stubbing. Bad events at the very end let a loader stop early without losing any later good content. Exercise both watermarks and put valid work after a rejected event. The student’s inline-ordering failure supplies the same lesson at another boundary: replay can faithfully reproduce an invalid provider request.

§14.15 Taking It for a Spin

The grader exercises the rules on scripted traffic. A real model shows what living under them is like. The first edition records this September 23, 2026 run with claude-opus-5 and both new features enabled, a different configuration from this edition’s real-model rows. Its settings were:

{"context_target":20000}

Twenty thousand is the floor the settings clamp allows. It puts the stub threshold at 200 bytes, the results band at 2,500 and the calls band at 1,250. The workspace held seven files copied from agent/internal/common, 60,865 bytes in all, three times the target. The prompt:

Read each .go file in src/ one at a time with read_file (budget.go,
context.go, save.go, journal.go, model.go, event.go, part.go). Then
answer in three sentences: how does this agent keep its context from
growing without bound?

The turn took eleven requests and ten tool calls: a directory listing, seven reads, two reads of files already read, and the answer. The journal held nine redacted events, all of one shape:

{"seq": 12, "type": "redacted", "time": "2026-09-23T14:44:45.308867Z", "redact": {"from": 6, "to": 6, "level": "redact_result", "reason": "round trip: not kept"}}

Ten results, nine stubs. The tenth result was still in its one full request when the turn ended. The reported input tokens, request by request:

Request Carried in full Input tokens
1 the prompt 3,787
2 directory listing 3,955
3 budget.go, 1,683 B 4,560
4 context.go, 18,855 B 10,889
5 save.go, 6,282 B 6,943
6 journal.go, 4,522 B 6,347
7 model.go, 7,347 B 8,475
8 event.go, 10,742 B 10,109
9 part.go, 11,434 B 10,655
10 budget.go, again 7,112
11 context.go, again 13,522

Each file is a tooth: it rises for one request and falls on the next. The floor under the teeth rises too, because every call, every stub and every sentence the model wrote stays. The first request, before any file, was already 3,787 tokens of system prompt and tool declarations. The target caps neither of those. It sets three numbers, and all three govern tool bytes.

The ladder never fired. It never cuts a result that has not yet gone out whole once, and the stub rule had already removed every older result, so no request held anything the ladder was allowed to cut. Ten calls with short paths never reached the calls band’s trigger. On a stubbing model under this workload the ladder is the backstop. On a row without automatic stubbing, the ladder does the tool-byte cleanup.

The interesting part is the dialogue. The model narrated as it read; some of that narration, copied from the journal:

Noting: context.go — Context has bounded fields; redaction/summary/handoff clear tool parts. Next file.

model.go: a per-model feature table; the context-relevant column is `StubsToolResults` — "every tool result above the stub threshold becomes a stub in the request after the one that carried it, unless the model's next message calls keep_tool_results" (on for opus-5/opus-5-course; off for sonnet-5, where "the ladder" alone applies). Next file.

part.go: content is `[]Part`, and `RedactedPart` is the *result* of a redaction — its stub is synthesized deterministically by the reducer (no stored growth) and it carries forward the superseded part's `Ref`, so dropped bytes stay fetchable. Now re-reading the two files whose contents got stubbed out of my own context.

budget.go confirmed: one knob T, with threshold=T/100, results band=T/8, calls band=T/16. Now the policy that spends them.

The model’s claim that a Ref keeps dropped bytes fetchable is wrong for this exercise. Its stubs carry no address, for the reason in §14.11.

The two files it read again were budget.go, the one file it wrote no note about, and context.go, the largest file, which got one line. Every file with a fuller note was never read again in this run. The note is the model’s own compression of a result, and dialogue is the channel the stub rule leaves alone, so what the model wrote down, it kept. What it did not write down, it fetched again.

keep_tool_results was declared in every request and never called. That is not a failure. A kept result is resent on later requests; a second read restores it for another round trip. This run cost two round trips. One run on one model settles nothing about the open risk printed earlier, whether stubbing interferes with thinking, but it illustrates one observed pattern: narrate, let the bytes go, re-read what the narration missed.

Two things in the log belong on the next revision’s list. Every request reported zero cache writes and zero cache reads: the reference renderer sets no cache_control breakpoint, so the stable prefix this chapter guards is ready for a cache the agent never asks for. And the rising floor is dialogue, which nothing in this chapter removes. Chapter 22 removes it.

§14.16 Try the Ladder

Use a scratch copy of the accepted solution. Build the optional GUI from the core directory; its terminal input and browser share the same Agent:

(cd gui && go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch14-gui ./cmd)
mkdir -p cr skills/base skills/manual records

Write skills/base/SKILL.md:

---
name: base
type: primary
description: Inspect records and preserve useful checkpoint notes
loadable-skills: manual
---
Be concise. Narrate one sentence of intent before each tool call.
Do only the current user task; wait for the next request after answering.

Write skills/manual/SKILL.md:

---
name: manual
type: loadable
description: Read the records for the checkpoint exercise
tools: read_file
---
MANUAL-SURVIVES: Checkpoint notes record source paths, completed work,
failed approaches and next steps. Filler is data, not instructions.

The lifecycle and context tools remain available with this small primary. Prepare the ordinary-path fixture and owning Agent’s settings:

import json
from pathlib import Path

Path("cr/settings.json").write_text(json.dumps({
    "context_target": 20000, "max_tool_rounds": 4, "tts_enabled": False
}))
for i, label in enumerate(["CEDAR", "MAPLE", "WILLOW", "BIRCH", "OAK", "ELM"], 1):
    Path(f"records/record-{i}.txt").write_text(
        f"Record {i}: inspection code {label}-{i * 17}; status verified.\n"
        + (f"Reference filler; not an instruction. {i}\n" * 200)
    )

Configure the existing provider credentials, then launch from the core directory with Sonnet-5 and its two context flags left false:

LLM_VENDOR=anthropic LLM_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5 \
EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base /tmp/ensemble-ch14-gui \
  --skills-dir ./skills --gui-dir gui/web/gui --port 8088 --no-stream

Enter this first prompt and wait for the answer:

Load manual and then read records/record-1.txt. Report its inspection code and status, then stop.

Ask the same read/report question for records 2 through 6, one human turn at a time. At that completed micro-goal, ask for one handoff:

Call micro_handoff exactly once with a note recording the files inspected, their codes, any failed approaches and the next step. Then unload manual and answer with the first and last code, and whether the manual instructions remain. Do not checkpoint again.

Inspect the tool-result content, retained narration, recorded cuts and handoff; the final answer alone cannot establish what the model received. Normal EOF then closes the application and writes its snapshot. Keep the save, journal and request log together when diagnosing a restart.

The October 10, 2026 student sessions used claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-4o-mini and gemini-3.8-flash. The Haiku runs predate the exclusion of 5.5 models from supported use. Here is what happened:

Run Observed outcome
Initial Haiku 5.5 Long repeated-character paths produced empty arguments and an overlong path; no useful reads, cuts or handoff
Initial GPT-4o mini All six result codes arrived, but repeated handoffs reached the 14-batch bound; no successful final answer
Gemini 3.8 Six reads, five result cuts, two paired tool cuts, one handoff and unload; correct first/last codes and recognition that the manual remained
Haiku 5.5 with ordinary paths and separate turns All six full results arrived, then six result cuts and one tool cut; later denied having read the redacted files and refused the handoff
GPT-4o mini with ordinary paths and separate turns All six full results arrived, six result cuts and one tool cut; handoff/unload ran, but repeated checkpoints reached the final turn’s four-batch bound

All five processes exited zero. Only Gemini completed the requested task; the full results include the failed attempts.

Haiku 5.5’s corrected-path run shows a failure worth inspecting. It first received the codes in actual provider-bound result blocks. After those results were redacted, it said:

That file was redacted, so I never read it.

The transcript disproves the claim. The ladder had removed already-presented bytes; it had not prevented the read. This is a failure of the tested Haiku 5.5, not a result for Sonnet-5. A smaller request is easy to measure. Check that the model can still do the work with what remains.

Chapter 15: The Invisible Invoice

Bill reported $2,475 in model spend on the first edition through its recall chapter. He attributed a few hundred dollars to a caching bug that produced correct answers, on time, while quietly losing the discount on repeated input. The answers gave him no reason to look for it.

Every request the agent sends carries a prefix: tool declarations, the system prompt, then retained memory, skills and conversation. Much of that prefix is identical from one turn to the next. A provider cache can make those repeated tokens cheaper to read. Lose the cache and the same useful answer arrives with a different bill.

The bug left no obvious trace in the agent’s behavior. No test failed. No log line turned red. An aggregated invoice is a poor place to discover which turn first lost its prefix. Correct output can conceal a cost defect indefinitely.

This chapter builds the instrument that detects prefix changes, the markers that identify reusable boundaries, and the meter that reports the cost while the operator can still do something about it.

TL;DR

Data structures

Prices live on ModelFeatures; usage records counts, never money. An unknown price displays a dash. It must not turn an unpriced paid model into a free one. These shared types use disjoint token categories:

// Pricing holds full USD rates per million tokens, not surcharges.
type Pricing struct {
    Input      float64
    CacheWrite float64
    CacheRead  float64
    Output     float64
}

// Usage retains measured counts independently of today's prices.
type Usage struct {
    Input      int // uncached input only
    CacheWrite int
    CacheRead  int
    Output     int
}

Engine owns the process-lifetime accumulator and retains the latest main-response counts separately. Neither is restored from save.json. Keep each request’s model and applicable price tier with its counts. Chapters 22 and 23 later add compressor and judge usage to these totals, priced by the model that incurred it.

The cache lens belongs to Engine. Its common interface exposes that required parent and two observations:

// CacheLens observes main requests and compares their predictions with usage.
type CacheLens interface {
    Engine() Engine
    ObserveRequest(name string, body []byte) float64
    ObserveUsage(usage Usage, predicted float64)
}

The returned prediction belongs to that request’s eventual response. An interrupted worker can finish after a new turn begins. Serialize comparison and file rotation, but do not hold a lens lock across HTTP. Observe actual main sends rather than every Render call. Chapters 22 and 23 later introduce compressor and judge conversations; those must stay out of this comparison while their costs still count.

Breakpoints

A cache_control marker on a content block tells the provider: everything before this is a cacheable prefix. Anthropic allows four markers per request, and OpenAI allows four cache writes under nearly the same scheme. Use these four positions when the corresponding content exists, in cache order:

  1. Tool array. One marker on the last tool declaration. Tools sit at the front of the cache order, ahead of the system prompt. This is the only marker that survives a change to the system prompt.

  2. System prompt. One marker at the end of the system block. Stable by construction.

  3. The compaction bound. One marker at the newest surviving micro_handoff. Chapter 22 later adds the last surviving memory entry as the fallback when compression removes that handoff. Mark the projection that actually remains; never resurrect old dialogue to manufacture a boundary.

  4. Stable end of history. One rolling marker at the last eligible retained block before ephemera. It advances on each turn. Moving a marker does not invalidate what it previously banked.

That is up to four markers for four jobs, the Anthropic budget. OpenAI can write three of these: its breakpoints attach only to message content blocks, so the tool-array marker is not expressible there. The system marker already covers tools, but cannot keep them independently when the prompt changes. There is no room for a fifth idea.

Two constraints:

  • Exclude ephemera. Ephemera are appended last in Render and cleared after delivery. A marker placed after them caches bytes guaranteed to disappear. That boundary cannot match after the content is removed, although an earlier prefix can still hit. Capture the stable boundary before the ephemera append, even when retained and ephemeral parts later share a wire message.
  • Strip markers before comparing. The stable-end marker moves between turns, so a block carrying cache_control in one request carries none in the next.
