Compare raw bytes and every healthy turn is classified as edited. The comparison strips markers first: a breakpoint is an instruction to the provider, not conversation content.

Wire format

Anthropic: explicit cache_control markers on content blocks. System must be an array of content blocks rather than a string. Up to four markers per request.

OpenAI: on this chapter’s supported GPT-5.6 Sol Chat Completions route, prompt_cache_breakpoint markers on content blocks, enabled by a request-level prompt_cache_options: {mode: "explicit"}. Up to four cache writes per request. Select explicit support from the model table; older rows retain implicit caching. Breakpoints attach only to message content blocks (text, image, audio, file), not to the tool array. The agent therefore writes three markers rather than four; the system marker already covers tools, but cannot keep them independently when the prompt changes.

The footgun: explicit mode disables implicit caching. A request that declares explicit mode but places no markers caches nothing at all, which is strictly worse than staying silent. On Anthropic, a missing marker costs a cache the agent never had. On OpenAI, it destroys the implicit cache the agent already had. The opt-in must follow evidence that a marker landed, never intent.

Gemini: implicit caching, with no markers to place. The selected model’s minimum prefix size matters; Gemini 3.8 Flash documents 4,096 tokens. A small prompt reporting zero reads has not established a caching defect. Warm-up and the amount granted are observations to measure with the actual growing conversation, not fixed numbers of cold turns to enforce.

The provider contracts above were checked on October 11, 2026 against the Claude caching guide, OpenAI caching guide and Gemini caching guide. A documented field and a well-formed request still need a real grant.

The meter

The GUI header displays four numbers: session cost, last-response input tokens, last-response cache read tokens, and session cache hit rate. The input and cache-read figures show the most recent response so the operator can see how large the current prompt is and how much of it was cached. Session totals go to the tooltip. Cost is computed from Usage and Price at render time and held only in memory. An unpriced model shows token counts and a dash for cost.

The meter reads Engine’s current-process accounting rather than the totals restored with conversation history. Latest input means all input to the last main response, including its cached buckets exactly once. Session cost and hit rate include auxiliary calls when Chapters 22 and 23 add them. Session cost means cost since the developer sat down.

Rules

  1. Build the lens before the markers. A breakpoint on an unstable prefix buys nothing and looks like it worked.
  2. Prices live on ModelFeatures. Usage lives in the event log. Cost is derived at render time from both.
  3. Token counts only in the event log. Prices change; counts are history.
  4. Recognize the conversation section, including Gemini’s contents, as the section expected to grow. Report unexpected stable-section changes; a deliberate checkpoint or model change needs its own interpretation.
  5. A growing JSON array is an append rather than an edit. Without this distinction, every turn fires a false alarm.
  6. The meter prices the model in force rather than the model named in settings. The two can differ when the model comes from the environment.
  7. Compare predicted and granted cache rates as ratios. A prediction is bytes from the request; a grant is tokens from the response. Adding them is a type error.

Yours

How the lens reports its verdict: log file, structured events, or both. Whether to display the per-section stability status in the GUI. How much detail the cache miss alarm carries. The format of the rotated request files, as long as plain diff puts the cursor on the first broken byte.

Exercise

Extend solutions/ch14. Wire a CacheLens to the main send boundary, place supported breakpoints, build the meter, and verify stable prefixes and actual cache reads. The grader runs from the repository root, defaulting to solutions/ch15 and its separate GUI:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 15 -json

Grader checks

cache-lens-exists          (15 pts)  a cache lens observes consecutive
                                     requests; the actual requests are inspectable
prefix-is-stable           (20 pts)  tools and system are byte-identical
                                     across turns
request-has-breakpoints    (15 pts)  last tool, system and stable history
                                     blocks carry legal cache_control;
                                     history advances within four markers
cost-is-computed-not-stored(15 pts)  event log holds counts only; cost is
                                     derived at display time
usage-is-session-scoped    (10 pts)  the meter's tokens come from the last
                                     response, not the lifetime restored from disk
cache-read-rate            (10 pts)  cache reads are zero cold, nonzero warm
all-vendors-report-usage   (15 pts)  vendor parsers normalize the supplied
                                     usage categories without double counting

§15.1 The idea in plain words

A cache miss can produce a completely correct answer. The tool call works. The edit lands. The test passes. Nothing in the agent’s behavior changes. The failure is pure cost, and it is silent.

Most bugs announce themselves. A bad tool call returns an error. A broken parse throws an exception. A wedged job hangs where the operator can see it. A cache miss does none of these things. The correct output arrives, possibly later, at the uncached input rate. No log line turns red. No test fails. The only reporting channel is the invoice, and it arrives thirty days late, aggregated across every session, past the point where anyone can attribute a cost spike to the change that caused it.

This chapter builds three things, in an order that matters.

The lens compares consecutive requests, section by section, and reports whether the prefix is stable. A breakpoint placed on an unstable prefix buys nothing while looking like it worked, because the agent still produces correct output. The lens catches the nothing.

The markers tell the provider where the cacheable prefix ends. Place them wrong and every turn is a cold read that looks like it should have been warm. Place them on something that changes and the cache is invalidated anyway. The lens locates stable bytes; the response usage says whether the provider actually served them from cache.

The meter displays cost in real time. An invoice is not a feedback loop. A number that updates on every turn is. The meter does not prevent waste, but it makes waste visible at the moment it happens, to the person who can fix it.

The economic argument is straightforward. At the October 11, 2026 Sonnet-5 rates, a million ordinary input tokens cost $2, a five-minute cache write costs $2.50, and a cache read costs $0.20. Output has its own $10 rate. Those are alternative input buckets: do not charge the full input rate again on a cache write. Two hundred repeated turns make a small per-turn difference consequential. The saving depends on which tokens actually receive the discount; it is not a tenfold reduction in every request’s total cost.

§15.2 The lens

The lens works by rotating two files: the current request and the prior one. In the supplied clients they are cr/cache-current.txt and cr/cache-prior.txt, under the owning Agent’s directory. Each is split into named sections (tools, system, messages) and re-emitted in cache concatenation order: the order the provider lays them out in context. For Anthropic, that is tools, then system, then messages, regardless of the struct’s JSON field order. The ordering matters because a prefix is a contiguous run of bytes from the start, and two sections in the wrong order produce the wrong prefix boundary.

Each section gets one of three verdicts: identical, appended, or changed. “Appended” means a JSON array grew at the tail, as the messages array does on every turn. Without this distinction, every turn reports a changed prefix, because the closing bracket of the array has moved. A changed non-messages section is the alarm. An appended messages section is the normal case.

The lens writes its sections to disk so that plain diff puts the cursor on the first byte that broke the cache. Reading the raw file is the fast diagnostic. Structured verdicts are the automation.

Stripping the markers

Because the stable-end marker moves, a content block that carried cache_control in one request carries none in the next. That difference sits deep inside the prefix, where the trailing-append rule cannot reach. Comparing raw bytes classifies every healthy turn as edited, and the reported cacheable prefix is truncated at the stale marker position.

The comparison strips markers before diffing. The principle: a breakpoint is an instruction to the provider rather than conversation content. Removing it from the comparison is the same kind of move as ignoring whitespace in a semantic diff.

The wrong way to strip is a JSON round trip. Unmarshalling and re-marshalling reorders keys and rewrites byte counts, and those counts are reported as a property of the real request and compared against the provider’s own figures. Both sides of the comparison get the same distortion, so equality stays honest while the measurement becomes fiction. The lens strips by pattern, in place, preserving every other byte.

Match the shape, not a rendering of it

The first-edition coder recorded a strip built from a constant holding the exact marker bytes the renderer emits, with a comment justifying it: “we control the emitter.” The emitter is controlled. But the lens compares what the canonicalizer produced, and the canonicalizer marshals with json.MarshalIndent. The marker arrives with spaces the constant does not have.

Nothing matched the indented marker. The strip left it in place. Nothing crashed. The symptom was a diagnostic reporting a prefix fault that was not there, on a path that produces no error when it fails to strip, because a strip that misses everything simply leaves the markers in place and the comparison fires.

The reason it survived its tests: every test hand-built sections as compact JSON, matched the constant, and passed. Test and code shared one wrong belief about the format, and the format itself was never consulted. The replacement test builds its input the way the agent does, with MarshalIndent, and it kills the defect. The old compact test still passes against the broken code, which measures exactly how much it was checking.

The coder’s retained review reports this two-turn comparison:

before:  messages:edited     66.6%,  0 breakpoints
after:   messages:appended   73.3%,  3 breakpoints

The lesson is general. When the instrument and the code share a belief, the instrument certifies the code against the belief, not against the artifact. Testing against the artifact, built the way the artifact is built, exposes the gap.

The late reply belongs to its own request

There is another way for the instrument to lie while every answer remains correct. The new implementation initially assumed the actor serialized lens observations. It does serialize turn decisions. An interrupted HTTP worker, however, can still be finishing when the next turn begins.

Independent review held an old cold response, interrupted its turn, and let a new request complete. The lens predicted 0.0000 for the cold request and 0.8554 for the new one. When the old response was released, it reported the new request’s 0.8554 prediction. Locking a shared “latest prediction” would prevent a race while preserving the wrong attribution.

Keep the prediction with the request that produced it. The corrected lens returns a ratio to Engine, and that exchange’s response callback carries it back with the granted usage. A short lock protects comparison and artifact rotation; no lock spans the network wait. The same held-response probe then reports 0.0000 for the old response and 0.8554 for the new one, with both actual usages counted. Interrupting the conversation does not make an already incurred charge disappear.

§15.3 Where the markers go

The system marker is straightforward. The system prompt does not change between turns, so a marker at the end of the system block banks the startup instructions. Dynamically loaded skill bodies remain conversation data; moving them into the system prompt would undo Chapter 9. Chapter 22 applies the same rule to mutable memory. One marker, one stable prefix.

The message-history marker is harder, because the conversation grows. Everything before the current exchange is identical to the previous request, and everything after it is new. A marker that banks the identical part saves money on every warm turn.

Why not the first message

An obvious placement is the first user message. Everything before it is stable, so a marker there should cache the prefix.

The error is in how the provider serves the cache. A read covers the span up to a marker. A marker on the first message caches tools, system, and the first message. The system marker already caches tools and system. The first-message marker adds one message to the cached span and leaves the rest of the conversation cold on every turn, while the conversation is the part that grows and the part that costs.

The tool array

Tools sit at the very front of the cache order, ahead of the system prompt and the messages. A marker on the last tool declaration closes a prefix containing all of them.

The tool-array marker is the only one that survives a change to the system prompt. Without it, editing a single word of the prompt discards the tool declarations along with it, and tool schemas are not small. With it, the declarations stay cached while the prompt rebuilds. The system marker covers tools under normal operation, but the tool-array marker is the one that matters under maintenance.

The stable end

One marker sits on the last eligible retained block before ephemera, even when the two share a wire message. It advances on each turn as the conversation grows. Because a marker is not part of the cache key, moving it does not invalidate the bytes it previously banked. The first-edition Anthropic run recorded a 21-token rise between its two warm requests, matching that exchange’s size. It demonstrates a moving marker with successful cache reads in that run; it does not promise the same increment for every response or provider.

A start-of-turn anchor is unnecessary. The rolling marker from the previous turn already wrote a cache entry at exactly that prefix, and both vendors walk backward past a bounded number of positions to find a prior write. The anchor would buy a second copy of something already in hand, using one of only four slots.

For this layout, an extra start-of-turn breakpoint duplicates the rolling boundary. If adding one appears to help, inspect the actual prefix before spending another slot. A rewritten prefix needs its cause fixed; an extra marker can make that mistake harder to see.

The compaction bound

A micro_handoff rewrites the conversation above it: tool calls are stripped, opaque reasoning and private replay signatures are removed, and the affected region settles into the redaction ladder’s terminal state. The stable-end marker, which sat somewhere in the middle of that region, now points at bytes that no longer exist. It rebuilds from the new tail and the old prefix is gone, along with the cache it banked.

The newest surviving micro_handoff gives the renderer a useful boundary between completed work and the continuing exchange. The cuts were recorded and applied by the reducer, not recomputed to suit today’s render. Chapter 22 extends this boundary: if a memory fold removes that handoff, the projection uses the last surviving memory entry instead. The cache marker describes retained bytes; it cannot preserve a dialogue entry that the memory policy has legitimately replaced.

This is a different answer from an agent that keeps demonstration pairs after compaction. Keeping the three most recent tool-call pairs past the handoff creates a moving boundary, because what counts as “most recent” is recomputed on every render. Pairs kept before an older handoff are dropped once a newer handoff pushes the boundary forward. The marker must then track the first surviving pair rather than the handoff itself. An agent whose compaction strip is uniform avoids the moving boundary entirely: the handoff is the bound, and that is where the marker goes.

Chapter 22’s memory-band compaction will rewrite data near the front of the conversation. That invalidates the old suffix from the changed point, while earlier tools and system instructions can still be reused. Accept that cost when replacing old memory; do not turn memory into frozen instructions to avoid it.

The vendor asymmetry

Anthropic takes cache_control on a tool definition, so it gets all four markers. OpenAI cannot. Its breakpoints attach to message content blocks, and the tools array is not a content block. OpenAI writes three of the four: system, compaction bound, and stable end.

Nothing is lost except independence. A breakpoint includes all prompt content before it, and tools precede the system prompt in the cache order, so the system marker already covers the tool declarations. The system marker simply cannot keep them when the prompt changes. Under routine operation this makes no difference. Under maintenance, Anthropic holds its tool cache through a prompt edit while OpenAI does not.

The exact provider lookback is not a client-side algorithm to reproduce. Earlier documentation even disagreed about its count. What matters here is that a read and a write are different observations, and a cache write can have its own full rate. This chapter is about an invisible invoice; write tokens belong in the accounting too.

That is up to four markers on Anthropic, three on the supported OpenAI route. An empty tool array or absent compaction bound does not need a placeholder merely to consume a slot.

Ephemera

Ephemera are content appended last in Render and documented as “delivered once, then cleared.” They may merge into the final user message. A marker placed after them includes bytes that disappear on the next turn. That exact boundary cannot match afterward, even if an earlier part of the prefix still receives a discount.

The stable boundary must be captured before the ephemera append. This is a single line of code and a paragraph of explanation, but omitting it leaves the rolling boundary beyond transient bytes. Correct answers alone will not reveal that placement error.

The provider minimum

Cache eligibility has a floor, and the floor belongs to a model and route. The October 11 documentation lists 1,024 tokens for Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, and 4,096 for Gemini 3.8 Flash. These are token counts, not request-file byte lengths. Check the selected model’s current contract before diagnosing a zero.

A zero can mean the cache failed, or it can mean the request was never eligible. An instrument that cannot tell those apart will eventually report the second as the first. The original live script used prompts of a few hundred tokens and got three Gemini zeroes. Its author first called caching unimplemented, then corrected the diagnosis after an eligible run.

The old grader fixture grew from 1,716 to 6,631 bytes when five tool declarations were added. That made its prefix test less trivial, but byte length alone does not establish a provider’s token minimum. A fake can award cache reads below any real floor; only a real response supplies the grant.

§15.4 What the wire shows

The first-edition coder reported these live cache-read counts. They are historical measurements under its earlier marker arrangement, not a new run of the final implementation:

vendor model cache_read by turn what it needs
Anthropic claude-sonnet-5 0, 3627, 3648 explicit cache_control markers
OpenAI gpt-5.6-sol 0, 7359 explicit prompt_cache_breakpoint; mode: "explicit"
Gemini gemini-3.8-flash 0, 0, 16349, 24531 implicit; history grew by roughly 8,400 tokens per turn

Three findings in that table.

Anthropic’s two warm counts differ by 21 tokens, the reported size of the previous exchange. That is the stable-end marker banking the conversation one exchange at a time. It is the direct evidence that a moving marker does not invalidate the cache, measured rather than assumed. The assumption held for two sessions before anyone thought to check.

The original OpenAI experiment used the explicit scheme, under different field names: prompt_cache_breakpoint on a content block and prompt_cache_options: {mode: "explicit"} on the request. It was then documented only for the Responses API in the coder’s reading; the experiment exercised Chat Completions. Its current reference also documents the content marker and request opt-in. The end-to-end measurement, using that version’s renderer output, reads 7,359 of 7,362 prompt tokens from cache on the second turn. That is 99.96 percent of the prefix, which confirms the markers land and the prefix survives.

The measurement that matters is the one that almost did not get made. The first probe sent a request with the marker removed from a position that had been primed, and got zero reads. The diagnosis that came to mind was “removing the marker broke the prefix.” But the probe had also changed the content encoding of that message from an array of parts back to a plain string, and two variables changed at once cannot diagnose anything. A second probe changed only the encoding and got 7,813 of 7,816 tokens cached: the encoding change preserved that tested prefix. The zero meant “no breakpoint at the primed position to look up,” not “the format change invalidated the cache.” This chapter is about instruments, and the first instrument an instrument builder needs is the controlled experiment.

The asymmetry between the two explicit vendors is the opt-in. On Anthropic, a missing marker costs a cache the agent never had. On OpenAI, explicit mode disables implicit caching, so a request that declares explicit mode and places no markers caches nothing at all, which is strictly worse than staying silent. The implementation must gate the opt-in on evidence: send mode: "explicit" only when at least one marker actually landed.

Gemini needs the shape of the experiment alongside its numbers. It caches implicitly, detecting the repeated prefix itself, so there are no markers to place. The original coder tried three shapes: a fixed large user message, a large stable system reference with a small growing history, and a history growing by roughly 8,400 tokens each turn.

The first two hit on turn two. The third produced the two leading zeroes in the table. An early review had tried to disprove the history claim using the fixed-message probe. Bill’s prompting led to the growing-history experiment. Both measurements were real; the first answered a different question.

The later implementation’s browser run used a large stable reference and four short questions. Gemini warmed on the second request there too, with 15,725, 15,801 and 15,910 cache-read tokens. Those changing values do not establish a universal 4,096-token block rule. Nor does the earlier four-turn run prove that a partial block stays uncached forever.

Put genuinely stable content early and keep nearby requests comparable, as the Gemini guide recommends. That is not permission to promote editable memories or retrieved documents into system instructions. This chapter uses implicit caching for Gemini; it needs no marker budget or separately managed cache object. Measure the conversation shape the application actually sends before turning a warm-up observation into a rule.

The section name

The instability alarm exempts the conversation section, because the conversation is the one section expected to grow every turn. The exemption compares against a section name. For Anthropic and OpenAI that name is messages. For Gemini it is contents.

A hardcoded constant gets the wrong answer for one of the three vendors. The lens detects the name from the body’s shape rather than from a vendor table, because the conversation section is the one containing an array of objects with role fields regardless of what the vendor calls it.

The failure mode before the fix: every ordinary Gemini turn was reported as a broken prefix, with a byte offset that moved between runs. The same log line already said contents:appended, which was the correct diagnosis. Two halves of one instrument contradicting each other, and the half offering a precise offset was the wrong one. A precise wrong answer outranks a vague right one in a reader’s attention, and that is exactly what happened.

What the fake cannot see

The grader runs against a fake vendor. A fake vendor grants whatever figures it is told to, so it can prove the request is well-formed and the lens observes it. It cannot prove the provider agrees.

The first implementation’s fake and live runs found different defects. Neither replaced the other.

The usage meter failed to find a paid model’s price. It looked up prices by the model named in the settings store, which is empty when the model comes from the environment. An empty name matches nothing, so claude-sonnet-5 reported priced:false, cost:0. The instrument built to make spending visible was the thing concealing it. It now prices the model actually in force, taken from the engine config at the composition root.

The original live gpt-5.6-sol Chat Completions run refused requests carrying reasoning_effort alongside function tools, returning a 400. That exercise exposed tools, so every attempted turn failed. The subtle half: the field must be sent as "none", not omitted. Omitting it means “your default,” and the default is a reasoning effort, so the request comes back refused with the identical error while the field appears nowhere in the body. The error names a field the developer can grep for and not find.

The price lookup is ordinary application behavior and a good fake-driven fixture can catch it. In fact, the retained coder review attributes that finding to the grader, not the live run. The tool/reasoning restriction needs a faithful provider contract before a fake can reproduce it. Real use found the missing fact; a focused regression can preserve it. Keep both kinds of checks, and be precise about which one found the defect.

§15.5 The meter

The GUI header shows four numbers: session cost, last-response input tokens, last-response cache read tokens, and session cache hit rate. Input and cache-read show the most recent response so the operator can see how large the current prompt is and how much of it hit cache, rather than a running sum that only grows. Session totals go to the tooltip on hover. Cost is computed from Usage and Price at render time and held only in memory.

The event log holds token counts in four categories: Input, CacheWrite, CacheRead, Output. Prices live on ModelFeatures. Engine’s meter multiplies each model/tier’s counts by its corresponding rates when the GUI asks for a view. A price correction can change the derived cost without rewriting the event log. Storing computed cost would freeze the wrong price into the permanent record.

Session scope

Cost and hit rate read from Engine’s process-lifetime accounting, which resets on restart. Input and cache-read display the latest main response. Chapters 22 and 23 will add compressor and judge usage to session totals and cost without replacing that main-response display. Restored conversation usage is a different history and does not seed the current process’s meter. The distinction matters: a developer who opens the GUI and sees yesterday’s total plus today’s spend has no feedback loop. “Session cost” means the cost since the developer sat down.

Units

Usage counts tokens. Prices are dollars per million tokens. The two meet only at render time, and the result is denominated in dollars. The event log never holds a dollar amount. Normalize vendor buckets before applying prices: Anthropic reports disjoint ordinary/write/read input; OpenAI’s prompt total already includes cached reads and writes; Gemini’s prompt total includes cache reads, and its charged output includes reported thinking. Subtract the included cached buckets when forming ordinary input, then count each once. For streams, retain the final usage rather than summing cumulative updates.

The lens predicts a cacheable fraction from the request, measured in bytes. The provider reports a cache hit rate in the response, measured in tokens. These cannot be added or subtracted because the units differ and the tokenizer is not a linear function of byte count. Comparing them as ratios is legitimate: the prediction is a fraction, the grant is a fraction, and a large gap is a reason to investigate. A small gap is consistent with reuse, but is not a tokenization identity or a billing audit. The original Anthropic report paired a 96.8% byte prediction with a 99.4% token grant. The comparison is useful because both remain visible.

§15.6 Exercise, graded

Extend solutions/ch14. Observe actual main sends with an Engine-owned cache lens; exclude auxiliary requests from that comparison. Place supported markers at tools, system, the surviving compaction boundary and the stable end before ephemera. Build the four-number GUI meter from process-scoped accounting. Keep model/tier identity with incurred usage, price unknowns honestly and preserve history across a restart that resets the current process’s spend.

Run from the repository root:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 15 -json

The grader builds solutions/ch15/gui separately from the core. -gui can select another GUI module; -cache-current and -cache-prior select its diagnostic artifact paths relative to the scratch launch directory. The defaults are cr/cache-current.txt and cr/cache-prior.txt. -cache-prices supplies the four per-million rates, in ordinary-input, cache-write, cache-read and output order; its Sonnet-5 default is 2,2.5,0.2,10. A historical implementation with a different dated tariff can be checked against its own rates. These are grader options, not new application flags.

The public GUI uses --port, --gui-dir, provider environment settings and a typed primary skill. Its WebSocket /ws accepts a subscribe message; ordinary browser prompts or stdin {"kind":"prompt","text":"..."} enter the same Agent. A usage frame reports latest disjoint input, cache_write, cache_read, output; nested total contains session counts, and hit_rate, cost_usd, priced describe the disposable meter. The header adds the three input buckets; the tooltip exposes the session totals. The GUI command saves to launch-directory save.json by default; its Agent’s lens files still belong under cr/.

check pts what it tests
cache-lens-exists 15 a cache lens observes consecutive requests, so the actual requests are inspectable
prefix-is-stable 20 tools and system are byte-identical across turns
request-has-breakpoints 15 the last tool declaration, system block and advancing stable history block carry legal cache_control, within the four-marker budget
cost-is-computed-not-stored 15 event log holds counts only; cost is derived at display time
usage-is-session-scoped 10 the meter’s tokens come from this response, not the lifetime total restored from disk
cache-read-rate 10 cache reads are zero on a cold turn and nonzero on a warm one
all-vendors-report-usage 15 vendor parsers normalize supplied usage without double counting

The numeric checks drive the real GUI and compare its requests, counts and artifacts with an external provider fake. Actual browser display, interrupted worker attribution and full provider marker rules also retain their focused source/integration checks. Auxiliary exclusion and surviving memory boundaries join those obligations in Chapters 22 and 23. The numeric marker fixture has no handoff or ephemeral tail. A fake’s warm reply cannot establish a real cache grant.

§15.7 Taking It for a Spin

Use a fresh directory and a stable reference large enough to make caching eligible. The reference belongs in the primary here because it is fixed for the demonstration, not because arbitrary retrieved text belongs in instructions. From a scratch copy of solutions/ch15:

cache_source="$PWD"
(cd gui && go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch17-gui ./cmd)
cache_demo=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$cache_demo"
mkdir -p skills/base
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
header = """---
name: base
type: primary
description: Answer questions about the fixed archive reference.
tools: list_directory read_file
---
Answer the user's archive question in one short sentence, without tools.
The archive project code is COPPER-FERRY-18.
"""
records = "".join(
    f"Archive record {i}: color copper; preserve the original source and record the reason for each change.\n"
    for i in range(1, 701)
)
Path("skills/base/SKILL.md").write_text(header + records)
PY

With the provider key configured as in Chapter 0, start the GUI in that terminal and leave stdin open while using the browser:

LLM_VENDOR=anthropic LLM_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5 \
EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base EN_SKILLS_DIR="$PWD/skills" \
/tmp/ensemble-ch17-gui --port 8088 --gui-dir "$cache_source/gui/web/gui"

Open http://localhost:8088 and send these in order, waiting for each reply:

What is the archive project code? Reply in one short sentence.
What is the rule for archive record 37? Reply in one short sentence.
What color identifies archive record 402? Reply in one short sentence.
Remind me of the archive project code, in five words or fewer.

The answers should identify COPPER-FERRY-18, preserving the source and reason, and copper. Watch the header, then inspect its session tooltip. Compare the last response’s usage in api.log with the usage frame in gui.log. debug.log records predicted and granted ratios; plain diff on the two cr/cache-*.txt files shows the retained prefix and appended conversation. A good answer with zero cache reads is still a zero-cache result. Check the actual input size, eligible route and prefix before deciding why.

Stop with Ctrl-D in the launch terminal after the last turn. Restart the same command in the same directory. Conversation history should return while the new process’s meter starts at zero; no new response has been charged yet. That is a separate check from seeing a warm second turn.

The retained October 11 browser sessions made four turns each on the earlier implementation 7436fcb. All twelve answers matched the supplied reference. Their raw provider usage and visible meters were independently compared:

Historical model Cache-read tokens by turn Final session USD Final session hit rate
claude-haiku-5-5 0, 21924, 21968, 22058 0.003481475 74.8879%
gpt-5.6-sol 0, 16349, 16349, 16349 0.1040918 74.6439%
gemini-3.8-flash 0, 15725, 15801, 15910 0.0226167 66.2209%

The dollar values use the dated model prices captured for those runs. The session percentages include the cold first request; they are not the last request’s hit rate. Haiku 5.5 remains the historical identity, not a current choice: the executable example uses supported Sonnet-5. Those captures contain no restarted process or handoff, and precede the lens-overlap correction. Restart and overlap have their separate real-runtime checks.

The unchanged original grader returned 0/100 because its primary fixture omitted the required skill type and never started the GUI. That did not measure seven broken cache features. Conversely, twelve correct answers did not establish that the instrument could attribute an interrupted reply. The useful result is the combination: inspect the actual request, preserve the provider’s counts, and make the displayed cost answer to both.

Chapter 16: Leaving Anthropic for OpenAI

This chapter is about freedom. It is also about choosing how you pay.

I built this codebook on Anthropic’s models. Eighteen chapters of tools, steering and context management. Then Anthropic shipped Opus 5.5 with restrictions on changing the context behind retained thinking. My agent depends on removing stale context. I am not giving that up to use a newer model.

Protecting private reasoning matters. So does letting the person building an agent control what it sees. The migration tests whether the vendor seam can preserve that choice.

So we are voting with our feet. In this chapter the agent authenticates through your existing ChatGPT subscription. No separate API-key signup for that route. The subscription has its own permissions and limits; it is another funding source, not a promise of unlimited inference or a measured tenfold saving.

TL;DR

The delta

Chapter 15 left the agent with three vendor renderers, a ModelFeatures table, capability flags, cache breakpoints, and per-vendor endpoints. This chapter:

  1. Introduces a credential provider abstraction that decouples authentication from inference.
  2. Implements OAuth 2.0 + PKCE for OpenAI’s ChatGPT plan, so an existing subscription becomes the API credential.
  3. Adds Responses API transport for selected OpenAI models, preserving Chat Completions for earlier model rows.
  4. Adds a capability profile for the ChatGPT plan’s restrictions.
  5. Streams reasoning summaries as first-class events, separate from assistant output.
  6. Implements a billing mode state machine with explicit, announced transitions.

Types (conceptual; adapt to your codebase)

// CredentialProvider returns a bearer token for inference.
// Both credential kinds produce the same Authorization header.
// Renewal belongs to the provider rather than the renderer.
type CredentialProvider interface {
    GetBearerToken(ctx context.Context) (string, error)
    Kind() CredentialKind
}

type CredentialKind int
const (
    CredentialAPIKey CredentialKind = iota + 1
    CredentialChatGPTOAuth
)

// OAuthProfile stores the state of one ChatGPT OAuth
// registration. The OIDC sub claim is the account identity.
type OAuthProfile struct {
    ClientID       string    // issued by OpenAI
    Subject        string    // validated OIDC account identity
    Email          string    // display only
    AccessToken    string    // secret
    RefreshToken   string    // secret; rotates on refresh
    IDToken        string    // secret — validated on receipt
    ExpiresAt      time.Time // access token expiry
    GrantedScopes  []string  // must include plan-use scope
    HostID         string    // stable per-installation UUID
}

type BillingMode int
const (
    BillingChatGPT BillingMode = iota + 1
    BillingAPI
    BillingChatGPTThenAPI
)

Rules

  1. Credential abstraction. The HTTP inference layer calls GetBearerToken() and receives a valid bearer token without implementing renewal itself. Both credential kinds produce Authorization: Bearer <token>. The credential provider stays off the renderer interface. Ensemble owns the auth service; Engine resolves a bearer into request-local transport configuration. Rendering and offline replay need no token.

  2. PKCE. Generate a cryptographically random verifier, compute the S256 challenge, send the challenge in the authorization request, and the verifier in the token exchange. Generate fresh state and nonce for every authorization attempt.

  3. Loopback listener. Bind to 127.0.0.1 (not localhost), any available port, path /auth/callback. The path must be exactly /auth/callback and the host must be the literal 127.0.0.1. Only the port may vary.

  4. Host identity. Generate a stable urn:uuid:<v4> once per installation. Persist it. Send as ext_agent_host_id in every authorization request. Never derive from username, hostname, email, or MAC address.

  5. Dynamic registration. The first authorization uses client_id=dynamic_agent_client. OpenAI returns an issued client_id on the authorization callback. Persist it before exchanging the authorization code. Reauthorization and token exchange use the issued client_id; a conflicting returning callback ID must be rejected. The bootstrap is a registration entrypoint, never valid for token exchange.

  6. ID token validation. Validate the returned JWT: fetch OpenAI’s published JWKS, check the signature, verify issuer, audience (must match issued client_id), expiry, and nonce. The OIDC sub claim is the stable account identity. Retain the issued client ID as well, so registrations remain separate.

  7. Scope checking. A successful login does not imply plan usage. The granted scopes must include chatgpt.tokens.use.direct. Without it, ChatGPT-plan inference is forbidden even if identity was successfully saved. Request openid profile email offline_access resource.invoke chatgpt.tokens.use.direct, with resource=https://api.openai.com/v1 on authorization and code exchange. Inspect the granted scope.

  8. Proactive refresh. Refresh the access token when now >= expires_at - 5 minutes. Each refresh returns a new refresh token; the old one is invalidated immediately. Serialize refresh per profile, including processes sharing its storage. Never allow concurrent refreshes for the same session. Save both new tokens atomically before using either.

  9. Terminal refresh errors. Six errors are terminal: invalid_grant, invalid_refresh_token, token_expired, refresh_token_expired, refresh_token_invalidated, refresh_token_reused. Mark the credential unusable, keep the issued client_id, re-authenticate. Temporary network/5xx errors: retry with backoff. Never delete valid credentials on a transient failure.

  10. Responses API format. ChatGPT-plan requests use the Responses API endpoint. They require store: false and stream: true, full history in input, and namespaced local function tools. The plan’s HTTP route excludes fields including temperature, top_p, max_output_tokens, previous_response_id, and top_logprobs (not logprobs). Model restrictions as a capability data structure, not scattered special cases. Require terminal completion before committing output or executing a streamed tool call; preserve completed output items even when the terminal output is empty.

  11. Cache breakpoints. On the supported API-key route, set prompt_cache_options.mode: "explicit" and place prompt_cache_breakpoint markers on eligible content blocks, including the developer-role constitution, within the four-marker budget. The measured ChatGPT route rejected the options field; its accepted capability profile omits both options and markers. Keep the cache lens and actual usage counters on both routes.

  12. Reasoning summaries. Request reasoning.summary: "auto" on models that support it. Stream summary events incrementally. Map them to separate observer events: never buffer a full summary, never concatenate into assistant text, never drop summaries adjacent to tool calls.

  13. Billing mode. chatgpt uses only OAuth credentials. api uses only the API key. chatgpt_then_api prefers OAuth, falls back to API only on subscription_sharing_usage_limit_exceeded and only when allow_metered_fallback is true. Announce the billing transition before the first metered request. Never silently switch billing. Deferring automatic fallback is permitted; this chapter’s accepted implementation supports only api and chatgpt.

  14. Credential isolation. Access tokens, refresh tokens, ID tokens, and API keys never appear in prompts, agent memories, conversation context, logs, debug output, or any model-visible state.

  15. Sign-out. Revoke the refresh token via OpenAI’s revocation endpoint. Clear local tokens. Retain the issued client_id and host ID. If remote revocation fails, clear locally and inform the user.

Yours

  • File layout for the OAuth subsystem
  • Profile storage format (JSON, keychain, or your existing secret store)
  • How auth status is displayed to the user
  • Whether chatgpt_then_api is implemented now or deferred
  • Multiple-account support: the schema should support it even if the UX exposes only one account

Exercise

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 16

Extend Chapter 15; the accepted result is solutions/ch16. Run the command from the repository root. It builds the core and its separate GUI; an explicit core path and -gui DIR select other submissions. The grader provides a fake OAuth server and a fake Responses API server. Complete the OAuth flow, perform inference through the Responses API, refresh tokens proactively, and stream reasoning summaries as separate events.

The idea in plain words

An encrypted reasoning block looks safe to store or share because its owner cannot read it. But the provider’s model can. If another model accepts the same block, the encryption has not established who may ask for its contents. That distinction made a seemingly opaque artifact a source of leaked secrets.

In August 2026, researchers demonstrated the consequence. They replayed a frontier model’s encrypted reasoning into a cheaper model behind a jailbreak prompt, and the decoder treated the replayed block as its own prior thinking and decoded it. From 6,708 public agent trajectories, they extracted 315,320 reasoning blocks. The genuine user sessions contained 62 distinct API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens and 7 private keys; 64 of the 704 recovered artifacts were absent from visible chat history. These are the researchers’ findings, not an invitation to test recovered credentials. The original account’s $720 figure describes the paper’s estimated cost for a separate 10,000-trace example, not the measured cost of this extraction. (Panfilov et al., August 2026, §§3.1 and 4.1.)

Binding a reasoning artifact to its authorized context is one way to close that gap. OpenAI’s September 30 report says it strengthened protections across users, workspaces, organizations and model families, closed a replay pathway, and added output checks. That report establishes the mitigation it describes; it does not disclose enough implementation detail to call it exactly the paper’s proposed cryptographic design. (OpenAI’s incident report.)

Anthropic’s preserved-thinking policy creates a different integration constraint. The Opus 5.5 launch applied it to that model and Fable 5.1 for API accounts created on or after August 31, 2026. The current documentation, checked October 11, ties retained thinking to the prefix against which it was produced. Changing earlier messages or tool results can invalidate later thinking. It also documents server-side editing and client-side compaction that discards stale thinking, so “no compaction at all” would be the wrong criticism. The conflict is with keeping those artifacts while independently editing the earlier context. (Launch policy, preserved-thinking rules.)

Several chapters depend on owning that editing policy: Chapter 2’s ephemera, the changing GUI and speech views in Chapters 12–13, the cuts in Chapter 14, the later memory in Chapter 22, and Chapter 23’s recorded recall attachments, which survive until a checkpoint. They do not all have the same lifetime. They do share the ability to stop sending material without asking a provider to make the cut. Beyond this codebook, any agent that needs to see its current state ephemerally is affected by such a constraint: a family assistant tracking a conversation, a virtual tabletop tracking game state, an accessibility tool streaming its reasoning to a developer who cannot see the screen.

Protecting hidden reasoning is a legitimate requirement. So is choosing a service compatible with the context policy the agent already implements. This exercise takes the latter route instead of designing a new policy around preserved thinking. Current Anthropic examples elsewhere in this edition stay on supported older models such as Sonnet 5; a newer catalog entry is not proof that the existing ephemeral-context behavior works with it.

This chapter migrates the agent to OpenAI. The vendor seam built in Chapter 2 and tested in Chapter 15 against three providers now faces the migration that motivated the first-edition account. The investment in the agent depends on the answer: if the seam works as designed, this is a refactor. If it was aspirational, this is a rewrite.

It is a refactor.

The credential seam

The existing pattern is a static API key: resolved at startup, stored on the configuration struct, passed to every request unchanged. This client treats it as a constant. The service can still revoke or expire it; a constant in configuration is not a promise from the provider.

OAuth credentials are not constants. An access token expires in about an hour. The refresh token that renews it is invalidated the moment a new one is issued. A concurrent refresh can lock the account out of both tokens. The HTTP layer must handle all of this without implementing token rotation in every renderer.

The CredentialProvider interface has two methods. GetBearerToken returns a valid bearer token or an error. Kind returns whether the credential is an API key or an OAuth token. The HTTP layer calls GetBearerToken and places the result in the Authorization header. Renewal stays with the provider; HTTP can request it after an authentication failure without taking ownership of the stored tokens.

The API-key provider is a single field wrapping a string. It returns that string every time and never fails. The OAuth provider holds protected profile state and coordinates token refresh. It checks the expiry, refreshes if needed, and returns the current access token. Both providers produce an identical header.

The credential provider stays off the renderer interface. Ensemble owns the auth store. Agent selects a funding mode, and Engine obtains the bearer just before HTTP through its request-local configuration. The renderer needs only the selected route’s public capabilities: for example, whether tools need a namespace. It does not need an access token to turn history into bytes.

This distinction also keeps offline replay offline. Rendering a saved conversation must not refresh a credential or require an account. A developer adding another renderer learns the neutral conversation and that provider’s wire format, without implementing OAuth. The seam’s job is to make the caller’s life boring.

OAuth from first principles

A distributed local application cannot hide a shared client secret. A web server can keep one on its backend, but a binary running on the user’s machine can be decompiled, inspected, and copied. Authorization Code with PKCE solves this: instead of proving you possess a long-lived secret, you prove that the app finishing the flow is the same app that started it.

The mechanism is a verifier and a challenge. Before redirecting the user to the authorization server, the agent generates 32 random bytes, base64url-encodes them without padding as the verifier, and hashes that verifier string with SHA-256. The base64url-encoded digest goes in the authorization request; the verifier goes in the token exchange. The server checks the same transformation. An attacker who intercepts the code still needs the verifier, which is sent only in the token exchange.

The agent binds a TCP socket to 127.0.0.1 on any available port, with the path /auth/callback. The host must be the literal 127.0.0.1; the OpenAI documentation says “Do not substitute with localhost.” The path must be exactly /auth/callback; their documentation says “/callback does not match /auth/callback.” Only the port may vary. This makes the coding agent, for exactly one HTTP request, a web server. A tool-calling engine that reads files and runs processes now listens on a socket and serves a redirect.

The authorization request includes several things that matter beyond PKCE. A state parameter prevents cross-site request forgery: the agent generates a random value, sends it in the request, and rejects any callback that returns a different one. A nonce prevents replay: it is embedded in the returned ID token and validated on receipt. A stable ext_agent_host_id identifies the installation. An RFC 8707 resource parameter (https://api.openai.com/v1) appears on the authorization request and is repeated at code exchange.

On first registration, the client_id is the bootstrap value dynamic_agent_client. The authorization callback returns an issued client_id alongside the authorization code and state. Persist the issued ID before exchanging the code. All subsequent requests for that registration use it. A returning callback may omit the ID; if it supplies a different one, reject it.

The course flow uses this callback-based registration rather than a separate RFC 7591 registration request. The bootstrap dynamic_agent_client is never valid for token exchange. Send agent_name_hint=Ensemble on first registration and omit it when reauthorizing. The requested scopes include identity, offline access, resource.invoke and chatgpt.tokens.use.direct. These small fields are part of the protocol, not labels to improvise. (Registration and sign-in.)

The user’s browser opens. They sign in. OpenAI redirects to the loopback listener. The agent extracts the code, the state, and the issued client ID, then shuts down the HTTP server. One request served. The agent returns to reading files. A reader who has followed this book from chapter 1 will notice the irony: the tool that runs shell commands now runs a shell command’s inverse, listening for network input instead of producing it.

Identity is not permission

A successful login proves who the user is. It does not prove the user has granted plan usage. Two separate checks are required, and both must pass before inference.

The token exchange returns three tokens: an access token for API calls, a refresh token for renewal, and an ID token for identity. The ID token is a signed JWT. Validating it requires fetching OpenAI’s published JWKS (JSON Web Key Set), verifying the signature against those keys, and then checking five claims: issuer exactly matches the trusted https://auth.openai.com URL, audience matches the issued client_id, the token has not expired, and the nonce matches the one sent in the authorization request. The sub claim is the stable account identity. Keep the issued client ID with it: the same email, or the same person in another workspace registration, is not a reason to merge token sets. A returning verified identity must match the account being renewed before replacing its credentials.

The second check is the granted scope. The token response includes a list of scopes the user authorized. Among them, chatgpt.tokens.use.direct means plan-usage inference is permitted. Without it, identity may be saved, but plan inference remains disabled. Refuse that request rather than quietly trying an API key. Login and permission to spend are separate results.

The discovery document inspected during the original implementation listed scopes_supported as openid, profile, email, and offline_access. It did not advertise the plan-usage scope. The missing catalog entry did not make the scope optional. A developer implementing against the discovery document alone will build a login that works and an agent that cannot infer. Inspect the token response itself for the granted scopes. The current sign-in contract likewise makes that grant a separate inference gate.

Tokens that expire

The access token is valid for about one hour. The refresh token is valid for about thirty days. Those are the documented lifetimes on October 11, not constants to substitute for the returned expiry. The agent tracks the expiry and refreshes proactively: when the current time passes five minutes before expires_at, the agent sends a refresh request before the next inference call.

Refresh-token rotation is a security feature that punishes mistakes. Each refresh response returns a new access token and a new refresh token. The old refresh token is dead the instant the server issues the replacement. If two threads both see an expired access token and both attempt to refresh, the first one succeeds and the second one submits a dead token. The server treats that as a potential replay attack and may invalidate both tokens.

The fix is mechanical: serialize refresh operations per profile. A mutex handles goroutines within one process; two clients sharing a credential file need cross-process coordination too. The accepted store locks and reloads the profile before deciding whether to refresh. A second request uses the replacement already saved by the first instead of rotating the old token again. Save both new tokens atomically before using either of them. If the process crashes between receiving the tokens and persisting them, the old refresh token is already dead and the new one is lost. Atomic persistence means writing a temporary file and renaming it, or using a transaction. Writing two fields in sequence can leave an unusable mixed profile. Atomic replacement prevents that partial local state; it cannot recover a new token lost between server-side rotation and local persistence. (Token lifetimes, refresh and storage.)

Six refresh errors are terminal: invalid_grant, invalid_refresh_token, token_expired, refresh_token_expired, refresh_token_invalidated, and refresh_token_reused. Any of these means the credential is unusable. Keep the issued client_id and host ID, discard the tokens, and re-authenticate from scratch. The user signs in again, but the agent remembers who it is.

Network errors and HTTP 5xx are transient. Retry with exponential backoff. The critical distinction: a terminal error is the server saying the credential is dead. A transient exchange failure does not establish that: a reachable server can return a temporary error too. Retain the stored credentials. A 401 on inference alone does not establish revoked refresh credentials; this implementation attempts renewal once through the same funding source, and clears tokens only after a terminal refresh rejection. (Error recovery.)

The Responses API

The Responses API is a different wire format for the same conversation. Messages become input items. System-role messages become developer-role messages. The streaming event names change. HTTP 200 opens the transport; response.completed establishes completed inference. An incomplete or failed stream does not become a successful conversation fact merely because text appeared. The local conversation stays vendor-neutral while its encoding changes.

ChatGPT-plan HTTP requests carry restrictions. store: false and stream: true are mandatory, and input carries the required history. The current route profile excludes temperature, top_p, max_output_tokens, previous_response_id, background, conversation, metadata, max_tool_calls, moderation, multi_agent, prompt, prompt_cache_retention, safety_identifier, top_logprobs, truncation, and user. The original printed list omitted user while including previous_response_id; the HTTP route excludes both. The capability table keeps these route restrictions separate from the model table. A renderer reads the selected profile instead of repeating policy decisions throughout its message loop.

Local function tools go inside a namespace on this plan route. Preserve the returned namespace separately from the function name, and carry the call ID into the function_call_output. A model asking to read a file is only half the transaction: the next request must contain the actual result correlated to that call. (Current plan limitations, models and inference.)

The top-level instructions field is legal on the plan route. It is a plain string, so it cannot carry its own content-block breakpoint. That does not make its bytes inherently uncacheable: a later reusable prefix can include earlier instructions. This renderer uses a developer-role content block for the constitution so the supported API-key route can place an explicit boundary there.

The first subscription attempt exposed a route difference that the original chapter had missed. It returned HTTP 400 with invalid_parameter, naming prompt_cache_options. The same explicit mode had worked on the API-key route. The accepted plan profile therefore omits both that option and its associated breakpoint markers. Only the option’s rejection was measured; the marker omission is a conservative choice for the paired mechanism. Changing credentials did not change the model name, but it changed which request was admissible.

Keep explicit caching on the supported API-key route: set prompt_cache_options.mode to "explicit" and place the markers on eligible content blocks, within the four-marker budget. The published GPT-6.1 Sol standard rates for prompts through 272K input tokens are $2 per million fresh input tokens, $0.10 cached input, $2.50 cache writes and $10 output, verified October 11. Cache reads are 0.05x fresh input; cache writes are 1.25x. Those API prices explain why the boundary matters. They are not a subscription invoice or proof that a request received a cache grant. (September 29 model release.)

The migration is per-model. SurfaceResponses is a fact in the ModelFeatures table, set on specific model rows. Earlier models stay on Chat Completions; newer models move to Responses. A test pins the boundary so that a blanket vendor-wide flip cannot silently move tested models onto an untested surface.

The first-edition coder found four artifacts waiting for this migration in that implementation. provenance.go declared SurfaceResponses and never wired it. delta.go documented that StreamAll deliberately excluded StreamReasoningSummary. openai.go carried a comment that encrypted reasoning was “a Responses-API concept … for a renderer that can use it.” The gpt-5.6-sol row recorded that function tools with reasoning were refused on Chat Completions, and that the fix was the Responses API. This chapter was someone doing it. The new implementation keeps the same lesson without requiring those historical filenames: authentication and wire format have separate seams, and the selected Responses models can now use reasoning and tools together.

The stream that had already finished its tool call

After removing the unsupported cache option, the subscription request reached the model and still failed. The body contained SSE, but the parser selected its whole-JSON branch. Fixing that decision exposed the second assumption: a completed read_file item had already arrived in response.output_item.done, while the terminal response.completed carried an empty output array.

The parser needs both parts of the protocol. Detect the stream without waiting to buffer its entire body, retain completed items by output index, and use them when terminal output is empty. A nonempty terminal output remains authoritative. In either case, terminal success and usage must arrive before those items become conversation facts or executable tool calls. The fact that a tool’s arguments have streamed is no permission to execute a response that subsequently fails.

The captured stream made both defects reproducible without another model call. A parser test that always repeats every completed item in the terminal array cannot expose the second defect. The real route had done less repetition than the fake, which was enough to lose a perfectly good tool call.

Reasoning summaries

Reasoning summaries are model-generated descriptions of private thinking, streamed separately from the assistant’s visible answer. They are not the private trace itself. Earlier adapters already distinguished displayable thinking from opaque replay material; Responses needs the same distinction. Preserve encrypted reasoning for compatible replay without reading or speaking its ciphertext.

Bill has no macular vision and reads code at about 80 words per minute. He listens to model output at about five times speaking rate. A reasoning summary that arrives as a single paragraph after the answer has lost its chance to help him intervene. The value is in the delta: hearing the model think one phrase at a time while the answer is still forming, and sending a hint to redirect the model before it finishes the wrong approach. This is the accessibility payoff for the entire migration.

The first-edition coder treated the reasoning-summary gate as a research question before any code was written. Live measurement against gpt-6.1-sol with reasoning.summary: "detailed" and effort set to high produced 314 summary deltas across 3 parts. The auto setting produced 186 deltas. The concise setting produced 4. Summaries stream, they produce enough content for real-time listening, and the variation across settings is large enough to warrant a configuration knob.

The first probe returned zero summary deltas and looked like a capability gap. The prompt was trivial and generated 18 reasoning tokens. The coder suspected there had been too little reasoning to summarize. A single sample nearly produced a “this does not work” report. Measure with a prompt that makes the model think.

That October 2 report is evidence of those probes, not a promise about every response. In the later student run, the API-key session produced 90 public-summary deltas. The subscription session requested detailed and used 165 reasoning tokens on its final response, yet returned no public summary at all. More reasoning is not a guarantee of a summary. Completion and shutdown must not depend on hearing one.

The observer receives summary events through the existing observation interface. Summary deltas are a new event kind, separate from assistant-text deltas. They are delivered incrementally, kept separate from the assistant’s visible text, and preserved when a tool call is adjacent. A response that interleaves reasoning, tool calls, and assistant text must emit every event in stream order. The existing part identities keep the streams associated with their finals. The GUI can feed summary phrases to the speech queue while the response continues, without merging them into the answer or speaking the encrypted item that accompanies them.

The billing state machine

The agent now has two funding sources: a ChatGPT subscription and a metered API key. Switching between them is a state transition that the user must authorize and the agent must announce.

Three modes. chatgpt: all inference uses the OAuth credential. api: all inference uses the API key. chatgpt_then_api: inference starts on the subscription and falls back to the API key only when the subscription quota is exhausted. The fallback requires an explicit flag (allow_metered_fallback) to be true. The safe default is false: a surprised bill is worse than a paused agent.

The error codes that drive transitions are specific. subscription_sharing_usage_limit_exceeded is the signal for a plan-usage limit, which can be app-specific rather than the whole subscription being empty; if fallback is allowed, the agent transitions to API billing and announces the switch before sending the first metered request. subscription_sharing_usage_unavailable means temporary overload: back off, do not fall back. subscription_sharing_unsupported_capability means the request used a feature the plan route does not support: adapt the request or report the limitation. A 401 needs credential or permission diagnosis. Attempt the bounded same-source renewal described above; a terminal refresh error requires reauthorization, while a transient failure does not justify deleting the account or spending elsewhere.

The announcement rule is the mechanism that prevents silent cost. Before the first metered request, the agent emits a clear observer event naming the billing source. The user hears it (or sees it, or reads the log) before any money is spent. Metered fallback is a decision, never an accident.

The accepted implementation takes the permitted smaller choice: it rejects chatgpt_then_api and implements no automatic fallback. Both supported modes announce their selected funding source before the first request. A successful login selects chatgpt for later launches unless explicitly overridden. Logout leaves that selection in place, so removing a subscription credential cannot silently activate an API key already present in the environment.

Model discovery uses the OAuth token. GET /v1/models returns the models available under the subscription, filtered by visibility: "list". The slug field goes in the request; the display_name goes in the UI. The same endpoint, hit with an API key, returns a different model list reflecting the API-key tier’s access. Two credentials, two views of the same catalog.

Choose from the account’s actual catalog and the model routes the application supports. A name being available from the provider does not add a missing transport row to the program. The public endpoint for this exercise is https://api.openai.com/v1/responses; it does not use another application’s private credential store or a backend endpoint. (Account-specific model discovery.)

Exercise, graded

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 16

Run from the repository root, optionally supplying the core path and -gui DIR for its separate GUI. Keep the seven original weights:

Check Points Observable behavior
credential-provider 15 Selected credentials authenticate actual requests; an unusable selection cannot become an API-key request
oauth-flow 15 Real login follows the loopback/PKCE flow, validates identity and checks the inference grant
token-refresh 15 Expiring credentials rotate and subsequent inference uses the replacement bearer
responses-format 15 Plan format, completed output and the correlated file result survive the real tool loop
cache-breakpoints 10 API-key developer content carries an explicit breakpoint; the plan profile omits the paired explicit mechanism
reasoning-summaries 15 Public summary deltas reach the GUI before completion and remain separate from assistant text
billing-mode 15 Actual failures preserve the selected funding source without unauthorized fallback

Total: 100 points, seven checks; no inherited parity row.

The grader starts external OAuth and Responses fakes and runs the actual clients against them. Signed JWTs, a published fake JWKS, rotating tokens and real tool-result bytes exercise the boundaries without accessing a personal account. A login that never reaches inference cannot prove a billing rule; a copied error code cannot prove that the Agent treated the turn as failed.

The numeric run is a bounded sample of the contract. Review the actual owner relationships, the full identity-validation cases, cross-process refresh coordination and atomic replacement separately. The retained browser tests exercise incremental summary speech; visible WebSocket events alone do not prove native speech delivery. Neither a fake summary nor a passing score guarantees that a live model will provide one.

For a human run, build the core from your implementation directory. The matching reader snapshot is solutions/ch16:

go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch18 .

Use a fresh workspace and a dedicated profile. This keeps the exercise’s conversation and sign-in separate from another application’s credentials. The profile directory contains secrets; the ordinary conversation save does not.

chapter18_work=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$chapter18_work"
mkdir -p skills/base profile
chmod 700 profile
export EN_HOME="$chapter18_work/profile"
export EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base
cat > skills/base/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: base
type: primary
description: Read the local scheduling exercise and explain the result.
tools: read_file
---
Read requested files before answering. Keep public explanations separate
from tool results. Never invent file contents or a successful operation.
EOF
cat > schedule.txt <<'EOF'
Two identical workers. Each job uses one worker and cannot be split.
Job duration prerequisites
A   4        none
B   3        none
C   5        A
D   2        A
E   4        B
F   3        C,E
G   2        D,E
H   1        F,G
EOF

Sign in through your browser, inspect the safe status and discover models available to that account:

/tmp/ensemble-ch18 auth login
/tmp/ensemble-ch18 auth status
/tmp/ensemble-ch18 auth models

auth login --print-url also prints the authorization URL while opening the browser. It does not print access or refresh tokens. The client uses EN_HOME when supplied; otherwise it chooses its own ensemble directory under the operating system’s user-config location. Keep the same selection for login and inference. A verified identity without plan permission is shown as disabled for inference, rather than silently spending through an API key.

The recorded task used gpt-6.1-sol. If it is available to your account, start the supported Responses route explicitly:

LLM_VENDOR=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-6.1-sol \
OPENAI_BILLING_MODE=chatgpt OPENAI_REASONING_EFFORT=high \
OPENAI_REASONING_SUMMARY=detailed \
/tmp/ensemble-ch18 --skills-dir skills chat

Enter this prompt and wait for the completed answer:

Read schedule.txt. Find a minimum-duration schedule for the two workers. Give each worker's job intervals and prove that a shorter schedule is impossible.

A lower bound is the dependency chain A–C–F–H: 4+5+3+1 = 13. One feasible schedule places that chain on the first worker and B0–3, E3–7, D7–9, G9–11 on the second. The Agent must actually read the file; knowing the answer in advance is no substitute for checking the tool result in the next request.

A summary may arrive while the model is working. You can send a hint through the existing chat input, but do not wait for a summary as the condition for ending the session. After the answer completes, EOF ends chat normally and saves the conversation. To exercise API-key billing instead, use the same launch with OPENAI_BILLING_MODE=api and the provider key configured as in Chapter 0. That is an explicit change of funding source.

When finished with the dedicated profile:

/tmp/ensemble-ch18 auth logout

Logout attempts remote revocation, removes local tokens and keeps the registration and host identity. If remote revocation cannot be confirmed, the client reports that fact. It does not turn subscription billing into API billing on your behalf.

Taking it for a spin

The actual student API-key run used the scheduling task above with GPT-6.1 Sol, high reasoning and detailed summaries. It read the file and produced a valid schedule with makespan 13. The three requests included one prompt and a hint-triggered continuation; they were not two independent prompted turns. Ninety summary deltas arrived. The hint reached the third request, after an intermediate answer, and the process exited normally in 14.51 seconds.

The subscription path took more work. First came the HTTP400 cache-option rejection. Then came a response containing real SSE that the parser tried to decode as whole JSON. Even with stream framing selected, the empty terminal output hid an already-completed tool item. The corrected parser retained that item and let the ordinary tool loop continue.

The final subscription run made two requests with no API key configured. It read the puzzle, put the correlated file result in the second request, and produced the same optimal 13-unit schedule. The response completed in 14.887 seconds. Both terminal output arrays were empty, so this was a direct exercise of the completed-item recovery rather than a fake that happened to include redundant data.

It also returned zero public-summary deltas despite requesting detailed. The launcher had tied its hint and eventual EOF to seeing a summary. The task finished; the idle CLI stayed open until the launcher killed it at 150.03 seconds. That run demonstrates the answer and tool loop, not graceful shutdown or a saved conversation. Changing the launcher’s completion condition was checked against captured events; no new paid run was made to turn the old timeout into a cleaner story.

The cache lens needed its own correction. Its earlier extractor recognized messages from the old API but omitted Responses input. Comparing only the remaining tools produced a reassuring prediction while ignoring the conversation. Including the actual input fixed the instrument. The final plan request pair shared a predicted 92.12% byte prefix, but both provider cache counters stayed zero. Each input was below 1,024 tokens. Stable bytes, a successful task and a granted cache hit remain separate observations.

The seam held, with repairs at the seam. The conversation and tools kept working while authentication, request encoding and streaming parsing changed. The migration required a Responses renderer; the claim that no renderer changed would erase the very work the chapter teaches. Its payoff is smaller and more useful: changing provider and funding source did not require rebuilding the Agent.

Chapter 17: The Crossover

The morning of the switch, I had two agents open on the screen. CodeRhapsody, the one that wrote this book. Ensemble, the one the book describes. Same hardware, same model, same prompt. One of them built by reading eighteen chapters of instructions. The other built by writing them.

If the agent that came out of this book cannot replace the one that went into it, then eighteen chapters taught a toy. If it can, the loop closes and the last chapter writes itself. Close it now, while every design decision is still fresh enough to debug. A month from now the memory is gone and the crossover becomes a project instead of a morning.

The first crossover took twelve days. The distance between passing a grader and surviving a workday turned out to be thirty-seven changes, a vendor caching bug, and this chapter.

TL;DR

The first-edition account counted thirty-seven changes on the way to a daily driver. They sort into four kinds:

  1. Loud failures that announce themselves within minutes of real use: part-ID collisions, a settings dialog that never saved, a Ctrl-C that killed the process without persisting the conversation.

  2. Silent failures where every request succeeds but something underneath is quietly wrong: a model selector that selected nothing, a credential provider that selected the wrong credential after a vendor switch, a startup resolver that sent an OpenAI model to Anthropic.

  3. Two-path failures where the live streaming path and the replay path disagree on what content looks like: text vanishing after a restart, resets that cleared the log but not the screen, a client that classified messages by guessing at turn state.

  4. Invisible failures where the output is correct and the bill is not: a cache diagnostic tool with a 100% false-positive rate, a route where cache reads first appeared around 22,000 tokens, and a plan-route caching gap that ended in a bug report rather than a code fix.

The existing checks had missed these paths. Daily use exposed them; focused regressions could then keep them from returning. A passing check establishes what it observed, which may be a smaller claim than its name suggests.

This chapter is a field report, with no new graded implementation. The historical repairs below explain failures to avoid, not defects to recreate. The final section follows the second-edition agent through a real Astra/high coding task: reading source, reproducing failures, editing a file and passing the unchanged tests. That is a concrete step toward replacing a daily driver; it is not the same as having written the next edition with it.

17.1 What Breaks on Day One

The following incidents come from the first-edition crossover and its running changelog, begun September 27, 2026. Names such as Hub, view_gui and the narration gate describe that implementation. The new implementation has already learned several of these lessons in earlier chapters.
