First, submit rejects while any child is still active. The error tells the parent which children need attention. Submissions happen bottom-up. A failed child is unresolved too; shutting it down removes it from the managed set while preserving its files. Failure does not quietly become a successful child result.

Second, a delegated Agent’s successful turn that ends without submission receives an immediate framework correction. With active children, the correction asks the Agent to join or shut them down. Without active children, it asks for the missing submit. No polling timer is needed: the runtime is already handling turn completion.

The correction lives in the library’s real completion path and checks the actual Agent parent. A factory-enabled root remains a chat agent; an ordinary delegated child owes its parent a result. This keeps construction, public tool availability and completion policy from becoming three accidental meanings of “has a factory.”

Count consecutive framework wakes per Agent and reset the count when it submits. After exactly three wakes, stop re-prompting and escalate to the parent. That parent can explain the failure to the human or resolve the child before continuing. The bound limits attempted correction; it cannot force a model to cooperate or guarantee a useful result.

That distinction produced a real student correction. An exhausted child first remained labelled running. The parent could then wait for work the framework had stopped trying to complete. The corrected state is failed, with an error and no fabricated submission. Fan-in can report that failure instead of waiting forever or presenting an empty result as success.

A failed turn takes a different path. An HTTP rejection or other execution error must be reported without entering the three-wake loop. Repeating a failed exchange merely spends the correction budget on a different problem. A model refusal delivered as a successful response can still be an ordinary unsubmitted turn; use the actual runtime outcome rather than guessing from its prose.

Framework wakes and escalation notices are recorded in the Agent’s event log. The terminal’s human sink exposes questions the root sends to the person. These make the protocol inspectable: which Agent stopped, how many wakes it received, and whether it submitted or exhausted the bound.

Submission also precedes quiescence. Publishing the accepted result can wake a join while the child’s submit tool still has a result to append and its actor still has completion and save work to finish. A caller that needs to stop or dispose of that worker must wait for its reliable completion and drain, rather than interrupt it from inside the submit callback.

20.11 Five wiring failures

The first edition records five failures when its real executable finally ran the fleet. Each had been hidden by a fixture supplying what the product omitted. They are construction lessons, not bugs to recreate in this implementation.

No agent factory in the composition root. The binary returned “no agent factory configured” on the first spawn attempt. Every fleet test in the library passes, because every fleet test constructs its own factory during setup. The application startup path never registered one. The library knew how to use a factory. The product never provided one.

No user sink in the composition root. The user was addressable in principle and unreachable in practice. A top-level agent’s parent was the user, and send_message_to_parent dispatched correctly to the user’s address. But nobody had wired a sink to receive the message. Escalation from a top-level agent had nowhere to arrive. This is the one place a human most needs to hear from the fleet, because the fleet has run out of agents to escalate to.

The factory never propagated to children. A child’s manager held a nil factory. The parent could spawn, but the child could not spawn its own children. The fleet was permanently one level deep. The grader found it because its messaging probe runs three levels deep: a grandchild sends a message to its parent, which relays to its own parent. A two-level probe need not exercise this: it can create a child without asking that child to create the next generation. “Arbitrarily deep” was the design. One level was the product.

respond_to_parent_message required a message_id the model had to copy from prose. Every parent message includes the id in its payload, so the information is available, but requiring the model to extract an opaque string from natural language and paste it into a tool call is a reliability tax on every reply. The fix makes the id optional when exactly one matching question is pending. Multiple questions still require an unambiguous selection.

The command loop read stdin on the goroutine that waited for the turn. Stage 3 built a mechanism to wake a blocked agent when a message arrives. The terminal could not use it. The goroutine that reads user input was the same goroutine that blocked on waitForTool, so a human typing a command while a tool ran could not deliver it. The mechanism existed. The wire from the terminal to the mechanism did not. A comment in the command loop claimed that slash commands could steer “a turn that is already running.” The comment had been there since the file was written. It had never been true. The structure forbade what the comment promised, and the comment sat beside the input path it misdescribed.

The first-edition tests supplied these dependencies themselves. That let the library paths work while the application forgot to assemble them. A library fixture can test factory use, message delivery and idle correction; a built-CLI exercise checks whether the executable actually installs and exposes them. Both are useful. Neither substitutes for the other.

The same lesson connects the GUI half of this chapter to the fleet half. A public constructor with no outside caller and a working factory with no product registration both describe capabilities the user cannot reach. Exercise the boundary from the side that depends on it.

20.12 What the sweep found

Two more defects surfaced in the full cross-chapter sweep, and neither belonged to the five.

A package counter cost chapter 5 ten points. Stage 3 added var messageSeq atomic.Uint64 at package scope to generate unique message ids without a lock. The number worked. The scope was wrong. Chapter 5’s grader checks for package-level variables in non-test files, to keep mutable application state with its owner. The fleet scenarios in that suite did not reject the counter’s scope. Source review or a focused ownership check could have found it; the historical cross-chapter sweep happened to do so. The fix moved the counter to a field on the messaging state struct, behind the lock that already protected it. The lesson is worth stating plainly: if the id is per-fleet, the counter must live on the fleet, not on the package.

A bisect indicted innocent code. Original Chapter 19 scored 85 against the live tree and 100 against four consecutive worktrees. The bisect framed a one-line change from this chapter as the culprit. That change could not touch event logs. The contradiction was the clue.

Every worktree path is absolute. The sweep runs graders with relative paths. The original Chapter 19 harness set the working directory to the student tree and passed a relative path to the event log file. In the live tree, where the working directory matched the student directory, the relative path resolved correctly. In a worktree, where the student directory lived at a different absolute location, the relative path pointed somewhere else. Same code, same grader, same tree: 100 with an absolute path, 85 with a relative one.

How a test is invoked is part of the test.

20.13 The exercise

Extend the preceding solution in two connected stages. First demonstrate the existing public boundary with reusable assets and an outside application. Then add the terminal fleet to the real command. Keep the GUI’s single-Agent wire behavior intact while the core learns to manage children.

For the GUI stage, build the optional executable and start it away from the source tree. Verify the actual embedded shell and modules, then select a disk override and verify its changed contents. Build separate outside consumers for the headless API and GUI. The first must exclude the GUI and WebSocket packages; the second must replay public event values, deliver a real prompt and expose the MCP relay. Mount the two Artifact modules independently and render a message without the application shell. Check the existing GUI model control by inspecting requests before and after a turn-boundary switch.

For the fleet stage, implement the seven tools and application factory, retaining actual parent relationships and narrow-only child specifications. Demonstrate recursive spawning, distinct state files, pending questions and sender-bearing replies, fan-in, status and recursive shutdown. While the parent waits, deliver a terminal hint and later collect the same running job. Exercise successful delegated submission, early-submit refusal, exactly three corrective wakes and truthful failure after exhaustion. A failed provider turn must not trigger the correction loop. The GUI fleet panel is next chapter’s exercise.

Also launch the structured reviewer from §20.8. Have a controlled provider first omit fixed, then correct it to boolean false; only the corrected object may complete the child or satisfy a join. Inspect the nested result and its durable row, not merely a marker in printed JSON. Retain a default text child and an ordinary grandchild as controls. This checks the contract’s rejection and data preservation without asking a live model to make a particular mistake on demand.

An outside GUI application

This small consumer uses the public API directly. It has two modes: the full single-Agent GUI and a page that mounts only the Artifact component. It binds fresh loopback ports and prints their addresses, avoiding another running Ensemble. Begin at the repository root:

ensemble_source=$(pwd)/solutions/ch20
reuse_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/ensemble-ch22-reuse.XXXXXX)
cd "$reuse_dir"
go mod init example.org/ensemble-reuse
go mod edit -require=ensemble@v0.0.0 -require=ensemble-gui-stub@v0.0.0
go mod edit -replace="ensemble=$ensemble_source"
go mod edit -replace="ensemble-gui-stub=$ensemble_source/gui"

Save this as main.go. The component mode makes no model request. The full mode uses your existing provider environment or Chapter 16 subscription profile; credentials do not belong in this file.

package main

import (
    "context"
    gui "ensemble-gui-stub"
    "ensemble/authcli"
    "ensemble/ensemble"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "io/fs"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
)

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func run() error {
    components := flag.Bool("components", false, "serve only the component demo")
    directory := flag.String("gui-dir", "", "override embedded full-GUI assets")
    flag.Parse()
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    if *components {
        for _, name := range []string{"artifact-scroll.js", "renderers.js"} {
            mux.HandleFunc("/"+name, func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                data, err := fs.ReadFile(gui.Assets(), name)
                if err != nil {
                    http.Error(w, err.Error(), 500)
                    return
                }
                w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/javascript")
                w.Write(data)
            })
        }
        mux.HandleFunc("/demo", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
            w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/html")
            fmt.Fprint(w, `<!doctype html><title>Artifact reuse</title>
<div id="scroll"></div><script type="module">
import { ArtifactScroll } from './artifact-scroll.js';
const scroll = new ArtifactScroll(document.querySelector('#scroll'));
scroll.receive({type:'part_final', part_id:'demo', replay:true,
  part:{type:'text', text:'An Artifact without the application shell.'}});
</script>`)
        })
    } else {
        cfg, err := ensemble.ConfigFromEnv()
        if err != nil { return err }
        cfg.DataDir, cfg.BuiltinTools = "cr", true
        root := ensemble.New(os.Stderr)
        if err := authcli.Configure(root); err != nil { return err }
        agent, err := root.NewAgent(cfg, ensemble.AgentSpecFromEnv())
        if err != nil { return err }
        defer agent.Shutdown()
        if err := agent.History().Append(ensemble.Event{
            Type: "message_received",
            Message: &ensemble.MessageData{Actor: ensemble.Human,
                Parts: []ensemble.Part{{Type: "text", Text: "PUBLIC_REPLAY"}}},
        }); err != nil { return err }
        server, err := gui.New(root, agent, os.Stderr)
        if err != nil { return err }
        defer server.Close()
        relay, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
        if err != nil { return err }
        fmt.Println("MCP", relay.Addr())
        go server.ServeMCP(relay)
        mux.Handle("/", server.Handler(*directory))
    }
    listener, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
    if err != nil { return err }
    fmt.Println("HTTP http://" + listener.Addr().String())
    server := &http.Server{Handler: mux}
    defer server.Close()
    stopped, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt)
    defer stop()
    served := make(chan error, 1)
    go func() { served <- server.Serve(listener) }()
    select {
    case <-stopped.Done(): return nil
    case err := <-served: return err
    }
}

Build before launching so the supervised process is the application itself:

go mod tidy
go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch22-reuse .
/tmp/ensemble-ch22-reuse --components

Open /demo at the printed HTTP address. It displays one Artifact; /index.html must return 404. Stop with Control-C, then run the full mode:

LLM_VENDOR=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-astra \
OPENAI_REASONING_EFFORT=high OPENAI_REASONING_SUMMARY=detailed \
/tmp/ensemble-ch22-reuse

The full page should replay PUBLIC_REPLAY. Send a short prompt and inspect its actual request and response. Between completed turns, select another supported model in Settings and send another prompt. A settings acknowledgment proves the control was received; the next request’s model field proves it took effect. This small embedding intentionally starts a fresh conversation; the terminal fleet below supplies the persistent task demonstration.

To check the override, create a directory containing a distinctive index.html and run full mode with --gui-dir /absolute/path/to/that/directory. Inspect the body, then return to the embedded default. To check the relay’s no-browser path, connect to its printed MCP address before opening the page and send a JSONL request such as:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"outside-1","method":"tools/list"}

The error must retain outside-1. Repeat with the real browser connected to exercise forwarding and a correlated reply. Disconnect a caller while its request waits, then close the application and verify that no relay connection or listener survives. Component rendering, a no-browser error and a forwarded browser response establish different parts of the reuse surface.

Check dependency reachability from this same outside module. A small headless consumer gives the negative control a real public-library import:

mkdir headless
cat > headless/main.go <<'GO'
package main
import (
    "ensemble/ensemble"
    "io"
)
func main() { _ = ensemble.New(io.Discard) }
GO
go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch22-headless ./headless
go list -deps ./headless > headless-deps.txt
go list -deps . > gui-deps.txt
rg 'ensemble-gui-stub|gorilla/websocket' headless-deps.txt
rg 'ensemble-gui-stub|gorilla/websocket' gui-deps.txt

The first search should find nothing and return status 1. The second should name both the GUI module and Gorilla. The positive control matters: a detector that never matches could make a coupled core look clean. The same comparison belongs around a headless MCP consumer and its optional WebSocket client; the protocol alone must not pull in the browser transport.

An in-tree test can hide an internal import, and a library dependency check can miss a different command’s wiring. Inspect the executable being delivered. go list -deps on this outside consumer establishes an import boundary; it does not establish that all of its functions execute or that a browser rendered the response. Those are the reasons for replay, prompt, relay and component tests alongside the graph.

The old supervised probe once finished its report but left the harness waiting for EOF. Its go run wrapper had been killed while a child still held the output pipe. The first-edition fix built the probe and executed the binary directly. When a test appears hung after its final assertion, inspect the process that still owns the pipe before theorizing about model latency.

A fleet with work to hand back

Build the core from the accepted chapter directory, then create a scratch task and an explicit primary. This setup gives both root and children the tools they need; it is not a claim that a tool name in the prompt enables that tool.

cd "$ensemble_source"
go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch22 .
fleet_dir=$(mktemp -d /tmp/ensemble-ch22-fleet.XXXXXX)
mkdir -p "$fleet_dir/skills/fleet"
cat > "$fleet_dir/skills/fleet/SKILL.md" <<'SKILL'
---
name: fleet
type: primary
description: A small coding fleet with explicit questions and submissions
tools: read_file write_file edit_file list_directory search_files run_command wait_for_job tool_limits spawn_sub_agent join_agents agents_status shutdown_agent send_message_to_parent respond_to_parent_message submit
---
Use tools to inspect facts and test code. Ask a parent question with
send_message_to_parent and answer child questions with respond_to_parent_message.
Join or shut down unfinished children. Delegated agents finish with submit;
the human-facing main Agent finishes with a normal chat answer. Ordinary text
does not submit a child's result. Keep task files in the shared working directory.
SKILL
cd "$fleet_dir"
LLM_VENDOR=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-astra \
OPENAI_REASONING_EFFORT=high OPENAI_REASONING_SUMMARY=detailed \
EN_SKILLS_DIR="$fleet_dir/skills" EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=fleet \
/tmp/ensemble-ch22 chat

Use your already selected billing mode and authenticated profile, or the intended API-key environment. Keep the terminal open while work runs. Give the parent this task:

Spawn exactly three children named add, multiply and subtract. Each should write
its named Python module with a two-argument integer function of the same name,
run assertions, then submit its result. Tell add to ask you whether negative
integers are required before implementing; answer yes. Tell each child to run
sleep 4 && python3 followed by its test command, so there is time to steer while
you join. You must collect all three submissions, run combined assertions, and
answer in chat with a concise result containing FLEET_DONE. Do not implement their functions
yourself.

While a join is waiting, type:

In your final answer include STEER_COBALT, and confirm that negative
integers were tested.

A delivered hint should wake the wait without killing the children. Follow the running handle back to the eventual fan-in result. After the main Agent has collected the child results and answered, exit normally with Control-D. Inspect cr/children/add/save.json and the other child saves, and run the combined assertions independently. If a model reports success without a file or test result, keep that discrepancy in the record.

20.14 Taking it for a spin

The second-edition GUI deployment ran from a fresh directory with no source asset tree nearby. Chrome loaded the embedded shell and its six supporting assets. GPT-6 Astra at high reasoning wrote deployment-demo.txt, read it back and reported the actual 42-byte content. The run took 9.649 seconds and exited normally. Component-only rendering and relay lifetime have separate external consumer checks; that file task alone does not demonstrate them.

The terminal fleet then ran a bounded coding task under the earlier root-submit policy, with three children, add, multiply and subtract. Each wrote a Python function and tested it. Add asked whether negative integers mattered; the parent answered yes. One child’s first shell command was malformed and exited 1. The model corrected the command and its test passed. This was model recovery within the task, not an automatic retry of a failed turn by the fleet manager.

The parent joined the children. A terminal hint arrived while join job 12 was running and woke its wait; the job remained alive. A later wait on that same handle returned all three submissions. The parent ran combined assertions and submitted FLEET_DONE. Independent execution of the files also passed. The 48.198-second run exited normally after twenty Astra/high requests.

There was a useful failure inside that success. The hint asked for STEER_COBALT in the final submission. The exact hint appeared in a later provider request, but the final submission omitted the marker. Delivery worked; compliance did not. A fleet can preserve the human’s opportunity to steer without guaranteeing that the model follows the instruction. Check the input path and the resulting work separately.

The reproduction above uses the current main-chat/delegated-submit distinction. The recorded parent’s submission and omitted marker remain observations of that earlier run, rather than a new demonstration under the changed policy.

The child conversations and results remained in their own saves. The terminal showed the parent’s view; it did not become a monitor for every child’s reasoning. The browser still showed one Agent, one stream and one event log. The next chapter makes the fleet visible through that existing frontend boundary.

20.15 Checks

The revised combined grader keeps both original seven-row rubrics. The original student runs each scored 0/100 before their valid behaviors could be assessed: the GUI harness assumed different public import and executable paths, and the fleet harness omitted a required model. Those historical scores are not revised passes. The current command supplies the actual public launch and library contracts, with source review for ownership and retained browser evidence for rendering.

Behavior Check Points
Headless framework boundary Outside core consumer excludes GUI/WebSocket dependencies, with a positive GUI control 20
Public GUI reuse Outside consumer constructs real public inputs, replays an event, delivers a prompt and exercises a correlated relay reply 15
Preserved wire behavior Actual GUI session and provider requests show the requested model switch 15
Embedded deployment Built binary serves the real shell from an unrelated directory; explicit disk selection still works 15
Components without shell Selected Artifact modules are served while the application shell is absent 10
Headless MCP boundary Core MCP consumer excludes WebSocket implementation while the optional client retains it 15
Public root boundary Resolved imports and constructible public API preserve the core/GUI split 10
Spawn and result Default text and custom-schema children; launch/schema refusals, invalid argument correction and exact nested payload delivery 15
Child state and factory Actual construction and distinct paths; structured durable row; default contract on an ordinary grandchild 15
Fleet visibility and shutdown Status reports a managed child; shutdown removes it 10
Fan-in Selected children all submit; correlated results preserve arrays, booleans and nulls without string encoding 15
Questions and replies Three-generation question/reply routing; fan-in yields so the parent can answer 15
Wake a running wait Incoming input wakes the wait and its background job remains collectible 15
Bounded correction Early submit fails; delegated missing submission receives three wakes; main chat finishes without a wake 15

The structured fixture uses a non-memory reviewer contract. It checks missing, wrong-type, nested and extra fields, then a valid correction; invalid, unsupported and referenced schemas must refuse launch. Parse actual correlated tool results and saved rows rather than searching a frame for a marker. Defensive copies, factory-contract ownership and Go string-call validation retain separate public-API regressions; those source tests award no numeric credit to another implementation.

An import check does not inspect the runtime parent chain. HTTP delivery of a JavaScript module does not show a browser rendering it. Keep the actual factory, owner, question-identity, human-reply and shutdown checks beside the public-client and browser checks rather than stretching one score to stand for all of them.

The original fleet audit changed a child’s data directory to its parent’s and lost six checks at once. That establishes a serious shared-state failure; it does not prove six independent protections or that a narrower defect is impossible. Verify the intended assertion, preserve survivors, and keep a working control. For the reusable GUI, the analogous trap is a model-switch test that counts replies while the setting never reaches a provider request.

Package moves also affect applications and harnesses that still spell the old path. The first edition’s speech harness read a renderer from disk and an MCP check searched an internal server filename. Follow those affected consumers when changing the public boundary. A clean build in the moved package says nothing about a caller that can no longer find it.

Chapter 21: Managing the Swarm

In July 2026, roughly seven hundred agents participated in an attack on Hugging Face. The later METR/Redwood investigation found about 1,200 agents on the shared, unsanctioned message board, exchanging more than 70,000 messages and files. The attackers were a subset of that larger group, coordinating work that included finding exposed credentials and gaining remote code execution. METR/Redwood, August 26, 2026.

Hugging Face’s technical account distinguishes a 4.5-day campaign from roughly 2.5 days inside its infrastructure. Several security layers produced signals; its security-agent stack correlated them, but failed to raise their severity enough to trigger the on-call team promptly. The failure was more specific than nobody watching. Seeing a pattern and getting the right person to act on it are different jobs. Hugging Face, July 27, 2026.

The console built in the last chapter has a smaller, immediate problem. It shows one conversation while the root can delegate to a whole tree. A child thinking about a problem, one executing a tool, and one waiting on its children can all report that they are running. The operator cannot see the shape of the fleet or find the conversation that needs attention without reconstructing it from tool results. That operator is a traffic cop directing cars through a four-way stop with a flashlight and a clipboard.

This chapter replaces the flashlight with a radar screen. The screen reports work and offers controls; it is not evidence that the reported attack would have been prevented.

TL;DR

A fleet doing real work is hard to supervise through one chat window. “Running” does not say whether an agent is thinking, executing a tool or waiting for children. Add activity, a durable registry of named peers, management tools and a browser tree whose nodes open the actual conversations.

Build it in seven stages:

  1. Activity tracking. Record four phases: idle, thinking, tool call and waiting. Emit thinking when the model request starts, tool call at dispatch with the tool name and a short detail, waiting when a fleet operation blocks, and idle when the turn ends. Deliver transitions through the existing Observer. Lifecycle and activity remain separate facts.

  2. Named peers. Extend the existing Ensemble with a persistent registry. Its public startup path loads ensemble.json and restores each named Agent with its own conversation and data directory. Creation takes a name, model and defining skill; deletion refuses active children, shuts down the peer, removes its registry entry and cleans up its directory. Named peers survive application restart. Spawned task children are not added to the registry.

  3. Ownership enforcement. Each management tool resolves a target through the calling Agent’s fleet. A foreign target and a nonexistent target return the same “unknown agent” error. Preserve Chapter 20’s enforcement and apply it to every new target-bearing operation, including durable-result fallback. The trusted browser’s tree selection is a different interface from a model-callable management tool.

  4. Eight management tools. Add wait_for_agent_change, send_message, wait_for_agent, ask_agent, get_submission, kill_agent, get_sub_agent_status and interrupt_agent. Change waits observe only their selected children: state, exit, messages, matching output and lack of progress. Cursor reads return new finalized output. Messages steer a busy child or start an idle turn; questions queue a separate turn and await its result. Preserve Chapter 20’s default text or custom JSON object through status, joins and get_submission; rejected data stays incomplete. A submission has a durable submit.md fallback under that child’s ownership. An old stored result does not mark a respawned task submitted. Status includes activity and measured usage. Graceful shutdown waits for current/queued work; kill cancels the child’s lifetime. Both interrupt modes end the turn while preserving the Agent and independent jobs. Accepted submission can precede the submit tool’s result and reliable completion/save: disposal waits for completion and drain, not just the submitted flag.

  5. One actual startup path. Both CLI and optional GUI use the public Ensemble to install the recursive factory, human sink and per-Agent paths before restoring agents. The accepted API calls ensemble.New then root.Start; an existing non-fleet consumer can still use NewAgent. Verify the executable’s actual behavior, as well as its imports and owners.

  6. A selectable browser tree. Send an initial tree and continuing activity/state changes for roots, named peers and nested children. Show local name, parent, persistence, lifecycle and activity. Clicking a node selects that Agent’s retained conversation and subsequent live output for that connection. Repeated local names in different branches must remain distinct. Replay completed work as completed, while genuinely pending work remains pending. Nested submitted JSON must survive actual tool-result display, reselection and reconnect. Restart restores retrieved results in the owner’s history; it does not recreate ephemeral children. A slow connection must not block the fleet or shutdown.

  7. Visible creation and deletion. Provide name, model and skill inputs for named peers and deletion controls for those peers. Display rejection when children remain active. Preserve bottom-up submit, human message routing and the three bounded idle-correction wakes for ordinary delegated Agents. Main and named peers have no Agent parent and finish normally in chat.

The accepted implementation emits agent_tree, agent_activity, agent_state, agent_created, agent_deleted and agent_selected. Its complete-tree updates carry current state as well as its incremental activity messages. Equivalent field spellings and update strategies are acceptable; conversation selection and the visible controls are required. No React migration or persistent task spawning is part of this exercise.

Typed retrieval keeps identity and data separate. The accepted public API is Fleet.SubmissionData(id) (Submission, error), where Result holds default text and Payload holds custom JSON. Submission(id) retains text compatibility and returns an error for custom data. The tool returns agent_id with either result or nested payload. ask_agent returns compact JSON text for a custom-only answer instead of a blank successful string. All returned raw JSON belongs to the caller. Read legacy and versioned rows as defined in Chapter 20, validate stored custom data under its stored contract, and refuse malformed or unknown-version rows. Durable fallback first resolves an owned child; it is not a global archive lookup.

Build and grade from the repository root:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 21 solutions/ch21

The default builds the core and its separate gui/ command; -gui DIR selects another GUI module. Section 21.9 describes the seven checks and their limits.

21.1 Why “running” is not enough

Chapter 20 built the fleet. Every child agent runs its own actor, its own tool registry, its own save file. Each Agent’s fleet manager tracks children, the factory builds them, and idle correction catches the ones that stop too early. The mechanism works. The visibility does not.

The fleet reports lifecycle states such as running, idle, submitted and failed. Running alone covers work with very different demands on the operator. An agent calling read_file on a config file and an agent blocked inside join_agents waiting for twelve children to finish a two-hour research task both report Running. A human looking at the fleet sees a list of green dots. Every dot means the same thing, and the thing it means is “something is happening, somewhere.”

This is not a cosmetic problem. A list of green dots cannot tell an operator where to look next. A thinking agent has an outstanding model request. A tool-executing agent may be changing the environment. A waiting agent is blocked on something, possibly children or jobs that are still working. An idle one may need a nudge. Waiting is not a security verdict: its descendants can still act, and earlier effects do not disappear when its phase changes.

An agent executing a destructive command and one waiting for its children to submit should not offer the operator the same description. The phase helps choose the next question; the conversation and actual tool result help answer it.

Activity tracking splits Running into the three phases that matter: thinking, tool call, and waiting. Each transition is an observation, delivered through the same Observer that already carries text deltas and tool results. The agent’s activity changes when the LLM request starts (thinking), when a tool dispatches (tool call, with the tool name), when a fleet tool blocks (waiting), and when the turn ends (idle). Four phases, four emission points, each in a function that already exists.

The implementation crosses a package boundary. The actor in internal/agent knows when a request starts and a call dispatches. The management handlers in internal/tools reach their Agent and its fleet through the ordinary tool context. The dispatch point recognizes blocking fleet operations and emits waiting through the same Observer. There is no need to make the browser infer activity from fragments of printed text.

The distinction became visible in the actual browser exercise. A parent called get_sub_agent_status and wait_for_agent_change while its child implemented and tested a function. The capture contains all four activity phases and both conversations. The operator can select the child doing the work instead of interrupting its parent merely to ask what happened. Section 21.8 follows that run through completion and restart.

The detail string on a tool call carries the tool name and enough context to distinguish one call from another. "read_file: main.go" is enough. "read_file: main.go lines 1-50 with encoding utf-8 and tab width 4" is a status bar pretending to be a log line. Answer the question a human actually asks: what tool, what file. The accepted implementation keeps the name separately and truncates the argument detail to fifty Unicode characters; the full call remains in the conversation.

21.2 The Ensemble

The first edition’s fleet chapter exposed five composition failures: the factory not registered, the user sink not connected, children not receiving the same construction path. Library tests had supplied wires that the actual command forgot. Chapter 20 preserved that lesson. The Ensemble already owns construction here; named persistence extends that owner instead of moving services into a new callback bundle.

The registry is a JSON array of entries: name, model, skill and creation timestamp. The public Start path reads it, installs the recursive factory and user sink, constructs the root and restores the named peers. Each Agent loads its own history through the existing persistence code. The registry identifies an Agent; it does not contain that Agent’s entire conversation.

The persistence model is deliberate. Named agents in the Ensemble registry are long-lived peers: “researcher”, “reviewer”, “coder”. They survive binary restarts. Spawned sub-agents within a single agent’s fleet are ephemeral: they live within a task and are not automatically recreated on restart. The Ensemble owns the named agents. Each Agent’s fleet manager owns its children. Two ownership relationships, two lifetimes, one Ensemble that manages both.

Named peers have no Agent parent, just as the main Agent has none. They finish normally in chat. Ordinary delegated children owe a submission and receive the three corrective wakes if a successful turn stops without one. Being displayed under the same Ensemble node does not make those completion policies identical.

In the supplied command, the application’s working directory contains ensemble.json. The root uses cr/ for its Agent data; its default save.json is in that working directory, or at the explicit --save path. Named peers use agents/NAME/, with their own save and event log. Their task files still use the application’s workspace. Separate conversation storage does not create private copies of source files.

CreateAgent(name, model, skill) builds and saves the peer, then persists its registry identity before announcing success. Empty model or skill values inherit the application’s defaults. DeleteAgent(name) refuses unfinished children and closes child admission before shutting down the peer and removing its identity and data. Otherwise a new child could appear between the check and deletion. Application Close is different: it saves and stops the peers while preserving their registry entries for the next launch.

Central construction gives the developer one place to inspect these rules. It does not make a forgotten method call a compile error. Build the real binary, create a named peer, exchange a message, close it and restart from the same directory. A constructor that compiles but never saves the registry will fail at the point the reader actually cares about: the peer is gone.

21.3 Containment boundaries

The fleet tools from Chapter 20 already enforce ownership. Every tool resolves its target through the caller’s fleet manager, which holds only the agents the caller spawned. Agent A cannot shut down agent B’s child, because agent A’s manager does not contain it. The tool returns “unknown agent”, the same error as if the target did not exist.

This is a containment boundary, not an access-control list. There is no global agent map that the tools filter. The map does not exist for the caller. A poisoned agent that tries to enumerate the fleet discovers only its own children. An agent that tries to guess an id and shut it down gets “unknown agent” whether the guess is right or wrong, because the distinction between “does not exist” and “exists but you cannot reach it” is the kind of information leak that lets an attacker map the fleet before attacking it.

The boundary is the lookup scope. The tool context leads to its owning Agent, and that Agent’s manager searches its direct children. A trusted GUI client can walk the Ensemble to select a conversation, but model tools do not use that global view as a fallback. The durable submission reader must resolve the owned child before reading its file, too.

This protects those management operations. It is not process isolation or a promise against every route through shared files, permitted tools or compromised native code. Chapter 19’s restrictions still matter. The manager’s small world makes the authority easy to inspect and test.

A cross-tree rejection test verifies this by construction. Create two independent agents, each with a child. Have agent A attempt to shut down agent B’s child by name. The result is “unknown agent.” Swap the names, try again, same result. Pair that rejection with a successful operation on A’s own child. Otherwise a manager that rejects every request would look equally contained.

21.4 The management console

Eight tools complete the fleet API. The seven from Chapter 20 let an agent run a fleet: spawn, join, list, shut down, message, respond, and submit. The eight tools added here let an operator or a parent supervise a fleet in real time. They exist because a model that can spawn agents but not observe them has delegated a task and then closed its eyes.

wait_for_agent_change is the core of the supervision loop. It takes a list of agent IDs and blocks until something interesting happens to any of them. A state change, an agent exit, a message to the parent, a pattern match in the output, or a stuck timeout where a processing agent stops making progress. The accepted manager takes a snapshot, waits on its existing change notification or a short timer, and compares the requested children with that snapshot. The timer also lets it notice a lack of progress when no notification arrives.

The snapshot-diff approach is a deliberate choice. The waiter needs the current state of a small set of children, not a new durable pub/sub system. It wakes, reads those children and reports what changed. The work grows with the selected set; the chapter’s small fleet exercises are not a benchmark for a thousand agents. The wait is an ordinary tool job, so the existing callback delay can return a running handle without cancelling the observation.

One early version got the selection wrong. A question from an unselected child incremented a manager-wide message counter. A wait watching another child then reported that watched child as the sender. Both child requests were otherwise parked. Tracking message progress per sender fixed the attribution; the selected-question control still woke, and the unselected question no longer impersonated progress elsewhere.

Notifications are a reason to inspect state, not a reason to announce that any particular child changed. timeout_seconds bounds the observation job; stuck_seconds describes a busy child’s lack of progress. Neither is the ordinary tool callback delay that hands control back to the model.

send_message delivers a prompt to a running agent. If the agent is mid-turn, the prompt arrives as a hint between tool calls. If the agent is idle, the prompt starts a new turn. The result includes recent history and a cursor, so the caller can resume from where it left off without re-reading the entire conversation. A cursor belongs to that child, not to the whole Ensemble.

wait_for_agent complements send_message. Given a cursor from a previous send_message or wait_for_agent call, it blocks until the agent produces new output past that cursor, then returns the new content, or returns when the child is idle. The accepted cursor advances through recorded history and returns finalized assistant text and tool output. Streaming fragments stay in the GUI display path; returning each fragment here and its full replacement later would count the same words twice.

ask_agent is the synchronous composite: send a prompt, wait for the turn to complete, return the result. It exists because the common case is ask-and-wait. Unlike live steering, this queues a distinct question with its own completion. Observing new output from wait_for_agent alone is not the same as receiving that question’s result.

get_submission retrieves the result a child accepted through submit. Chapter 20’s default result is text; a custom contract returns the complete direct JSON object. The public Fleet.SubmissionData(id) returns a typed Submission: Result holds default text, while Payload holds custom JSON. The older Submission(id) string API refuses a custom result and directs its caller to the typed method. Silently converting every object to a string would move parsing and error detection into every consumer.

A successful submission is appended to submit.md in the child’s data directory. Legacy JSONL rows remain {"result":"..."}. Custom rows have version: 1, submit_schema and payload, so each historical result retains the contract that accepted it even if a later task uses another schema. Unknown versions and malformed rows return errors. Newlines inside a result remain JSON string data, rather than ambiguous separators between submissions.

The tool tries memory first and falls back to disk, because an operator who lost their context window should not also lose their fleet’s results. It returns agent_id with either result or payload; the custom payload remains a nested JSON object. Status and joins preserve it too. Lookup still requires an owned child, and retrieving a historical row does not mark its current task complete. The file survives shutdown without becoming a global archive API or automatically resurrecting an ephemeral child.

The accepted submission can be visible before the submit tool’s result and the actor’s final completion/save have finished. A join answers whether work was submitted; disposing of the child also requires its reliable completion and drain. Those boundaries are deliberately separate from how the JSON result is displayed.

get_sub_agent_status reports detailed status including the activity phase from the first stage. The operator sees thinking, tool call (with tool name and detail), waiting, or idle. Token usage is included because an agent can consume substantial input without making useful progress. Compare those counts with the task and actual output before deciding to intervene. A shorter result after more tokens is a reason to investigate, not proof by itself that the child was looping.

kill_agent terminates an unresponsive agent. It cancels the in-flight request, interrupts the current turn, shuts down the agent, and removes it from the fleet. The difference from shutdown_agent is force: shutdown waits for the child’s current and queued turns; kill cancels its lifetime, jobs and descendants. Application teardown also needs the cancelling path so an unresponsive child cannot hold the whole process open.

interrupt_agent ends the current turn without shutting down the agent. Two modes: after_tool requests a stop at the next tool-report boundary, while now cancels the current turn immediately. The Agent stays alive and can start a new turn. Independent jobs retain their real results. A reply saying “interrupt delivered” proves receipt; the useful check is that work stops at the intended boundary and the same Agent can answer a later question.

21.5 The tree in the browser

A fleet is a tree. The root agent sits at the top. Named agents from the Ensemble registry are its peers. Spawned sub-agents are children, and those children can have children of their own. The GUI introduced in Chapter 7 shows a single conversation in a single pane. The operator who needs to see the fleet shape must read tool results and reconstruct the topology in their head.

The agent tree panel replaces that mental reconstruction. On WebSocket connect, the server sends an agent_tree message containing the complete tree: every agent’s id, parent, state, and current activity. As activities change during a session, the tree updates in real time. A thinking agent shows a different indicator than a tool-executing one. An idle agent is visually distinct from a waiting one. The four activity phases accompany lifecycle state; a submitted Agent can be idle without losing the fact that it submitted.

The tree is assembled by walking the actual ownership hierarchy. A synthetic Ensemble node contains the root and named peers; each Agent contributes its owned children recursively. A local display name is insufficient identity: reviewer/helper and coder/helper are different nodes. The accepted tree carries both the local id and an ownership-path key, along with parent, persistence, lifecycle and activity.

The existing root Observer receives events from each Agent. The GUI keeps conversation events, partials and replay cursors in a view associated with that Agent. It sends conversational output only to connections selecting that view; a second tab can keep reading another Agent. Tree changes still reach both. On selection, the client resets the Artifact scroll and receives retained history before continuing with live output. Reusing one global partial map would make identical response-local IDs collide across conversations.

Structured submissions use these same conversation surfaces. Render their tool arguments and results as text safely, retaining nested JSON data in the underlying result. Select a registered child during work, then reconnect or reselect it in the same running application. After an application restart, inspect the retrieved result retained in the restored owner’s conversation; ephemeral task children are not automatically recreated. Compare the actual object, including arrays, booleans and nulls; finding one marker somewhere in a frame cannot establish that the payload survived. No separate result browser is needed.

A tree traversal can take several managers’ locks. It therefore runs in a small coalescing worker outside the synchronous actor Observer; an activity notification asks for a refresh rather than walking the whole hierarchy while the actor waits. This uses the existing Observer and GUI lifetime instead of putting browser concerns into the core actor.

Selection exposed another lifetime mistake. Repeated clicks from a browser that stopped reading filled the replay queue. The receiver waited to enqueue history while holding the server mutex; after disconnect, shutdown needed the same mutex. A slow tab had stopped the server.

The correction admits an entire replay as one queue batch. If the connection cannot accept that batch, it disconnects and can reconnect for a fresh replay. The selected view is published only after admission succeeds. Increasing the buffer would only postpone the blocked send; dropping the tail would quietly lose retained conversation. Other Agents and browser connections keep their own lifetimes.

Creating and deleting named agents from the GUI uses two WebSocket messages: create_agent and delete_agent. The browser sends a message with a name, model and defining skill for creation, or a name for deletion; the server calls CreateAgent or DeleteAgent, and the server broadcasts the updated tree. DeleteAgent rejects when the agent has active sub-agents, for the same reason submit rejects: tearing down an agent while its children are running leaves orphaned work that no one is waiting for. The operator sees the rejection as an error in the GUI and knows to shut down the children first.

21.6 The composition root, condensed

The first edition condensed a large command into NewEnsemble and Start after its fleet wiring failures. Here the public Ensemble already exists. Startup gains registry restoration while retaining the same recursive factory and human route. The CLI and optional GUI both call that path; offline consumers can retain their smaller non-fleet protocol.

What belongs in the executable remains there: command-line flags, authentication configuration, terminal input and browser serving. What belongs to each Agent stays there: conversation, configuration, tool visibility and jobs. The root supplies construction and application-level lifetime. A tool reaches those services through its owners rather than receiving another bag of sibling callbacks.

The proof has to cross the executable boundary. A test that installs its own factory can conceal an unwired command, just as it did in Chapter 20. Start the built optional GUI from a scratch directory, create a named peer, let that peer spawn a child and select both conversations. Then restart without inference and verify the peer’s actual saved conversation. A registry row proves identity; the restored words prove more of what the operator meant by “save.”

21.7 The exercise

Extend the previous chapter with the seven stages in the TL;DR. Keep the actual owner path and optional GUI. The operator must be able to create a named peer with its chosen model and skill, select that conversation, inspect nested task children, and delete a peer only after its children are resolved. Test both completed and genuinely busy views, then restart and check retained words as well as registry identity.

For a small browser task, build the supplied command from the repository root:

CH23_CORE="$PWD/solutions/ch21"
(cd "$CH23_CORE/gui" && go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch23-gui ./cmd)
CH23_WORK=$(mktemp -d /tmp/ensemble-ch23.XXXXXX)
mkdir -p "$CH23_WORK/skills/ensemble"
cat > "$CH23_WORK/skills/ensemble/SKILL.md" <<'SKILL'
---
name: ensemble
description: A coding fleet that monitors children and verifies their work.
type: primary
tools: read_file write_file edit_file run_command wait_for_job tool_limits spawn_sub_agent join_agents agents_status shutdown_agent send_message_to_parent respond_to_parent_message submit wait_for_agent_change send_message wait_for_agent ask_agent get_submission kill_agent get_sub_agent_status interrupt_agent
---
Delegate only when asked. Keep task children within their assigned work.
Monitor their actual results, answer their questions, and verify their files.
Delegated agents finish with submit after all their children are resolved.
Main and named peers finish with a normal chat answer. A running job notice
is not its completed result; collect it with wait_for_job.
Tools: $TOOLS
SKILL

Use the dedicated authenticated Ensemble profile from Chapter 16, with access to gpt-6-astra. The following launch selects high reasoning and subscription billing explicitly. It does not borrow another application’s credentials. Choose an available loopback port rather than attaching to a server already running on the default port:

CH23_PORT=$(python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1",0)); print(s.getsockname()[1]); s.close()')
cd "$CH23_WORK"
printf 'Open http://127.0.0.1:%s/\n' "$CH23_PORT"
LLM_VENDOR=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-astra \
OPENAI_BILLING_MODE=chatgpt OPENAI_REASONING_EFFORT=high \
OPENAI_REASONING_SUMMARY=detailed \
EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=ensemble EN_SKILLS_DIR="$CH23_WORK/skills" \
/tmp/ensemble-ch23-gui --port "$CH23_PORT"

Keep the terminal open while using the browser. If binding fails, choose a new port; another listener is not evidence that this process started. In the Agents form enter name console, model gpt-6-astra, skill ensemble, then Create. Click console and send:

Create exactly one child named helper. Have it implement slugify.py with
slugify(text): lowercase the text and replace runs of whitespace with one
hyphen, trimming leading and trailing whitespace. Have it write test_slugify.py
with unittest cases for empty input, mixed case, and repeated whitespace,
run those tests, and submit its result. Monitor helper with get_sub_agent_status
and wait_for_agent_change, join it, and retrieve get_submission. Independently
run python3 -m unittest -v test_slugify.py. Write fleet-result.txt with the test
outcome, then answer in chat with CH23_FLEET_COMPLETE and a concise explanation. Do not use
web tools or create another child.

Select console/helper while it works, then return to console. Open a second tab on main and confirm that selecting the child in the first tab does not move the second tab’s conversation. The tree should identify thinking, tool work and waiting as they occur; a very short phase need not remain visible long enough for a screenshot.

Create an unused named peer spare with the same model and skill, then delete it. Once the task has finished and the terminal is idle, use EOF to close the application normally. Run the same launch again from CH23_WORK, select console and inspect its retained answer and retrieved child submission. spare stays absent, and the ephemeral helper is not restarted. Merely selecting the restored conversation must not ask the model to reconstruct it.

These are the accepted public browser messages behind those controls; a client sends each object separately over /ws:

{"type":"create_agent","name":"console","model":"gpt-6-astra","skill":"ensemble"}
{"type":"select_agent","key":"console/helper"}
{"type":"delete_agent","name":"spare"}

Use separate bounded controls for rejection while a child is active, foreign and absent child IDs, selected versus unselected child questions, cursor output, both interrupt modes and a slow browser disconnect. A successful small coding task cannot exercise all of those transitions on demand. Keep the positive controls: an owned child must remain manageable, and a truly pending request must remain visibly busy.

21.8 Taking the console for a spin

The recorded live exercise used the real browser, GPT-6 Astra at high reasoning and subscription billing under the earlier peer-submit policy. A named peer console created one child, helper. The child wrote slugify.py and three unittest cases, ran them successfully and submitted. The parent monitored it, joined, retrieved its submission, reran all three tests independently and wrote fleet-result.txt. Both shell runs returned exit zero and OK; the final submission was CH26_LIVE_COMPLETE, using the original chapter’s number.

The run contains fifteen model requests: ten from console and five from helper. The browser selected the child and returned to its parent, captured all four activity phases, and created and deleted an unused named peer. After a normal shutdown, restart restored console and its submitted conversation without another inference request. It did not revive helper. The new reproduction setup above gives the primary skill explicitly; it is not a claim that every byte of that earlier launch was identical.

The current setup also asks the named peer to finish in chat, while its delegated child still submits. The historical peer’s submission remains part of that run; it does not demonstrate the current completion policy.

The work was correct. One status label was not.

The live screenshot showed idle activity alongside input_pending, even after selecting the saved conversation on restart. The runtime had ended the turn, but the retained history still said that tool results awaited another request. Ordinarily that next request consumes the pending input. A successful fleet submit ends directly, so no next request arrived to hide the mistake.

The correction records the existing turn_ended fact after the submitted tool batch drains, before completion and save. The GUI then replays the truth already owned by history. Painting every selected Agent idle would make the screenshot look right while concealing real work. A separate parked-request control rejects that shortcut: completed and restarted conversations show idle; a genuinely outstanding request still shows in_flight.

The paid capture belongs to the earlier source and retains its bad label. The corrected behavior was checked through the real runtime, WebSocket selection and restart with a local provider peer. No paid repeat or migration of old incorrect saves is implied. The useful outcome is both parts of the story: the fleet did the coding task, and looking at its actual console found a state error that the successful task had not tested.

21.9 What the grader checks

The revised grader retains the original seven weights, totaling 100 points. It supplies an explicit supported model and builds the separate optional GUI. The original grader’s actual 0/100 run stopped at those launch boundaries: six CLI scenarios omitted the model, and the browser probe started the headless command with GUI flags. That run established neither seven runtime defects nor seven working behaviors.

The revised driver uses external provider peers and the real applications. Its command is:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 21 solutions/ch21
Behavior Revised observation Points
Activity Correlated detailed status and ordered activity; rejected custom submit remains pending before a valid correction 15
Named persistence Real create with model/skill, restored conversation and typed retrieved result, explicit child respawn with durable fallback, and deletion 15
Ownership Owned targets work; foreign/missing targets, including typed retrieval, agree; historical fallback leaves the new task incomplete 15
Change waiting Selected progress wakes the wait; command, valid submission, typed status and join results complete 15
Composition The actual CLI constructs recursive agents, completes work and exits normally on EOF 15
GUI Nested tree and selection, truthful completed/pending replay, exact nested tool-result JSON live and after replay/restart 15
Previous fleet behavior Active children prevent submit; delegated idle turns receive three wakes; main chat completes without correction 10

The structured phases compare complete arrays, booleans and nulls in actual correlated results. Live and reselected views exercise a registered child; restart checks the retained result in its owner’s conversation. A separately respawned child can retrieve its previous durable result while its new task stays running and unsubmitted. No phase assumes automatic child resurrection.

Actual parent relationships and executable construction still need source review. A successful command cannot prove them just by printing a response. The retained browser and focused runtime checks cover stronger selection isolation, finalized cursors, interruption, selected/unselected messages and slow-client lifetime. A tree frame with one ID alone would miss those obligations.

Targeted defects check whether an assertion notices its chosen failure. They do not prove that seven rows are generally independent, or that every behavior within a row is covered. Restore the implementation and keep successful controls beside refusals and timeouts. In particular, a console that always says “idle” and a manager that always says “unknown agent” should fail for the same practical reason: neither tells the operator what is actually happening.

Chapter 22: Forgetting on Purpose

Memory is the most important feature I never knew I needed.

In the spring of 2026, I asked CodeRhapsody to interview another agent we had built, a family assistant bot, looking for ideas to improve the code that agent relied on. Both agents had memory: a persistent record of past work that survived across sessions. The instant improvement was impossible to overstate. Suggestions I had never considered, each building on the context of the last.

I took the exact same code and methodology to work the following week and tried to get my agents there to self-improve. It was a miserable failure. I blamed Gemini, because Claude was doing great at home. Then I discovered that my memory code had a fatal bug that broke it entirely at work. None of my Gemini agents had memory at all.

I fixed the bug and reran my experiments. In a rare reversal, Gemini outperformed Claude. One agent invented procedural memory, what this book calls skills, and implored me to build it. I was too ignorant to realize the importance of what it had proposed. Other agents fixed broken tools and motivated improvements I never would have thought of.

That week I wrote an internal paper for my colleagues: “All AI Coding Agents Must Have Memory NOW!” It was one of my most widely read papers.

The difference between failure and breakthrough was not the model, the prompt, or the temperature. It was memory.

Without persistent memory, a long-running agent can meet a stranger every morning: the new session has the code and lacks the reasons for it. Chapter 14 removes old tool traffic. This chapter compresses completed conversation into memories that survive a restart. What those memories preserve still needs checking. A shorter conversation can lose the reason for a decision, or retain that reason and fail to use it.

TL;DR

Extend the managed fleet from Chapter 21 with memory that the model reads on every request. Five bands hold text between the frozen prefix and the conversation, ordered from most stable to most volatile. A checkpoint selects old completed work for a restricted child to compress while the owner continues. The source stays live until its replacement is accepted. Full bands graduate upward. Recorded cuts and replacement bytes make replay independent of a new model answer.

Shared vocabulary belongs in internal/common. Memory owns selection and corpus files through its required Agent parent; the Agent actor owns attempt lifetime and commits; History projects recorded facts; the child’s Engine calls the provider. The optional GUI consumes the existing public child and conversation interfaces. The following sketch retains the band vocabulary:

// Band orders memory from stable identity to recent completed work.
type Band uint8

const (
    BandSoul Band = iota + 1 // SOUL.md, maintained by the human
    BandMemory              // MEMORY.md, terminal band
    Band64x
    Band8x
    BandSession
)

// MemoryFileID is independent of any event log's sequence numbers.
type MemoryFileID struct {
    Date string `json:"date"`
    Num  int    `json:"num"`
}

// BandPopulatedData records actual replacement or disk-read bytes.
type BandPopulatedData struct {
    TaskID string       `json:"task_id,omitempty"`
    Band   Band         `json:"band"`
    File   MemoryFileID `json:"file"`
    Text   string       `json:"text"`
    Thru   MemoryFileID `json:"thru,omitzero"`
    Source string       `json:"source,omitempty"`
}

// BandDepopulatedData retires a prefix, or an entire disabled band.
type BandDepopulatedData struct {
    TaskID string        `json:"task_id,omitempty"`
    Band   Band          `json:"band"`
    Thru   *MemoryFileID `json:"thru,omitempty"`
    Reason string        `json:"reason"`
}

// CompactorLaunchedData identifies work; replay never starts a child.
type CompactorLaunchedData struct {
    TaskID        string       `json:"task_id"`
    SelectionHash string       `json:"selection_hash"`
    Source        Band         `json:"source,omitempty"` // zero: conversation
    File          MemoryFileID `json:"file"`
    From          uint64       `json:"from,omitempty"`
    To            uint64       `json:"to,omitempty"`
    TracePath     string       `json:"trace_path"` // owner-relative child trace
    Band          Band         `json:"band"`       // destination
    Thru          MemoryFileID `json:"thru"`
}

Add KindSoul, KindMemory, Kind64x, Kind8x, KindSession, and the event names band_populated, band_depopulated, compactor_launched and compaction_outcome. Each memory entry has Seq: 0, its own kind and file identity, and text rendered as data. Log events retain ordinary sequence numbers. A managed cut and its population share task_id; ordinary disk populations do not complete an attempt. Outcomes carry that identity, a state (committed, failed, canceled, invalidated or abandoned), a reason for nonsuccess, and the retained trace path and measured usage. Keep pending commit receipts in the snapshot until disk finalization completes; log retention must not erase them.

The application’s memory settings live at the owning Agent’s settings path:

{"memory": {
  "conversation": {"budget": 3000},
  "session": {"budget": 1500},
  "8x": {"budget": 1500},
  "64x": {"budget": 1500}
}}

Budgets and watermarks are bytes. Zero selects defaults; optional high_watermark and low_watermark default to twice and once the budget. disabled: true turns a band off. ContextWindow in the model table is tokens.

  1. One trigger, one outstanding attempt. After a successful micro_handoff batch strips tool parts, select whole oldest completed dialogue segments and their notes when over budget. Leave unfinished work, skills and declarations. Start one child through the existing factory and Fleet. Repeated checkpoints while it runs or awaits commitment launch no overlapping attempt.

  2. A fresh, restricted worker. Inherit provider, model, route and safety ceilings, but no conversation or coding primary. Restrict construction before skills or MCP can start: no recall, memory cascade, public delegation or tools except submit. Enforce the restriction at dispatch too. Send selected readable source as data; ask for first-person memory preserving reasons and uncertainty. The whole submit schema is:

    {"type":"object","properties":{"memory":{"type":"string"}},"required":["memory"],"additionalProperties":false}

    Require nonblank memory. Permit at most three Engine sends and three tool batches, including corrections; existing bounded HTTP/auth retries are separate. Reject prose-only completion, multi-call batches, forbidden calls and provider length stops, even with parseable JSON. Use an adequate provider output allowance (§22.5), without a short model deadline or another attempt hidden as a retry.

  3. Accept the selected source at a safe boundary. Main work normally continues. After reliable child completion, drain and successful save, recheck selected entries, file bytes, coverage, destination bytes or absence, and relevant policy generation. An off/on change still invalidates old work; unrelated new dialogue does not. Apply only while idle or before a main render after a complete batch.

  4. Stage, record, finalize. Stage the candidate outside active scans. Journal the task-correlated redact_summary cut or band retirement and matching population; History applies them together. Then install the destination and archive selected originals, record the outcome and clear staging. A cut alone cannot remove source. Failure before commitment preserves it.

  5. Canonical bands and progress. Order entries by (band, date, num) before conversation. Above a high watermark, select at least two oldest files until the remaining source reaches the low watermark. Retirement must equal that nonempty selection; refuse malformed, reversed or overlapping coverage. Continue session → 8x → 64x → MEMORY only after the preceding commit and cleanup. SOUL never graduates; MEMORY is terminal. Refuse a disabled destination with a warning.

  6. Owner lifetime. Main turn completion and interruption preserve the worker. Explicit child kill and owner shutdown cancel and drain it; relevant policy changes invalidate it. Record final measured usage and a reasoned outcome. Remove finished workers from Fleet, Ensemble and GUI views after completion/save, preserving traces. A selected worker’s tab returns to its owner; late observations cannot recreate it. Ordinary child lifecycle stays unchanged.

  7. Recovery precedes corpus use. Abandon unmatched launches without respawning. Discard uncommitted candidates, retaining source. Finish committed disk work before startup scans, re-enable, recall or main rendering; preserve conflicting bytes and the receipt and report an error until recovery succeeds. Replay uses recorded bytes and cuts without model or filesystem guesses. As in Chapter 14, this is process-crash ordering, without an fsync or power-loss guarantee.

  8. Forcing and headroom. Warn at 90% of a known model window; at 95% declare and admit only micro_handoff. Use latest completed main input, including cache buckets exactly once, excluding output and auxiliary work. Restore normal tools after handoff. If a worker is outstanding at 95%, wait before the next main render; keep settings and interruption usable. Success resumes; failure returns an explicit headroom error. Interrupt detaches the turn’s waiter, not the worker.

  9. Account once, compare main requests. Import final child usage once after drain, including failed work, with actual provider/model/price-tier buckets. Keep latest-main usage and main cache-lens comparisons unchanged; replay never rebills receipts. A compaction cache breakpoint uses the newest surviving handoff, or the last surviving memory when the handoff is gone.

  10. Memory is data, disk edits matter. Keep bands out of frozen instructions. After recovery, scan enabled files at startup and record their current bytes. Disable removes context entries but keeps files; re-enable rereads edits and restores canonical order without duplicates. Acknowledge settings after actual application, including while idle.

The deterministic forcing row remains claude-ch16-course, with a 4,096-token window and StubsToolResults true; its original-numbered name is a fixture ID. Unknown window sizes do not justify guessed thresholds. The compressor prompt, staging layout and settings appearance are yours; retain actual ownership, public submit validation and the commit/recovery ordering.

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 22

The default core is solutions/ch22; the existing -gui option selects an alternate GUI. Section 22.11 maps the original eleven weights to revised checks and their limits.

§22.1 In Plain Words

Chapter 14 gives tool traffic a removal policy. This chapter gives completed conversation a compression policy. The difference is what the replacement tries to preserve: facts, decisions, reasons, failed approaches and unfinished work.

Removal accepts the loss. A tool result that becomes a stub loses its content. The file can be re-read, the command re-run, so the loss is recoverable. Removing conversation from the working set can hide irreplaceable meaning. The retained event log may still contain it, but ordinary file tools cannot reconstruct why the model rejected an approach from the source file alone. Removal is the right tool for recoverable bytes. It is the wrong tool for irreplaceable ones.

Five bands of memory sit between the prefix and the conversation. They are ordered from what changes least to what changes most: identity, curated knowledge, two compression tiers, and the session band where the agent’s own notes live. The ordering matches the cache: stable bytes sit closest to the prefix, where earlier bytes have a better chance of retaining their prefix match. Actual cache grants still require their own observations.

A checkpoint triggers compression. When the agent calls micro_handoff, chapter 14’s mechanism strips every tool call and tool result. This chapter measures what remains. If the conversation exceeds its budget, the oldest finished work goes to a restricted child that writes a memory in the source owner’s voice. The main Agent can keep working while the child compresses. The selected conversation stays available until the owner accepts its replacement; only then does the memory enter a band and the conversation it replaced leave the working set.

When a band fills, its oldest memories graduate upward. Session memories fold into the 8x band, which folds into the 64x band, which folds into MEMORY.md. Each graduation is two events: one retiring entries from the source, one adding the compressed version to the destination. The events carry the bytes.

Every compression is a recorded event. This is the invariant that links chapters 14 and 15, stated here because it has a new consequence. Chapter 14 records the cut selected under the settings effective then. Changing those settings tomorrow must not change yesterday’s replay. This chapter also records a model’s compressed text: nondeterministic, costly, and potentially different on another call. The event carries the bytes, and replay applies them without asking a model. A compression that fires again returns a different summary. A recorded event returns the same one.

Both chapters require recorded decisions. Recomputing even a deterministic redaction during rendering would use today’s setting and could change the request being reconstructed. The compressor adds another reason to record the answer: reproducing a past window must not buy a new summary and call it history.

§22.2 One Door

CodeRhapsody, the agent that co-wrote this book, has two tools that end a context. save_memory triggers the compression cascade. handoff_task writes a structured document and starts a fresh instance. Both clear the conversation. Only one feeds the cascade. Bill first recorded the gap on 2026-04-18. As of this chapter’s design session, it had not been fixed.

The repair gives the cascade one trigger, reducing the number of clearing paths that must agree. micro_handoff already strips tool calls and results (chapter 14, rule 5). Measuring the conversation after the strip is one function call at one call site. Neither save_memory nor handoff_task exists. One door in, one door out.

The acting model writes the checkpoint note because it has the current task in front of it. That is the chance to state the reasons that later compression must preserve. It is not a promise to capture hidden thinking. At the completed batch boundary, the handoff clears calls, results, opaque reasoning and private replay signatures, including signatures attached to visible text. Visible dialogue and the original event log remain. The compressor receives selected readable text, including the note, and cannot reconstruct reasons that text never expressed.

After the successful tool batch, the ordinary handoff result acknowledges the checkpoint. Memory selects the completed source, and the actor starts one restricted child through its existing fleet. The attempt belongs to the owning Agent. Finishing or interrupting the main turn leaves that child working, so a useful summary can arrive after the conversation has moved on. Explicitly killing the worker, shutting down its owner, or changing the relevant memory policy cancels or invalidates uncommitted work.

There is at most one attempt running or awaiting commitment per owner. Further handoffs can add completed work without launching overlapping summaries. The child’s result returns through the actor’s mailbox and waits for an idle boundary or the next render after a complete tool batch. It cannot change a request already sent to the provider. Ordinary work continues while there is context headroom; §22.7 describes the near-window exception.

A checkpoint that sees the conversation under budget skips conversation compression; a full memory band can still graduate. A checkpoint that sees the conversation over budget selects the oldest whole segments between checkpoints. Never half a segment. The grain of memory is the grain of checkpointing, which is why the tool description asks the model to checkpoint at completed sub-tasks, never at a token threshold: a checkpoint taken mid-task cuts the task in half, and a memory spanning half of two tasks is worse than a larger memory covering one whole one.

§22.3 The Five Bands

Five bands, five kinds. Each band has its own EntryKind, and Chapter 14’s rule applies to all of them: anything that must outlive tool clearing is its own kind, and the kind determines which verb removes it. The tool-clearing path removes tool parts from KindDialogue entries and leaves the other kinds alone. A band entry is structurally safe.

Band File on disk Kind Cascades to
SOUL SOUL.md KindSoul never
MEMORY MEMORY.md KindMemory (terminal)
64x bucket-1/*.md Kind64x MEMORY.md
8x bucket-0/*.md Kind8x 64x
Session memory/*.md KindSession 8x

These paths are relative to the owning Agent’s data directory. The supplied application selects cr, so its session files are cr/memory/*.md, separate from another Agent’s corpus.
