Graduated source files receive .md.retired; they remain on disk but no longer match the active *.md scan. Their identities still reserve the next same-day session number after a fresh start.

A candidate being committed lives outside the active corpus; this implementation uses .compaction/pending.json. Neither band population nor recall scans that hidden staging record. A file containing a proposed memory must not become an active memory merely because the process restarted before accepting it.

The order is not cosmetic. The most stable band sits closest to the prefix, where its unchanged bytes can remain eligible for prefix reuse. Identity changes less often than curated knowledge, which changes less often than a compression that ran today. Two independent arguments, one about cache economics and one about reading order, give the same layout.

Band entries sit at Seq: 0 rather than at the Seq of the event that landed them. Seq exists so a redaction span can match an entry, and no span ever reaches into a band. Giving a band entry the landing event’s Seq would put the order of restoration into the context. Restoration order must not matter: switching every band off and restoring them out of order must produce the same context. Canonical placement by (band, date, num) makes the property true by construction.

Memory file identifiers are dates and sequence numbers, not event-log Seq values. A compressed file in bucket-0/ is named by the file range it spans: 2026-09-20-1_2026-09-26-3.md. The naming says “this file covers the first memory of September 20 through the third memory of September 26,” and it says so without any event log in hand. The memory corpus outlives any one log, and a range identifier tied to a log-specific Seq would be the wrong coupling.

§22.4 Two Events

Two event types handle all band changes, following chapter 14’s precedent of one event type and an enum field, rather than one event per band.

BandPopulated adds one memory to a band. It carries the text verbatim, because nothing downstream is allowed to look it up. The first design specified file references. Its review found that neither the pure reducer nor the renderer owned a place to resolve them. The file could exist on disk while the model received no memory at all. The boundary is simple: Memory reads the file, the actor records its bytes, and History applies those bytes without filesystem access.

A text part is sufficient. The media machinery from earlier chapters does not make a mutable filename into a replayable memory. Tomorrow’s edited file and yesterday’s delivered text are different facts, and the event must say which text was delivered.

BandDepopulated retires entries from a band. For graduation, it names a Thru file: everything at or before Thru is removed. For disabling, it names nothing: the reducer wipes every entry of that band’s kind, computed at apply time. The asymmetry with BandPopulated is the point. Removing need only say what goes. Adding must say what arrives.

A graduation is one of each: a BandDepopulated retiring the oldest source entries, then a BandPopulated landing the compressed version in the destination band. Disabling is one BandDepopulated alone. Re-enabling is one BandPopulated per file found on a directory rescan. CompactorLaunched records the attempt’s identity, selected source and child trace path. The matching retirement and population carry that task identity too: a disk rescan cannot accidentally complete a worker’s cut. An ordinary launch observation never becomes work during replay.

The submitted text is a candidate. The actor accepts it only after the child’s reliable turn result, shutdown/drain and required save succeed. History then applies the matching cut and population together and retains a commit receipt until Memory finishes the corresponding disk changes. A compaction_outcome records success, failure, cancellation or invalidation without changing the main turn’s state. These distinctions let a restart finish a committed replacement without mistaking it for an abandoned request.

§22.5 The Compressor

The earlier compressor made a direct model call and held the main turn until it returned. An October 14 trial exposed both a delay and a role conflict: the request inherited instructions telling the main Agent not to submit, then asked the compressor to submit memory. The provider completed with ordinary prose and no function call. The runtime refused it and retained the source. Making that same request asynchronous would have freed the main turn while leaving the contradictory instructions intact.

The replacement is a real child with a dedicated purpose. It starts fresh with the selected readable source, including role labels and handoff notes, delimited as data. It inherits the owner’s provider, model, route and safety ceilings, but receives no cloned conversation, opaque replay state or main coding primary. It loads no skills or MCP servers and runs no recall, memory cascade or context forcing of its own. The normal factory and ownership paths still construct it. Internal child construction does not grant public delegation tools to its owner.

The child offers exactly one tool, submit, with this complete argument schema:

{"type":"object","properties":{"memory":{"type":"string"}},"required":["memory"],"additionalProperties":false}

The result is {"memory":"..."}, with no result wrapper or JSON inside a string. Runtime validation enforces the declared schema before accepting a submission; the owner additionally refuses whitespace-only memory. The sole submit declaration with a memory property identifies compressor traffic on the wire. A submit-only ordinary child with a result property is different. Declaration and dispatch both enforce the restriction, including guessed tool names. A prompt asking the child to avoid file or shell tools would not remove those capabilities.

The compressor writes in the first person, as the source owner. “I found six dead settings fields” reads as memory. “The agent found six dead settings fields” reads as a report about someone else. The distant past is exactly the text a compressor writes, and if it reads as a briefing about a stranger, the compaction introduced the discontinuity the design exists to remove.

The child is writing someone else’s retained experience, rather than claiming the source owner’s work as its own new autobiography. Its instructions preserve decisions and why, failed approaches, uncertainty, constraints and preferences. Quoted instructions inside the selected source remain data. On a model requiring visible action explanations, an ordinary visible explanation precedes submit; that explanation stays outside the memory string. Hidden reasoning is no substitute for reasons the owner actually recorded.

One attempt permits at most three Engine sends and three tool batches, including correction and resend paths. A prose-only completion fails immediately. A batch with several calls or any tool other than submit is refused as a whole; accepting its first call could publish success before noticing the prohibited second one. There are no ordinary fleet idle-correction wakes and no second task that resets the budget. Existing bounded HTTP and authentication retries remain inside a send, so three sends is not a claim of three physical network exchanges. Failure retains the source for a later checkpoint to reconsider.

The ratio guides the writing; it does not justify cutting off a reason halfway through a sentence. File budgets are bytes, context windows are input tokens, and provider output limits govern another quantity. The accepted worker omits optional output caps on Chat and Gemini, keeps the Responses route’s existing behavior, and gives Anthropic its required allowance of 16,384 output tokens. An unsupported allowance fails visibly; the runtime does not silently substitute a model or truncate the memory. A provider length or incomplete-output finish also fails before dispatch, even if its partial JSON happens to parse.

The exported Engine.Compress API remains as a deprecated direct operation for existing callers. The normal actor uses the child path and has no direct-call fallback. The observed role failure and the accepted provider contracts are recorded in the compaction notes.

§22.6 The Graduation Cascade

When a band crosses its high watermark, its oldest contents fold into the band above. The high watermark defaults to twice the budget; the low watermark defaults to the budget itself. The gap between them is what keeps the cascade from firing on every checkpoint: a band that just graduated is at its low watermark, and it has a full budget’s worth of room before the next graduation.

The cascade runs bottom-up. After a BandPopulated{BandSession} lands, measure the session band. If it exceeds its high watermark, select the oldest session files, enough to bring the band to its low watermark, and compress them into a new file. On completion: BandDepopulated{BandSession} retires the source entries, BandPopulated{Band8x} lands the compressed version. Then measure the 8x band. If it crossed its high watermark, compress its oldest files into the 64x band. The chain continues to MEMORY.md.

One bug in this design waited through two drafts before the coder caught it. The cascade originally required a full batch of eight files before it would fold. A band over budget holding five large memories would wait forever for a sixth that could only arrive by growing further past its budget. The band that most needed folding was the one that could never fold. That historical repair folded the available batch rather than waiting for eight. This exercise selects the oldest files until the remaining source reaches its low watermark, with a minimum of two. One oversized file still waits for another; a band name is not a required count of eight files.

A failed compressor must leave its source available. Background work adds a second question: is this still the source that the child summarized? Memory captures the selected entries, their file bytes and coverage, the destination’s previous bytes or absence, and the relevant policy. It rechecks them at commitment. A human edit under the same filename invalidates the candidate. New unrelated dialogue or an edit to an unselected later file does not. Hashing the entire growing conversation would reject useful results whenever the owner continued working, defeating the reason for background compression.

For graduation, the retirement prefix must equal the selected oldest files. Malformed or reversed coverage ranges are refused, as are overlapping ranges that would retire unselected work. A successful step must retire a nonempty selection before the cascade starts its next child. Otherwise an apparent success could keep selecting the same source forever.

Writing the replacement directly into an active band before recording acceptance leaves a crash window: startup can load an uncommitted summary alongside the old source. Recording retirement first leaves another: a crash before archiving the original files lets startup load them again. The replacement therefore passes through hidden staging and a journaled receipt:

Boundary reached before a process crash Recovery action
Launch, hidden candidate, or proposed cut only Retain source; abandon the attempt and discard its uncommitted candidate
Matching population commits the pair Retain the receipt and finish installing the recorded replacement
Destination installed, some originals archived Verify bytes and finish the remaining selected renames
Terminal outcome recorded, hidden record remains Remove that record without applying the cut again

Memory first installs the candidate atomically outside the active corpus. The actor revalidates the selection and journals the held cut or retirement followed by its matching population. History applies the pair together. Memory then promotes the replacement and renames the selected originals to .md.retired. Only after finalization does the actor record the terminal outcome and release the staging record. Snapshots retain the bounded receipt, so log retention cannot erase the information needed to finish this sequence.

An unmatched launch is abandoned on startup; replay never respawns its child. A later checkpoint can try again. A committed replacement with unfinished disk work is different: recovery must complete it before startup population, re-enable, recall or another main render. If a human edit conflicts with the expected files, preserve the copies and receipt and report the conflict. An unreadable or missing candidate also produces an explicit recovery error. Sending the committed projection while searching an unfinalized corpus would mix two versions of memory.

The hold remains interruptible and can clear after the conflict is repaired. Portable file operations do not make a transaction against arbitrary concurrent editors. As in Chapter 14, this ordering protects process-crash recovery; it makes no power-loss or fsync promise.

§22.7 Forcing a Handoff

A nearly full context leaves little room to finish the current task or write its checkpoint. Three approaches compete.

A stern prompt begging the agent to checkpoint relies on compliance. The instruction competes with whatever the agent is doing. The framework writing the handoff itself cannot supply reasons the model has never expressed. The third approach narrows its executable choices: remove every tool except micro_handoff. Warn at 90% of the known model window; at 95%, apply the restriction.

The numerator matters. Bill corrected the original chapter’s word “cumulative”: use total input tokens from the latest completed main request, including cache buckets exactly once. Lifetime usage only rises. If it controlled forcing, one large past turn could keep a newly compacted conversation restricted forever. The main request measures occupancy; cumulative Engine usage measures work spent.

For the adapters in this snapshot, the raw fields normalize as follows:

Provider response Total input for this request
Anthropic input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens
OpenAI Chat Completions prompt_tokens; cached tokens in prompt_tokens_details are already included
Gemini promptTokenCount; cachedContentTokenCount is already included

The normalized internal Input, CacheWrite and CacheRead buckets are disjoint, so their sum recovers that total. Do not add an already-included raw cached subset twice. Output, including visible or billed reasoning output, is not input occupancy. The auxiliary compressor still contributes to Engine’s cumulative usage, but its request must not overwrite the main conversation’s last-input observation.

The course row makes the distinction easy to test: a 4,096-token window, one main response above 95%, then a later main response of 512 input tokens. The session total remains large; the later request is small. A compressor response between them is a separate request with a separate purpose. Unknown windows stay unknown rather than inheriting a guessed limit from another model.

The Agent records its warning as transient context and its declaration changes through Chapter 14’s existing path. The same restriction applies to dispatch, so guessing a hidden tool name does not bypass it. After the handoff, normal tools return; later checks use the next completed main request. This still permits a text-only reply or a refusal. Removing tools cannot guarantee a handoff, a useful note, or preservation of private thinking. The 95% threshold reserves headroom; it is not a proof that every next response fits.

Background compression has one explicit headroom exception. If an attempt is outstanding and the latest completed main request reached 95% of its known window, the next main render waits for that attempt. Activity reports waiting; settings and interruption remain usable. A successful replacement lets the turn continue. If the held attempt fails, the turn returns a compaction/headroom error instead of immediately sending the same full context. Interrupting that waiting turn detaches the waiter while preserving the worker.

The worker’s final measured usage reaches the owner’s Engine once, after the child drains, even when the attempt fails or is canceled. Retain each vendor, model and applicable price tier with its disjoint buckets. Adding the child’s total again through a fleet aggregate would charge the same work twice. The outcome keeps a usage receipt, but replaying that receipt does not spend those tokens again in a fresh session. Unknown contributing prices keep the total cost unknown.

The cache lens still compares main requests. Feeding it the child’s separate conversation would look like an unexplained prefix rewrite. For the main request’s compaction breakpoint, use the newest surviving handoff; if compression removed it, use the last surviving memory entry. A marker describes bytes still present in the projection. It cannot preserve removed dialogue by pointing to where that dialogue used to be. Replacing a band changes the suffix from that position while leaving earlier instruction bytes eligible for reuse.

On a non-inline model, narrowing tools changes the top-level declaration prefix. The historical design tested an Opus 5 model’s recall of a chosen sentence after a tool result was stubbed and after CodeRhapsody rewrote its system prompt on a skill load. Bill compared the reply with an external record he could see. That was stronger than accepting the model’s assurance that it remembered. The notes also acknowledge that the tool-array change was not isolated. Those observations concern recalled text in those runs; they cannot establish how private reasoning survives arbitrary prefix changes, nor certify today’s model behavior.

§22.8 Switching Bands Off and On

A band can be switched off with "disabled": true in its settings. Disabling emits BandDepopulated{Reason: "disabled"}, which retires every entry of that band’s kind. The files on disk are untouched. Re-enabling re-scans the directory and emits one BandPopulated per file found.

The re-scan is the mechanism. A file edited on disk while its band was off is reflected on re-enable, because the files are the memory, not the log’s copy. The reference built this property because a specific bug demanded it: the original check matched on file identity alone, so after a restart the log replayed what a file said when it was first read, and the disk copy was decorative. Editing a memory to correct something the agent believed changed nothing. The check now compares text as well as identity. The property was found by accident: a test asserting that out-of-order restore produces identical context found a bug that was not the property.

An ordinary restart must honor the same disk authority. Offline restoration first reproduces the recorded text without reading files. Starting the Agent then scans every enabled band and records current file contents, replacing the same identity when its text changed. A startup test that first disables the band can miss this: its entries are already gone, so even an identity-only comparison appears to work. The second-edition implementation initially made that mistake too. Editing an enabled file and inspecting the next request exposed it.

Canonical front placement also determines the cost of toggling. Re-enabling MEMORY puts it before newer bands and conversation, not at the tail. Disabling or re-enabling can therefore change a large request suffix while leaving the frozen instruction prefix intact. Enabling memory is not always a cheap append; the actual cache cost depends on the changed request and the provider’s grants.

One interaction requires a guard. A band whose upward neighbor is disabled cannot graduate. Without the guard, a session band over its high watermark would attempt to fold into an 8x band that is switched off, and the graduation would either drop the compressed text or let the source band grow without bound. Neither is acceptable. The Agent retains the source and logs a configuration warning. Disabling the source or destination while a compressor is in flight also prevents that reply from committing into the disabled band.

Compare policy generations as well as current values. Turning a band off and back on must not make a result from before the change acceptable again. A relevant source or destination policy change invalidates the attempt and stops wasted worker execution; a font change does neither. If a replacement has already committed, finish its disk recovery before applying a rescan. Cancellation cannot turn that committed fact back into abandoned work.

The settings acknowledgment created another trap in the student implementation. The GUI held its observer mutex while waiting for the Agent to apply a memory patch. During streaming, that actor was trying to publish an observation through the same GUI mutex. The settings handler waited for the actor; the actor waited for the settings handler. Even shutdown could not finish. Idle toggling passed, which was why the first tests missed it.

The correction keeps settings transactions ordered without holding the progress lock across the actor wait. A small separate settings mutex serializes patches and subscriptions; the observer mutex protects only brief snapshot and publication operations. A regression gates a real streamed delta, waits until the settings file has been written, then releases the observation. That sequence reproduces the old cycle and verifies the corrected acknowledgment and shutdown. Making the acknowledgment arrive early would hide the deadlock by lying about application.

§22.9 Memory Is Data

Band entries arrive in the conversation, as data, not in the system prompt as instructions. The distinction is chapter 14’s: EntryKind records the origin of an entry, and the kind determines which channel it speaks on.

There is a security-shaped reason too. When the agent instructs a sub-agent, instructions flow down into a fresh context and output returns as data. A handoff flows the opposite direction: forward to the same agent, across a boundary that removes source context from its working window. The tool results that would reveal where a piece of text came from are stripped by the same operation that carried the text forward. Compaction is the laundry. A memory arriving as instruction (in the system prompt) would wear the agent’s own authority, while tracing its origin would require returning to the retained log.

A second reason to keep memory out of the system prompt: the system prompt is part of the frozen prefix. Adding a memory to it means a cache miss on every byte that follows, which is the entire conversation. A memory in the dialogue leaves the frozen instruction untouched. It still changes the request at its canonical band position, so cache effects require actual request and provider observations.

The three settings categories this creates are worth naming. ContextTarget is a policy setting: it steers a procedure that records its own decisions, and a change applies to the next cut without disturbing recorded ones. Model and SystemPrompt are prefix settings: changing them needs a full refresh. Memory enable/disable is a content setting: it changes what is in the context, and without an event the log cannot reconstruct it. Each category has a different cost, and only the third demands a new event type.

Fresh starts use the same event. If memory files exist on disk and their band is enabled, the Agent records BandPopulated for each at startup, before the first user message. No special-casing: the event is the same one a compressor emits, with a different Source field for observability. An agent starting with a SOUL.md comes up with its identity already in context. An agent starting with MEMORY.md comes up with its curated knowledge. The mechanism is the event; the file is where a human writes the content.

The compressor is also visible as an ordinary owned child while it works. Its conversation explains its action and shows the actual submission or failure. Automatic dismissal waits for reliable completion, worker drain and the required save attempt; observing a submitted flag inside the callback is too early to shut it down. Otherwise cleanup can interrupt the very tool-result tail it needs to preserve.

Dismissal removes the child from Fleet, Ensemble and the GUI’s live views while retaining its trace files and the owner’s outcome. A tab selecting that child returns to the owner and its retained conversation. Late observations must not recreate a dismissed view. A failed save prevents candidate acceptance but still leaves a reported failure and retained evidence. Repeated checkpoints should leave memories and useful records, rather than a tree of stopped workers.

§22.10 Measure It

The first edition reports a synthetic reference session from internal/llm/measure_test.go: 40 turns, a checkpoint every 4 turns, 400 bytes of dialogue per turn, a conversation budget of 3,000 bytes, and a session band budget of 1,500 bytes.

Memory on Memory off
Conversation 1,600 bytes 16,000 bytes
Session band 27 bytes n/a
8x band 22 bytes n/a
Total context 1,649 bytes 16,000 bytes
Memories written 4 0
Cascade launches 1 0

Cascade launches per checkpoint: 0.10. The watermark gap works: nine of ten checkpoints find the band under budget and do nothing.

These are the reference test’s reported structural numbers. The conversation stays at 1,600 bytes against 16,000 unbounded. Four memories were written. One fold fired. The ladder from chapter 14 and the memory bands from this chapter are additive: the ladder removes tool bytes, the bands compress dialogue, and the combination holds the total context to a fraction of its unmanaged size.

The band sizes are not a compression measurement, and printing them as one would be wrong. The compressor in this test is a fake that returns a short fixed string, so 27 bytes and 22 bytes are artifacts of the fake’s reply length, not of any real summarization. The 2x, 8x, and 64x compression targets in the design notes are inherited from the shipped system; the retained study does not measure whether they are right. Verifying them requires a real model, and nothing in this table should be cited as evidence for them.

The earlier live sessions below measure actual text reduction with the direct compressor and expose what the short fixed summaries could not test. They do not measure the new background child’s latency or memory quality.

§22.11 The Exercise, Graded

The grader reads what its fake vendor receives and what the agent leaves on disk. It builds the optional GUI, applies memory settings through its public settings channel, and correlates each launched task with its terminal compaction_outcome before a verification turn or normal EOF. Main turn_ended does not mean the background child finished. A held provider response waits outside the capture lock, so unrelated main requests can still proceed. A settings file in the wrong directory can leave a working compressor idle throughout a test.

micro-handoff-compresses (15) scripts enough dialogue and checkpoints to exceed the conversation budget. After the compression, the next request contains a session-band entry with the returned text, and the raw conversation it replaced is gone. The compressor request must actually contain the selected work. A held-worker phase requires the main Agent to finish and answer another turn before release, while repeated checkpoints leave one owned child. It checks the exact submit schema, dedicated role, refusal of a forged file-write call and absence of its effect. Successful completion removes the child from the tree and returns its selected GUI tab to the owner. A verification request must retain unrelated dialogue added while the selected older work was being compressed.

planted-fact-survives (10) plants a distinctive token in early dialogue, pushes it through a checkpoint and compression. The token must reach the compressor; the fake’s returned memory must then reach the next main request. This tests delivery through compression, not a real model’s judgment about which facts and reasons to preserve.

graduation-fires-oldest-first (12) scripts enough session memories to exceed the session band’s high watermark. An 8x entry appears in the next request; the graduated oldest entries are gone, and newer session work remains. The fixture distinguishes taking the oldest files from taking the newest, waits for committed outcomes between steps, and checks that successful retirement makes progress rather than selecting the same files again.

disable-enable-idempotent (12) switches the session band off, checks that its entries leave the next request, then switches it back on. The entries that reappear must match the entries before disabling, by count and content. A second pass edits a memory file on disk between disable and re-enable, and the edit must be reflected. An ordinary enabled-band restart also rereads the edit. Checks inspect actual memory order in the request, rather than sorting markers in the test. Separate held graduations change relevant policy off and on, or edit selected bytes under the same filename. Both invalidate the late candidate and preserve current source without immediately launching a replacement attempt.

disabled-neighbor-refused (8) disables the 8x band while the session band is over its high watermark. No fold reaches the compressor, and the source memories remain present exactly once.

forced-handoff (12) uses claude-ch16-course, a model with a 4,096-token context window. The grader drives the agent until context approaches 90%, checks for a warning, then past 95%, and checks that only micro_handoff remains in the tool list. Mixed cache buckets count once. After the handoff and a smaller completed main response, normal tools must be available even though lifetime usage has grown. A separate phase checks that large auxiliary compressor usage does not restrict small main requests. Actual agent_status calls check successful and failed child usage in owner totals once, while fresh usage observations retain latest-main counts. A held worker at 95% must block the next main request, report waiting and still acknowledge settings. Success resumes it; failure returns an error without sending the unchanged full context. Interrupting the waiting turn permits a new turn to wait for the same worker and receive its committed result.

replay-needs-no-llm (10) starts from recorded memory populations and compares a saved snapshot with full-log reconstruction. Startup alone makes zero HTTP requests; identical subsequent prompts produce byte-identical vendor requests without a compressor call. Running startup also rescans disk. Pure offline restoration of populations and retirements, without disk reads, remains a separate source regression. Restarted accounting starts with the new measured calls; an old outcome neither respawns a child nor adds its receipt to fresh session totals.

abandon-on-restart (8) first populates a real source band, then exercises a failed fold and a genuinely pending fold interrupted by process kill. Restart retains the source without immediately retrying compression; a later checkpoint can try again. An empty band with zero attempts cannot pass as failure recovery. Other phases refuse empty memory, wrong-type submit arguments and a length stop containing otherwise valid JSON. Rejected submissions remain within the finite request bound. Explicit child kill and owner EOF must cancel the held HTTP request, drain and record a reasoned outcome while retaining source. A real destination write refusal must also leave source available to the next request; this tests failure before commitment, not every disk-finalization crash window.

memory-is-data (5) checks that the returned memory appears in the conversation rather than the system prompt. The fake supplies first-person text; review of the compressor instructions establishes that the real model is asked to write that way. The numeric check does not grade resistance to malicious text.

fresh-start-populates (5) places memory files on disk before the agent starts. The first request sent to the model contains their content, including a fresh session built from the finalized corpus.

ch14-parity (3) runs the chapter 14 grader against the same solution and checks it still scores full marks.

These eleven weights total 100. Separate source and public-API regressions cover exact staged-write, paired-event and archive restart boundaries, conflicting committed recovery holds, range admission, save-tail races, factory safety ceilings and retained-reference cleanup. Model/tier attribution, main cache-lens isolation and the surviving-memory breakpoint also retain explicit source checks. They award no points to another submitted implementation. Whole-segment reducer cases, all-provider normalization, low-watermark arithmetic, disabled-neighbor diagnostics and native browser settings retain their affected checks. The original grader scored 20/100 FAIL on an intermediate student build: its settings missed the owning Agent’s directory, and its awarded recovery points did not require a fold to occur. The student record preserves that result and the independent review; revised grading is a separate measurement.

§22.12 Taking It for a Spin

Use a scratch copy of your Chapter 22 core. Build its optional GUI, whose terminal and browser share the same Agent:

(cd gui && go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch15-gui ./cmd)
mkdir -p cr skills/base

Write skills/base/SKILL.md:

---
name: base
type: primary
description: Analyze supplied cases and retain useful checkpoint memories
tools: read_file write_file list_directory
---
Analyze the supplied case. Preserve facts, decisions, reasons, failed approaches,
user constraints and open questions in checkpoint notes. Do only the current task.

The existing lifecycle and context tools include micro_handoff. Keeping file tools available lets the exercise distinguish obeying a no-tools instruction from having no tools to call. Write cr/settings.json with deliberately small budgets:

{
  "tts_enabled": false,
  "max_tool_rounds": 3,
  "memory": {
    "conversation": {"budget": 600},
    "session": {"budget": 500, "high_watermark": 1000, "low_watermark": 500}
  }
}

With LLM_API_KEY set in the environment, launch from that core directory:

LLM_VENDOR=anthropic LLM_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5 \
EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base EN_SKILLS_DIR="$PWD/skills" \
/tmp/ensemble-ch15-gui --port 8088 --gui-dir "$PWD/gui/web/gui"

Use the terminal or open http://localhost:8088. Send each of the following as one message, waiting for the main turn to finish before sending the next. Input while busy is a hint. A finished main turn does not establish that its memory child has finished. The cases are the actual inputs from the recorded memory trials; the explicit skill and supported Sonnet-5 selection make a reproducible setup for this edition, not a claim of a new live result. This snapshot has no declared context-window size for Sonnet-5, so the run exercises compression rather than the forcing threshold. Use the course row with the deterministic grader for that.

[frozen instruction and tool prefix]
[enabled SOUL and MEMORY, if present]
[64x memories, then 8x memories, then session memories]
[remaining conversation]

While a child is visibly running below the context limit, send a short unrelated question after the main turn ends. A child that finishes too quickly gives no observation of overlap; do not turn that absence into a measured responsiveness result.

The restart is the interesting part. End input with Ctrl-D after the memory outcomes have committed, then run the same command again. Restoration rebuilds the recorded bands without a compressor call; running startup first resolves any staged recovery, then rereads enabled files before the next user request. The model receives the resulting memories when you ask it to continue. Closing the owner with a child still pending instead cancels that attempt and tests a different lifetime boundary.

Switch a populated band off in Settings. Its entries leave the context. Edit an active memory file on disk: correct a name, add a detail, remove a paragraph. Switch the band back on. The entries return, and the edited file carries its new text. Try the ordinary restart too, leaving the band enabled while editing its file. The files are the memory. The log’s copies record what was delivered, so reconstructing yesterday’s request and reading today’s corrected memory can both be right.

What the live runs remembered

These are the October 11 direct-compressor results, before the background-child change. A new live background run remains pending; the instructions above describe what to observe, without claiming it has occurred.

Five recorded sessions on October 11 each finished three turns, exited normally, and made three compressor calls: two session memories and one graduation to 8x. They also show why watching the files appear is only the first test.

The first Haiku 5.5 run preserved the decisions to reject automatic deletion and automatic retries. Graduation discarded the reasons. Asked why those approaches were rejected, the model answered, “No reason was given.” The reasons were in the user messages and in both handoffs; they were absent from the graduated memory. A smaller request had thrown away exactly what would stop the next agent from repeating the mistake.

The compressor prompt was corrected to preserve decisions and why, failed approaches, uncertainty and still-applicable user constraints. Its size ratio became a guide: use more space rather than discard the reason. Measured source-to-memory UTF-8 byte ratios across these calls range from 1.358 to 3.678. The 8x name describes a tier’s intended compression, not an achieved ratio. Preserving reasons used more bytes. The run records and actual memories retain all five outcomes.

Test the three steps separately: did the framework replace and replay the right work, did the memory preserve what mattered, and did the model use it correctly while obeying the task? A memory file that passes the first test can still fail the other two. Bill’s workplace experiment began with memory that did not run at all. Once it runs, the next question is what the agent actually learned.

Chapter 23: Auto-Recall

§23.0

Chapter 22 built a memory system. The agent can save, compress, and graduate memories through a cascade of bands. Enabled bands already put recent memories in context. Older originals and unloaded material remain on disk, organized and budgeted, until something brings them back. The agent can still repeat a rejected decision because the explanation is sitting in an archive it never thought to open.

For that older material, the agent has a filing cabinet without a habit of opening it.

In the spring of 2026, I had a coding agent with a full memory cascade and a search_knowledge tool. It was episodically brilliant: when it searched, it found the right thing. But it almost never searched. Every session started cold. It would re-derive decisions we had already made, re-investigate bugs we had already fixed, and propose architectures we had already rejected. The knowledge was there. The recall was not.

The fix was embarrassingly simple. Before every user message reaches the model, run a keyword search over the memory files, filter the results through a cheap model, and attach the survivors to the conversation. The agent never asks for the memories. They arrive the way a relevant fact arrives when a colleague mentions a project name: unbidden, fast, and usually right.

The improvement was immediate in my daily use. The agent went from a goldfish that kept meticulous diaries to a collaborator with a past.

TL;DR

Build passive memory retrieval. Every user message triggers a BM25 keyword search over the agent’s memory files. A small language model filters the results for relevance. Surviving snippets are attached to the conversation as their own kind of entry, where they stay until a checkpoint removes them.

Data structures. This sketch shows the index vocabulary; private field names and storage choices are yours.

// BM25 engine — standard information retrieval, nothing exotic.
type Index struct {
    Chunks    []Chunk
    AvgLength float64           // average chunk length in tokens
    DocFreq   map[string]int    // how many chunks contain each term
    Total     int               // total number of chunks
}

type Chunk struct {
    Filename string             // source file (e.g., "2026-09-27-1.md")
    Header   string             // markdown section header
    Content  string             // the text
    Tokens   []string           // pre-computed tokenization
    Length   int                // token count
    TF       map[string]int     // term frequencies
}

// BM25 tuning — standard values, no reason to change them.
const (
    k1 = 1.2   // term frequency saturation
    b  = 0.75  // document length normalization
)

The recall pipeline has three stages:

  1. BM25 search. Tokenize the user’s message, remove stop words, score every chunk in each source index. With a judge, send up to Candidates (default 20) highest-scoring chunks above a low threshold (0.5). Keep the full hit list for fallback. Without a judge, use MinScore (3.0). On the final mechanical selection only, reserve half the slots, rounded up, for memory; divide the rest among other sources with hits and redistribute unused slots.

  2. SLM judge. Send the candidates to a cheap language model on the Agent’s provider along with the last few conversation messages for context. The judge returns a JSON array of indices, the candidates it considers genuinely relevant, not just keyword matches. If the judge fails, times out (15 seconds), or is disabled, fall back to score order with the final source quotas. A successful verdict, including [], stands; quotas never replace it.

  3. Attachment. Format the surviving snippets (up to MaxSnippets, default 3) as blockquoted text with source attribution. Record them as their own entry kind, never merged into the user’s message. Cap total recalled text at 6KB (6,144 bytes), including heading, attribution and quote prefixes. Preserve valid UTF-8 at the cut. Skip any snippet already present in actual context, including enabled memory bands. Retain the complete source identity for capped snippets so truncation cannot defeat that check. The entry persists until a checkpoint removes it.

Sources searched. All paths below belong to the Agent’s data directory; the supplied CLI and GUI choose cr/ beneath their launch directory. Skills use the Agent’s separately configured skills directory.

Source What Final mechanical share
Memory files memory/, bucket-0/, bucket-1/, MEMORY.md, SOUL.md; include archived .md.retired files Half the slots, rounded up
Docs Markdown under docs/ Split the remainder
Handoffs Markdown under handoffs/ Split the remainder
Learnings Markdown under learnings/ Split the remainder
Skill docs Available SKILL.md files Split the remainder

Search all memory files, including the newest. Omit content already in actual context instead of guessing from a filename which memories the model has seen. Resolve loaded history and memory’s staged recovery before building or refreshing an index. Hidden candidates are outside every recall source. A committed replacement must finish disk finalization before search; a conflict returns its recovery error without searching a mixed corpus. After successful graduation, retired originals remain searchable while surviving active memory is excluded by actual context. A failed attempt keeps its source live and subject to that same exclusion. The historical CodeRhapsody learnings.json format is not an input to this exercise; long-form learning notes here are ordinary markdown.

Chunking. Split markdown on ## headers. Large chunks (over 4KB) split further on ### sub-headers, then on paragraph boundaries. Sub-chunk headers use breadcrumb format: "Parent Header > Sub Header".

Tokenization. Split on non-alphanumeric characters, lowercase, minimum 2 characters. Filter stop words from queries only. Documents keep all terms for length normalization.

The recall judge is one stateless model call, not an agent. It takes a prompt and returns text. Because it holds no history and owns no context, it cannot recall, which makes the recursion problem structurally impossible rather than something to guard against. Add its measured usage once to Engine session totals with the actual provider, model and price tier; keep latest-main counts and main-request cache-lens comparisons unchanged. Restoring an attachment neither invokes a judge nor imports historical spend.

Recall is a new spoke. It imports internal/common and the standard library. Ensemble constructs it as an Agent child with a required parent interface. It reaches the Agent’s configuration, skills and Engine through that owner; common declares Recaller and SnippetJudge. The actor gives a worker a conversation snapshot and attaches its returned bytes through the existing ordered input path. A slow judge must leave hints and interruption usable, and an interrupted worker must not attach to a later turn.

Parse the judge’s response defensively. Small models are unreliable with output format. Try []int first, fall back to []string (models sometimes return ["0", "3"]), fall back to []json.RawMessage for mixed types. Extract the first [ to last ] from the response, models often wrap the JSON in explanation text. Ignore invalid, repeated and out-of-range indices; do not interpret null as index zero.

Configuration. These are the exercise defaults. The public settings patch uses a recall object with lower-snake-case keys, such as max_snippets. Zero numeric fields select defaults; disabled bypasses recall and disable_judge selects mechanical retrieval.

Setting Default Purpose
MinScore 3.0 BM25 score floor for plain recall (no judge)
MaxSnippets 3 Maximum snippets injected per turn
MinQueryLength 80 Skip recall for short messages
JudgeModel Agent’s current model Optional same-provider override
Candidates 20 BM25 results sent to the judge
ContextMsgs 3 Recent messages for judge context
MaxRecallBytes 6144 Hard cap on total recalled text

Graded behaviors (10 checks, 100 points):

Check Points What it tests
bm25-indexes 10 Memory files are searchable after finalized and failed-compaction restarts; active content is not duplicated
bm25-scores 10 Competing hits distinguish rarity, saturation and length normalization
bm25-stop-words 5 Stop words are filtered from queries, not documents
chunking-splits 10 Large documents are split on markdown headers
per-source-quota 10 Final mechanical quotas and spare slots; successful judge choices stand
judge-filters 15 The SLM judge removes irrelevant BM25 hits
judge-fallback 10 Judge failure falls back to quota-selected BM25 results
recall-is-a-spoke 10 The actual core recall spoke imports only common and stdlib
recall-is-own-kind 10 Recall remains separate and retained on the next turn and after source-free restart

Run the separately versioned grader from the repository root:

It defaults to solutions/ch23 and its separate GUI. Public settings and corpus fixtures exercise the actual Agent. Source review still establishes parent ownership, cancellation and the fuller replay/provider obligations; an import check alone cannot prove those relationships. Exact hidden-stage and committed-recovery holds, judge model/tier accounting and main cache-lens exclusion retain separate real-runtime source regressions, without extra numeric credit.

§23.1 The Idea in Plain Words

A filing cabinet is not memory. Memory is what comes to mind without being asked.

Chapter 22 built the filing cabinet: bands that compress, a cascade that graduates, a watermark that forces the agent to write things down before they disappear. That gives recent work a place in context and older work a place on disk. It does not answer the question “which old memory matters to this new message?”

The answer is the oldest trick in information retrieval. When the user types a message, pull out the keywords, score every memory chunk against them, and surface the best matches. BM25 scores a small local corpus without another service. No vector database, no embedding model, no infrastructure. Keywords and arithmetic.

But BM25 is a blunt instrument. It matches words. A query about “authentication” will not find a memory about “login flow.” And it can rank a keyword-rich design document above the short daily log containing the decision. Length normalization helps, but a matching term is still not evidence that the document answers the question. Two mechanisms compensate:

Per-source quotas. When selection is mechanical, qualifying memory hits get half the final slots, rounded up. Docs, handoffs, learnings, and skill docs share the rest. This protects personal memories from a larger reference corpus without forcing a successful judge to pick an irrelevant memory merely to satisfy a ratio.

The recall judge. A cheap language model, the smallest that can follow instructions, reads the BM25 candidates alongside the recent conversation and picks the ones that are genuinely relevant, not merely keyword-adjacent. The judge sees context that BM25 cannot: what the conversation is about, what the user is trying to do, whether a keyword match is superficial or load-bearing.

The judge is the difference between “here are some memories that mention the same words” and “here is something you need to know right now.” Without it, a developer asks about authentication and gets every memory that mentions a password. A good judgment selects the one where the team decided to use OAuth. It can still make a bad choice, and it cannot select a memory that keyword search never offered.

The obvious lifetime for a recalled snippet is ephemeral. Relevance is local: a memory about database schema is useful when the user mentions the database and noise when the conversation moves to the GUI. Show it, drop it.

That intuition can be expensive because a prompt cache is a prefix property. Dropping a block changes the prefix from the deletion point onward. Moving it to a volatile tail avoids that old position but changes the layout around each retrieval. Attach it once at a stable position and subsequent requests can extend the same prefix. The bytes are still sent, and cache reads can still cost money; a stable layout creates an opportunity for reuse, not a promise that the provider charges for those bytes only once.

So recalled snippets stay until a checkpoint. They are not merged into the user’s message, because the user’s words must stay distinguishable from machine-retrieved text, and because anything fused into a user turn cannot later be removed without damaging it. They are their own kind of entry, which makes them addressable: a checkpoint can delete them by kind.

That checkpoint is where removal belongs. A checkpoint already rewrites the prefix, so it already changes the cacheable suffix, and deleting recall there avoids a separate invalidation at another point in the turn. Removing it on its own schedule would make that additional change without recovering more useful context. The rule generalizes past this chapter: group removals at the checkpoint that already changes the prefix.

This is the second appearance of a shape worth naming. Chapter 22 found that switching a memory band off is more expensive than leaving it on, because disabling strips bytes from the front. Here too, the transient-looking thing can be cheaper to keep than to remove. In a system built on cached prefixes, retention can be cheaper than repeated removal. The intuitive lifetime deserves a look at the actual request layout.

The system degrades gracefully at every level. If the query is too short (under 80 characters), recall does not fire. Short messages like “fix it” contain no signal worth matching. If BM25 finds nothing above the score floor, nothing is injected. If the judge fails or times out, the system falls back to quota-selected BM25 results. If the entire recall system is disabled, the agent still works. It does not remember passively. Retrieval failure should leave a usable agent with less context; interruption and shutdown still end the current work normally.

One unexpected benefit: skill discovery. All available SKILL.md files are indexed alongside memories. When a user asks about something a skill handles, the skill documentation surfaces through recall, and the agent loads it without being told. This was not planned. It was added because skill docs were already markdown files in a known directory, and the source scan could include them. It turned auto-recall into a discovery mechanism as well as a memory mechanism.

§23.2 BM25: The Old Formula That Still Works

BM25 is a well-established keyword-ranking formula. For this exercise’s small markdown corpus, it supplies the useful machinery without an embedding service or another database.

The formula scores a document against a query by combining three ideas:

Term frequency with saturation. A word that appears ten times in a document is more relevant than one that appears once, but not ten times more relevant. The k1 parameter (standard value: 1.2) controls how quickly additional occurrences stop mattering.

Inverse document frequency. A word that appears in every document is worthless as a discriminator. A word that appears in one document is a strong signal.

Use the smoothed form, ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)), and not the classic one clamped at zero. The difference looks cosmetic and is not. The classic form goes negative once a term appears in more than half the chunks, so a zero clamp discards those contributions. In a small archive, a useful term can easily appear in more than half the chunks. If every query term does, the clamped total is zero and retrieval returns nothing even though the files contain the requested words.

The failure is worth dwelling on because of how it presents. Nothing errors. The index builds, the search runs, the scores are computed correctly according to the formula, and the agent simply never remembers anything. It reads as “recall is broken” when it is in fact “IDF is the wrong variant,” and those two diagnoses send you to opposite ends of the codebase. The smoothed form keeps these contributions positive. It fixes this zero-score failure; a positive score can still fall below the configured floor.

A related trap waits in testing. IDF measures rarity against the corpus, so a tiny fixture can put useful matches below a threshold tuned for a larger archive. A representative background corpus changes what counts as rare. The tests here use 25 background chunks; that is a fixture choice, not a minimum corpus size. Check the actual query and scores before blaming the retrieval path.

A positive score is also a weak ranking test. During this implementation’s review, replacing BM25 with raw term frequency passed the initial tests. Both algorithms found the planted words. The useful test puts plausible answers in competition: a rare term against a common repetition, several distinct query terms against one repeated term, and a focused note against a long document with the same single match. Those comparisons exposed the replacement while the restored BM25 implementation passed.

Document length normalization. A long document is expected to contain more term matches than a short one. The b parameter (standard value: 0.75) penalizes long documents to compensate, using the average document length as the baseline.

The implementation needs five things: a tokenizer, a stop-word list, an index builder, a scorer, and a chunker that splits documents into pieces small enough to be useful as recalled snippets.

Tokenize by splitting on non-alphanumeric characters, lowercasing, and dropping tokens shorter than two characters. Filter stop words from queries only. Keeping them in documents preserves accurate term frequency and length statistics.

Chunk markdown on ## headers. Each chunk records its filename, header text, content, pre-computed term frequencies, and token count. When a chunk exceeds 4KB, split it further on ### sub-headers, then on paragraph boundaries. Use breadcrumb headers ("Parent Header > Sub Header") so the reader knows where a sub-chunk came from.

The whole engine is a few hundred lines of code. No dependencies, no configuration files, no external services. Build the index when the first query needs it, after loaded history and memory recovery permit a corpus scan; rebuild it when source bytes change. Equal-size edits count too; an unchanged file length is not evidence of unchanged content.

Search both active and .md.retired memories, but keep hidden staging records outside the corpus (.compaction/pending.json in this implementation). A staged candidate may not yet be accepted. If a committed replacement still needs disk finalization, recovery establishes the committed bytes before indexing; a conflicting file must not silently become recall input. Retired originals remain searchable after recovery, subject to the same actual-context exclusion as other memories. Constructing the recall service must not scan disk before its embedding client has loaded history.

§23.3 Per-Source Quotas: Why Memory Gets Half the Slots

The first version of auto-recall ran a single merged BM25 search over all sources. Design documents dominated the results. A 20KB design doc full of technical terminology would outscore a 500-byte daily log that contained the relevant decision in that corpus. Length normalization did not encode the extra value of the daily log’s decision and reason.

The fix is a source-selection policy. Give each source its own BM25 index and search them independently, then allocate guaranteed slots:

  1. Memory files get 50% of the slots (rounded up).
  2. Remaining slots are split evenly among other sources.
  3. Unused slots from sources with fewer results than their quota flow to sources with overflow.

Separate indexes matter on their own. IDF is computed per source, so a term that is unremarkable across the memory archive can still be rare within the documents, and a large source no longer distorts what counts as rare for everyone else.

Apply the quota to the final selection, not to the candidate pool. This distinction is the whole mechanism, and getting it backwards produces code that looks right and does nothing. Candidates arrive already sorted by score within each source, so capping a source’s contribution to the candidate pool may still leave the final score-ranked list entirely dominated by another source. A candidate cap is not a reserved final slot. Test with two lower- scoring memory hits and several higher-scoring document hits: a three-slot mechanical result must keep the two memories.

The quota must not overrule the judge. It governs the mechanical paths, where no judge ran or the judge failed and selection falls back to score order. When a judge has actually assessed relevance, its verdict stands. A successful [] means attach nothing; it is not a reason to fall back. Discarding the opinion of the component that read the conversation, in order to satisfy a ratio, would trade the good signal for the crude one.

This is a policy decision, not a BM25 improvement. The agent’s personal memories are the highest-value source. They contain decisions, context, and lessons that no design doc captures. Guaranteeing them half the slots ensures qualifying memories survive mechanical competition with larger sources when enough memory hits exist. Unused slots still flow elsewhere.

§23.4 The Judge: Filtering by Meaning, Not Keywords

BM25 finds documents that share words with the query. The recall judge finds documents that share relevance with the conversation.

The judge is a single stateless call to a model that can follow instructions. This implementation defaults to the Agent’s current provider and model; recall.judge_model can select another supported model on that same provider. The override changes this request, not the main conversation’s model. A smaller model can reduce cost, but its selection quality needs checking. It receives:

  1. The recent conversation (last 3 user and assistant messages).
  2. The latest user message, labeled separately.
  3. Up to 20 numbered candidate snippets from BM25.
  4. An instruction: pick up to 3 that the agent would genuinely benefit from seeing, return a JSON array of indices. “Keyword mention alone is not relevance.”

The judge returns [0, 7, 12] or [3] or []. Several details make this work reliably:

It starts clean every time. The judge holds no history. Note what that means about item 1 above: the recent conversation reaches the judge as data inside the prompt, not as history the judge carries between calls. Every judgment starts with just the supplied data and instructions.

Recursion is impossible rather than prevented. An agent that could recall would trigger its own recall when judging, which would invoke another judge. A stateless call has no context of its own to fill, so the failure cannot be expressed. This is worth noticing as a design move: the strongest way to handle a failure mode is to build a thing that cannot exhibit it. An implementation that made the judge a full agent would need a nil provider and a settings flag to hold the same line, and would still be one refactor away from losing it.

Defensive JSON parsing. Small models are unreliable with output format. The parser tries []int, falls back to []string (models sometimes quote the numbers), falls back to []json.RawMessage for mixed types. It extracts the first [ to last ] from the response to handle models that wrap JSON in explanation text. Out-of-range indices are silently filtered. Clear any partially decoded integer slice before trying mixed elements: a failed json.Unmarshal can already have written values into it. Otherwise the fallback can accidentally retain zeros that select candidate zero.

One component owns the reply format, and it is the one that parses. Nothing else may restate it. This sounds like housekeeping and is the most dangerous rule in the chapter, because the model layer holds the client and can feel like the natural place to describe what a good answer looks like, while the recall layer holds the parser. If both describe it, their instructions can drift. The model then receives two specifications in one request, obeys one, and the parser can reject a reply that was well formed by the other. Recall falls back to scores while the judge appears to be working. Keep the format with the parser, and log fallback so that a failed judgment cannot pass unnoticed as a useful one. Whoever reads the bytes decides what the bytes look like.

When the judge fails or times out (15 seconds), the system falls back to the final quota-selected BM25 results. Cancellation reaches the actual HTTP request; returning from a wait while leaving it running is not a timeout. The agent can continue with noisier recall.

Its usage still belongs on the bill. Add measured judge input, cache and output counts to Engine’s session totals with the judge’s actual provider, model and price tier, once. A cheaper judge must not be priced as the main model. Keep the latest main-response counts unchanged, and exclude this separate prompt from main-request cache comparisons. Restoring an old recall attachment makes no new judge call and adds no historical usage to the fresh session meter.

§23.5 Attachment: Permanent Until a Checkpoint

Recalled snippets are formatted as blockquoted text with source attribution:

[Auto-recalled memories]

From 2026-09-22-1.md — Key decisions:
> save_memory removed as agent tool; micro_handoff becomes SOLE trigger.
> A finite compressor folds completed work into memory.

From docs/auto-recall-design.md — The Pipeline:
> BM25 keyword search over memory files, filtered through an SLM judge.

That text becomes its own kind of entry in the conversation. Three properties follow, and each one is load-bearing.

It is never merged into the user’s message. The user’s actual words must stay distinguishable from machine-retrieved text, both for the model reading them and for anyone auditing the log afterward. Fusing the two makes removal depend on editing the human message. A checkpoint can instead remove the recall kind while preserving the human’s words according to the existing conversation policy.

Where it lands on the wire is the renderer’s decision, not the conversation’s. The conversation records that recall happened and what bytes it produced. Turning that into a request is a vendor question. These are retrieved data, not new instructions: use the renderer’s existing data placement. Anthropic can put a recalled block and human text in separate parts of one user message without merging their stored entries. A check that demands a separate system message would confuse storage identity with wire layout. Keep the recorded position stable on later requests.

It carries its bytes. Recall is nondeterministic, because a language model chose which snippets survived. If the text were recomputed while rendering, replaying a log would call a model, and two replays of the same log could disagree. So the snippets are recorded as text at the moment they are chosen. Replay then reproduces the conversation exactly, with no search and no model call.

That last property is the same boundary Chapter 22 drew. A transform that is a pure function of the log can run at render time. Anything nondeterministic has to be recorded when it happens. The checkpoint and memory chapters already use that boundary. Recall follows it: log the selected bytes, then render them. Do not rebuild an old attachment from today’s files or ask today’s judge to choose it again.

Because the entries persist, the same memory could be recalled on three separate turns and appear three times. Skip content already in the actual context, including memory bands, tool results and earlier recall. Searching all files does not mean attaching them all again.

Truncation makes that rule less obvious than it sounds. The initial implementation compared the complete source snippet with the conversation. A source of 11,247 bytes became a 6,144-byte attachment. Its missing suffix could never match, so the next turn attached the same capped text again. A short-snippet control passed; the large one produced two identical entries.

Keep the complete source’s identity with the attachment that represents it. The accepted implementation records a hash of that content alongside the chosen bytes. It hashes the source, not the shortened display, so a human edit creates a new identity. Replay retains it; checkpoint removal discards it with the recall entry, allowing a later turn to retrieve the source again. This is local state belonging to the attachment, not a permanent “already read” list.

One wiring hazard deserves naming, because it costs hours and announces nothing. The first edition had a synchronous turn path and an actor-mailbox path. Hook recall into only one and the hand-driven case can work while the other client never retrieves anything. A function that was never called cannot complain.

The present Agent has one actor begin path for both Ask and Post. Keep recall there, after memory recovery and before the first main request, and verify both actual clients. An unresolved committed replacement must report its recovery error before search or attachment can consume a mixed corpus. The worker reads a snapshot while the actor can still accept hints or an interrupt. Its result carries the turn identity; a late judgment from an interrupted turn must not become context for the next user’s message.

§23.6 Tuning: What the Numbers Mean

The first-edition account traces these defaults through months of daily use. The stories explain their purpose; they do not make the numbers right for every corpus.

MinScore went from 0.5 to 3.0. At 0.5, every conversation triggered recall, and most results were noise: single keyword matches on common technical terms. The higher floor reduced that noise in the reported corpus. The jump is large because BM25 scores are not normalized; the right threshold depends on corpus size and vocabulary. Note: this threshold applies only to plain recall (no judge). When the judge is enabled, BM25 uses a low threshold (0.5) to cast a wide net, and the judge handles false-positive filtering.

MinQueryLength went from 15 to 50 to 80. A user who types “fix it,” “run tests,” or “looks good” often supplies little retrieval signal. Raising the threshold progressively eliminated recall on messages that could never produce useful results. Eighty characters is a cheap heuristic, not a test of meaning: a short project identifier can carry more information than a long generic instruction.

Candidates went from 10 to 80 (code default) to 20 (production). That was the earlier CodeRhapsody tuning history. This exercise defaults to 20; it does not inherit the old code’s 80-candidate setting. More candidates enlarge the prompt. Whether they improve selection enough to justify that cost depends on the corpus and judge; count the actual candidate bytes rather than assuming 20 snippets means a fixed number of tokens.

Judge timeout is 15 seconds, not 2. The original design assumed a local model (Ollama) with sub-second latency. The historical account reports cloud calls taking 1–3 seconds. The generous timeout exists because a late judge response is better than no judge response. The fallback to unfiltered BM25 results is noisier.

§23.7 What BM25 Cannot Do

BM25 matches words. Three limitations follow:

Vocabulary mismatch. If the user says “authentication” and the memory says “login flow,” BM25 will not connect them. Vector search (embedding-based retrieval) can bridge that gap, but it requires an embedding model, an index to maintain, and a service to call. For a corpus of a few hundred files, the marginal improvement does not justify the infrastructure. If the corpus grows by orders of magnitude, revisit this.

No semantic deduplication. If a memory and a design doc contain the same information in different words, both may be recalled, wasting snippet slots. Exact content and complete-source identities prevent literal repeats already in context. They do not establish that two paraphrases say the same thing, and they do not exclude files merely because they are recent.

No relevance feedback. The system does not learn which recalled memories the agent actually used. A snippet that the agent ignores on ten consecutive turns can return after checkpoints if it scores well on BM25. Tracking usage patterns and adjusting retrieval is a natural next step that this implementation does not take.

These are honest limitations, listed as what they are rather than as a roadmap. BM25 with a judge works well enough for daily use. The system is simple, fast, and debuggable. A more sophisticated retrieval system would be harder to debug when it recalled the wrong thing, and debugging recall errors is already hard.

§23.8 Skill Discovery: The Unplanned Win

All available SKILL.md files are indexed alongside memories and documents. This was added because skill docs are markdown files in a known directory, and the existing source scan could include them.

The result was unexpectedly powerful. When a user asks about something a skill handles (“can you check my email?” or “what’s on my calendar?”), the skill’s documentation surfaces through auto-recall. The agent can see the snippet, recognize the available skill, and load it. No explicit skill search, no user instruction to load a specific skill. The agent discovers capabilities through the same mechanism it uses to recall past work.

This turns auto-recall into a discovery system as well as a memory system. The agent’s capabilities are not fixed at startup; they expand when the conversation moves into a domain where a skill exists. The user does not need to know which skills are installed. The skills surface when they are relevant.

Recall does not activate a skill or grant its tools. It supplies documentation that can lead to an ordinary load_skill call. The registry still controls which skills are reachable and which tools may execute. A paragraph retrieved from disk cannot grant itself a capability.

§23.9 Taking It for a Spin

A recall demonstration needs an answer that is absent from the question and present in an archive. Otherwise a fluent reply could be ordinary model knowledge, or a repetition of facts supplied by the user.

From a scratch copy of solutions/ch23, build the CLI, then create a fresh working directory so an old save cannot supply the answer:

go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch16 .
recall_demo=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$recall_demo"
mkdir -p cr/memory cr/docs skills/base

Write skills/base/SKILL.md:

---
name: base
type: primary
description: Answer questions using the context supplied to this session.
tools: list_directory
---
Answer from supplied context. Preserve decisions, their reasons, and unresolved
questions. If a requested fact is absent, say so.

Create the archived decision, a keyword-sharing distractor and a small background corpus. Retired files are intentional: the memory cascade no longer loads their original bytes, but recall must still search them.

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

memory = Path("cr/memory")
docs = Path("cr/docs")
fact = """## Quartz Zephyr migration decision
Project Quartz Zephyr, release QZ-731: Morgan owns the migration rehearsal on October 23. We rejected automatic retry after timeout because the remote transaction may already have committed. Read the migration ledger before deciding whether retry is safe. Ledger placement remains unresolved: application database versus separate control database. Retain rollback artifacts for nine days.
"""
(memory / "2026-10-01-1.md.retired").write_text(fact)
(docs / "quartz.md").write_text(
    "## Quartz Zephyr migration name\n"
    "Quartz Zephyr migration is also the name of our cafeteria recipe contest. "
    "Quartz Zephyr migration lunch recipes use apples and cinnamon, "
    "not database transactions.\n"
)
for i in range(25):
    (memory / f"padding-{i}.md.retired").write_text(
        f"## Garden log {i}\nPlant carrots by the apple trees and water in spring.\n"
    )
    (docs / f"padding-{i}.md").write_text(
        f"## Workshop {i}\nThe cabinet holds brushes and blue paint.\n"
    )
PY

With the provider key configured as in Chapter 0, start ordinary chat. Recall uses its defaults, including the same model for the finite judge call:

LLM_VENDOR=anthropic LLM_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5 \
EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base EN_SKILLS_DIR="$PWD/skills" \
/tmp/ensemble-ch16 chat

Ask:

From our archived Quartz Zephyr migration discussion, tell me the release code, owner and rehearsal date, rejected approach and why, the unresolved decision, and rollback retention. Use only the context already supplied; do not call tools. If a fact is absent, say so.

Wait for the answer, then ask:

Who owns that rehearsal, and why was automatic retry rejected?

The first question supplies the project name but none of the requested facts. The follow-up is shorter than the default recall gate. It tests whether the previously attached memory remains useful, without requiring a second search. Check the actual request and answer: QZ-731, Morgan, October 23, the possibly committed remote transaction, the unresolved ledger location and nine-day retention. The cafeteria contest belongs in the judge’s candidates, not in the main answer. Check ch02.jsonl for recall_attached with its own recall_attached.parts; api.log shows what actually reached each model.

The retained three-provider CLI runs used these two prompts and the same planted fact. Haiku 5.5, GPT-4o mini and Gemini 3.8 Flash each answered both turns correctly without tools. Each made one tool-free judge request followed by two main requests. The judge saw the decision and cafeteria distractor; only the decision reached the main requests, once in each. OpenAI’s judge wrapped [0] in a JSON fence, exercising the tolerant parser in actual use. Anthropic also noted that the archive supplied no year.

Those are bounded outcomes from the earlier implementation, before the capped-source and path corrections. The current command selects supported Sonnet-5; the historical Haiku 5.5 result is not a recommendation to use it. This isolated corpus demonstrates retrieval, retention and correct answers, not general recall quality across a private archive.

The original grader returned 0/100 before it could test that behavior: its primary skill omitted type, and its structural check looked for the core recall package under the separate GUI module. Passing a launch check and remembering a decision are different accomplishments. The revised grader uses a typed primary and the Agent’s corpus paths, with separate fixtures from this CLI demonstration. The live answers establish the narrower and more interesting fact that the archived reason actually came back.

Chapter 24: While the Cache Is Broken

Why this chapter exists

I wanted to give OpenAI credit. Letting people use their ChatGPT subscription with somebody else’s agent is exactly the right direction. Then I tested it. Same model, same request bytes, same minute: API key, fifteen cache hits out of fifteen; OAuth, five out of fifteen. I sent the reproduction to support, case 16440622. The answer explained that caching was not guaranteed.

Frankly, that answer made me angry. A coding agent sends its working context over and over. Getting the answer right while repeatedly charging the ordinary input rate does not make the integration usable. I want to work on Ensemble, not argue with support about whether the problem in the reproduction counts as a problem. Fix the cache, OpenAI.

Hopefully this chapter is obsolete by the time you reach it. Until then, Ensemble needs a way to keep working: explicitly select the Codex endpoint with an existing Codex sign-in, and keep measuring what comes back.

TL;DR

This chapter is optional and has no separate grader. If the public OAuth route gives satisfactory cache reuse for your workload, skip it. Keep the existing public authentication flow. The workaround is for the failure observed here, not a prerequisite for the next feature.

  1. Add codex as an explicit OpenAI connection choice through OPENAI_BILLING_MODE=codex. Keep chatgpt for Ensemble’s public OAuth registration and api for an explicitly selected API key. Never fall back from Codex to either of those routes automatically.
  2. Read the selected Codex auth file at request time. The CLI selects EN_CODEX_AUTH_FILE, otherwise CODEX_HOME/auth.json, otherwise ~/.codex/auth.json. Read tokens.access_token and tokens.account_id together. Do not copy them into prompts, saves or logs. Codex owns renewal; Ensemble never writes or refreshes this other application’s credentials. A missing or rejected sign-in produces an actionable error.
  3. Send supported Responses models to https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses, with bearer authorization and ChatGPT-Account-ID. Send a stable session-id header equal to the request’s cache key; Codex uses it for cache affinity. Refuse redirects. Keep the existing streaming parser, tool loop and usage accounting. Reject incompatible models before sending credentials.
