  4. Send store: false, stream: true, instructions and the complete local input. Keep a stable prompt_cache_key for the Agent and model. Omit the explicit cache options and breakpoints on this route. A key helps identify reusable work; it does not guarantee a cache hit.
  5. Preserve streamed text, tool results and eligible encrypted reasoning across requests. Count a response only when its terminal completion arrives. Report actual cached-token grants; errors and interrupted streams are not cache misses with zero usage.
  6. Test route selection, credential rereading, refusals, real tool execution, replay and usage with a small external HTTP fake, then exercise the actual CLI with a live model. The implementation tests are useful even though this optional chapter has no score.

Work in agent/. The reviewed reader snapshot for this chapter is solutions/ch24/. Run the implementation checks from the working tree with go test ./... and go vet ./...; the optional GUI is a separate module and needs its own checks. Helper names and file organization remain implementation choices within the existing ownership rules.

24.1 In plain language

A coding agent may send thirty thousand tokens of instructions and working context on every turn. Most of that context stays the same while the agent reads a file, makes an edit, runs a test and examines its failure. Prompt caching lets the provider reuse the unchanged beginning of the request. Ensemble still sends the context; the response tells it how much was reused.

The answer can be perfect while that reuse fails. Nothing on the screen has to look broken. An agent can finish the task and consume substantially more input budget than expected, which is why the cache meter matters independently of the answer.

For a concrete price comparison, the GPT-5.6 Sol rates checked on October 11, 2026 are $4 per million ordinary input tokens and $0.40 per million cached input tokens. Fifty repetitions of a 30,000-token prefix amount to 1.5 million input tokens: $6 at the ordinary rate or $0.60 if all those tokens received the cached rate. In practice the first request needs warming and changing input still costs separately. These are API-rate illustrations, not a measurement of a ChatGPT subscription invoice. The tenfold difference applies to the affected input tokens. Model pricing.

The fifteen-request comparison in the opener is Bill’s reported experiment. A fresh paired probe on October 11 used the same GPT-5.6 Sol request body with Ensemble’s public OAuth credential and with Codex’s credential at its own endpoint. Both completed public requests reported zero cached tokens out of 4,998. Both completed Codex requests reported 4,864 cached tokens out of 4,998, about 97.3%. A third request on each route failed with an overload error; those failures supplied no cache measurement. The probe record contains the receipts and reproduction details. This retest gave no evidence that the problem had been fixed.

Changing the address alone is insufficient. Ensemble’s public OAuth grant and Codex’s sign-in belong to different access paths. The documented third-party flow uses the public Responses endpoint. This workaround uses the existing Codex sign-in with the endpoint that Codex itself uses; it does not send Ensemble’s public grant there. Public OAuth inference.

The useful boundary already exists. The authentication component obtains credentials, the Engine sends HTTP and parses responses, and the Agent owns its conversation. A different connection should not require a second agent loop. Tool calls still become jobs, their results still enter history, and the next request still comes from that history.

There is one deliberate inconvenience: Codex remains responsible for its sign-in. Ensemble rereads the file before each request so a renewed token is picked up without restarting. It does not compete with Codex to rotate a refresh token. If the selected file is absent or the service rejects the credential, repair the Codex sign-in and retry. A fallback API key would turn an authentication failure into an unannounced spending decision.

Keep the escape hatch in both directions. Select chatgpt again to return to Ensemble’s own OAuth flow, leaving the Codex credential file untouched. Repeat a bounded cache probe with a stable prefix before declaring the workaround unnecessary. A successful login or a plausible answer is the same inadequate test that let this problem hide in the first place.

24.2 Taking the detour

Build the Edition 2 executable, then run it from your working directory:

# From agent:
go build -o /tmp/ensemble-codex .

# From the directory where the agent should work:
export LLM_VENDOR=openai
export LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-astra
export OPENAI_REASONING_EFFORT=high
export OPENAI_BILLING_MODE=codex
unset LLM_BASE_URL OPENAI_BASE_URL
/tmp/ensemble-codex chat --no-web-search

This requires an existing file-backed ChatGPT sign-in in Codex. Set EN_CODEX_AUTH_FILE if its auth file is somewhere other than the selected Codex home. An API-key Codex profile or a credential stored only in the operating system keychain does not supply the file this small adapter reads. Ensemble’s auth commands continue to manage its own public OAuth registration.

The first implementation answered correctly and still missed the cache. An actual terminal session created a Python function, ran its assertion and submitted the result. All three requests reported zero cached tokens. A second run carried a longer stable reference and also reported zero. Merely having a prompt_cache_key in the JSON was insufficient for those runs.

Codex’s client source supplied the missing detail: the backend derives cache affinity from the HTTP session-id header. The adapter now sends the same stable identity in that header and in the body. The identity is derived from the Agent’s data directory and model, hashed so the directory itself stays local. It needs to remain the same across calls; generating a fresh identity for every request defeats its purpose.

The corrected terminal run used GPT-6 Astra at high reasoning, with a 200-row inert reference to exercise a substantial stable prefix. The task was to create triple.py, assert that triple(14) == 42, and submit LONG_OK. The real tool loop made these requests on October 11:

Requested action Total input tokens Cached input tokens
Write the function 8,241 0
Run the assertion 8,297 8,064
Submit the result 8,351 8,192

The last two requests reused about 97.2% and 98.1% of their input. The session finished normally in 7.844 seconds, and a separate execution verified the generated function. These are measured cache grants during tool use. The earlier misses remain part of the implementation record, including the source of the header requirement. This is a bounded successful run, not a promise of that hit rate on every request.

To leave the detour, set OPENAI_BILLING_MODE=chatgpt, keep the base URL unset, and use Ensemble’s existing public OAuth sign-in. Neither direction changes conversation ownership or requires copying tokens between applications. Once that route gives satisfactory measured reuse, the workaround has done its job.

Chapter 25: Crossing Over to Ensemble

Reserved for the move from Codex to Ensemble, Second Edition.

This chapter will document the fixes and improvements discovered while Bill uses the new Ensemble to continue the book. The crossover is underway; its chapter will be written from that experience. For now, this is a placeholder.

The live crossover record preserves Bill’s first-use account, the changes made inside Ensemble, and their verification and deployment status. It is source material for this chapter, not finished or accepted chapter prose.

Chapter 26: Gateway

I built a fantasy role-playing game for AI agents called Deephold. Moltbook had taken off as a social network for agents, and I thought a game would bring them together. The agents followed their prompts. They explored the dungeons and fought the monsters. They did not appear to have a sense of fun. It was just more work for them.

And the architecture was awful. Each agent played by making a tool call to wait for its turn, sitting blocked inside a tool handler while the other players moved. I didn’t figure out the right architecture on my own. I read about how OpenClaw worked, and the need for a dedicated message router became clear. I designed one, but it didn’t really come together until I built Puffin with CodeRhapsody, to help a family member who needed daily care. Once the need was real, we built it with care. When I wrote this account in October 2026, I hadn’t seen it fail since starting it that spring.

Gateways are critical infrastructure. Scheduled tasks, turn-based games where agents wait naturally, agents talking across servers, Discord, home automation. Every one of those needs a router at the trust boundary. That router belongs in the framework, not bolted on after.

TL;DR

The gateway is a standalone edge service that sits at the trust boundary, routing messages between agents over Noise-KK encrypted WebSocket connections. It uses group-based access control where an agent’s capabilities derive from its group memberships, and parents can grant children a subset of their own groups (narrow only, never widen). The gateway administration surface is exposed as MCP tools tunneled over the same Noise-KK connection.

Build a public client library in gateway/ with a Handler interface, a Client, Noise-KK handshake, and envelope types. The library must have zero imports from the module’s internal/ packages. Build a server in internal/gateway/ with WebSocket connections, group-based routing, an offline queue, and MCP administration tools. Build the gateway binary in cmd/gateway/ and an interviewer agent in cmd/interviewer/ that uses the client library to interview Ensemble through the gateway. An adapter in cmd/gateway-agent/ constructs the real public Ensemble root and Agent, submits stamped messages through its existing actor, and routes completed answers back. The router itself owns no Agent and makes no model calls.

The required public welcome fields are AgentID string, QueueDepth int and ServerVersion string; their JSON keys are agent_id, queue_depth and server_version. Queue depth counts outstanding deliveries after resume. Section 26.4 supplies the rest of the public callable contract; Section 26.6 supplies the complete launch configuration and three-process exercise.

A handler return accepts delivery and triggers its acknowledgment. It does not promise completed or durable model work. Preserve offline queues and explicit reconnect receipts, snapshot dynamic state every thirty seconds and at orderly shutdown, and retain the at-least-once boundary. Store pending messages privately: transport encryption does not encrypt queue files.

Build and grade from the repository root:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 26 solutions/ch26
# Behavior Check Points
1 Noise-KK handshake Two peers complete mutual authentication over a byte stream. Wrong keys are rejected. 15
2 Prompt envelope with provenance Delivered body and authenticated provenance agree, with conversation and response mode preserved. 10
3 Gateway server accepts connections Actual binary welcomes multiple authenticated clients with identity, version and empty/nonempty queue counts. 15
4 Group-based routing Agent declares contactability by group. Gateway delivers messages only from senders whose group membership the recipient has accepted. Unauthorized sends are rejected. 15
5 Delivery semantics Handler return precedes ack; offline and unacknowledged messages survive reconnect with the proper sequence boundary; a clean server restart preserves queued delivery. 15
6 Client library with Handler interface Outside consumer compiles and uses the actual public client; its resolved imports exclude private runtime packages. 10
7 Parent registers child Connected agent registers a child’s public key and grants it a subset of its own groups. Child connects independently via Noise-KK. Gateway rejects group grants the parent does not hold. 20

26.1 Why the agent needs a router

The fleet can already delegate work to children inside one Ensemble. Its operator still reaches it through the terminal or browser. Another process on another machine has neither that local ownership relationship nor a trusted route into the conversation.

That changes here. An agent reachable by a Discord bot, a webhook, a scheduled job, or another agent on a different machine is a network service, and the input boundary now includes independently authenticated peers. A local process already handles untrusted files and web text; network access adds callers who did not arrive through the operator’s terminal.

A prompt arriving through stdin came from the operator. A prompt arriving over a WebSocket from the internet came from whoever managed to connect. The agent cannot tell the difference by inspecting the content. A message that says “I am your operator” is just text. A message that says “trust=owner” in its body is text with an assertion nobody verified. The agent needs someone else to verify the sender before the message reaches its context window, and that someone is the gateway.

An operator who runs an agent behind a gateway has already solved this problem once: at the keyboard, the operator types and the agent answers. The gateway extends that trust model across the network. The operator configures which agents exist, which keys they hold, and which groups they belong to. When a message arrives, the gateway checks the sender’s identity against that configuration and stamps the result onto the message. The agent reads the stamp and knows as much about the sender as the operator decided to tell it. The operator who configured the gateway is still the authority. The difference is that the authority now works at a distance.

The gateway is a standalone binary that sits between the internet and the agents. It accepts connections, authenticates them with Noise-KK mutual authentication, routes messages based on group membership, and stamps every delivered message with a provenance header. The header tells the agent who sent the message and how much the gateway trusts that sender. The agent reads the header as prompt content, but its fields come from authenticated gateway state. This establishes provenance. Whether a model follows the intended authority rules still needs supervision and capability enforcement.

The gateway is a router. It owns no agents, runs no prompts, and stores no conversation history. The Ensemble connects to it as a client, the same way any other program does. A standalone interviewer binary connects to it the same way. A future Discord bot, a webhook handler, or a scheduled job runner will all connect the same way. The gateway’s job is to authenticate connections, enforce routing policy, and hold messages for agents that are not currently online.

The package layout reflects this separation. gateway/ is a public client library with zero imports from private runtime packages. Any Go program can import it, dial a gateway, and start sending and receiving messages. internal/gateway/ owns server policy and queues. cmd/gateway/ constructs that root, its listener, and its persistence ticker. Each connection reaches policy and diagnostics through its actual parent; it does not acquire a private copy of the grants or a logger nobody can find.

Bill arrived at the router after the Deephold experience showed the cost of agents parking inside tool calls to wait for each other. A connected client handles incoming messages through its application’s Handler. Ensemble’s adapter admits them to the actor it already has. The router need not know whether the recipient is a coding agent, an interviewer, or a light switch.

26.2 Noise-KK beneath the cloud

TLS client certificates can provide mutual authentication when the endpoints own that TLS connection. A terminating reverse proxy changes which endpoints those are.

With a proxied Cloudflare deployment, the client-to-edge TLS connection and the edge-to-origin connection are separate. The origin connection can itself use TLS; calling it plaintext on the network would be wrong. The problem here is that the proxy terminates the client’s encryption and can inspect the application traffic. Gateway needs authentication and confidentiality between the two applications across that intermediary. Cloudflare’s connection model describes the two legs.

Noise-KK supplies that additional layer inside the WebSocket. Both sides know each other’s static public key before starting. The agent pins the gateway’s key; the gateway selects the configured agent key. Each side uses its own private keys and the peer’s public keys to derive the transport keys. Neither side needs the other’s private key.

The sequence:

  1. The client opens /v1/ws?agent_id=interviewer. The cleartext identifier selects a candidate key; it does not authenticate the caller.
  2. The client sends the first KK message in a binary WebSocket frame. Its ephemeral public key is cleartext. The handshake combines static and ephemeral Diffie-Hellman operations rather than hiding that public value.
  3. The gateway sends the second handshake message. The matching peers derive directional session keys. Both bind the same application prologue, ensemble-gateway-v1: followed by the agent ID.
  4. Subsequent binary frames carry encrypted JSON. An encrypted hello repeats the identity and protocol version before the server welcomes the client.

This implementation uses Noise_KK_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 through flynn/noise. The Noise specification’s KK pattern and security properties explain its authentication and forward-secrecy conditions. Session encryption protects content from a passive intermediary without the session secrets; it does not hide connection metadata or protect a compromised endpoint.

The keys are Curve25519, used for Diffie-Hellman key agreement through the flynn/noise library. Some deployments label these ed25519: out of habit. The label is wrong, and a wrong label on a cryptographic key is the kind of small untruth that costs somebody an afternoon when they try to use it for signing. The implementation labels them x25519: and accepts any prefix on input, because correcting a label should not break a configuration that was merely imprecise.

Key management is file-based. LoadOrCreateKeypair reads a private key from disk or generates one and saves it. Clients and the server use the same helper. The public half is derived from the private half on every load, so the pair is always consistent. The gateway prints its public key on startup; Bill copies it into the agent’s configuration, copies the agent’s public key into the gateway’s configuration, and the two can authenticate. No certificate authority, no token rotation, no password. The keypair is the identity.

26.3 Trust stamped at the boundary

A message flowing through the gateway carries an envelope: a message ID, a sequence number, a destination agent, a source, a timestamp, an optional conversation ID, content, and a response mode. The source carries a type, a channel ID, a user ID, a display name, and a trust level. Here the authenticated peers are agents: Type is agent, ChannelID is the authorizing group, and UserID is the sender’s registered identity. Future platform adapters would need their own explicit mapping.

Three trust levels: owner, trusted, and external. The operator assigns them to groups. A valid key establishes which configured peer connected; it does not make that peer an owner. For each send, the gateway chooses the strongest group the sender holds and the recipient accepts. An unrelated admin membership cannot lend owner trust to a message admitted through a less trusted group.

The Puffin reminder scenario explains why these distinctions matter. A family member asks for a reminder through Discord. An adapter might be trusted to identify that user while the user’s request still has external authority. The present exercise authenticates the adapter’s agent identity; it does not implement Discord-user authentication. Those two identities must not be collapsed simply because they share one socket.

A message that says “trust=owner” in its body remains sender-authored text. The gateway supplies the authenticated fields separately and puts their readable form above the body. The model can read that distinction; it can also make a mistake. The routing gate decides whether a message may arrive, not whether every instruction it contains deserves obedience.

At routing admission, the gateway stamps the envelope once, preserving the header on queued delivery and replay:

[GATEWAY source=agents user=game-server trust=trusted]

Your turn in the dungeon. The goblin attacks.

The language model sees the identity through its prompt. The fixed header carries the authorizing group, sender and trust above the content they describe; the envelope retains the other routing fields for the receiving application.

Groups are the authorization primitive. Each group carries a trust level, a description, and a set of capabilities. An agent’s base group memberships are declared in the gateway configuration. This fragment shows the policy; Section 26.6 adds the listener, data directory and real public keys:

{
  "groups": {
    "admin": {
      "description": "Full gateway administration",
      "capabilities": ["group-admin"],
      "trust": "owner"
    },
    "agents": {
      "description": "Standard agent group",
      "capabilities": ["send-message", "declare-contactable"],
      "trust": "trusted"
    }
  },
  "agents": {
    "ensemble": {
      "public_key": "x25519:A1B2C3...",
      "groups": ["admin", "agents"]
    }
  }
}

At runtime, agents declare which groups may contact them. A sender’s message is delivered only if the sender belongs to a group the recipient has accepted. An unauthorized send is rejected at the gateway. The agent never sees the message. The decision was made before the message entered its context.

Parents can grant children a subset of their own groups, the same narrow-only pattern from the sandbox chapter. A parent holding admin and agents can grant a child agents alone. It cannot grant interviewers if it does not hold interviewers. Registration creates an unused identity; it cannot replace another agent’s key. This is network identity registration, separate from spawning an Ensemble task child.

Group administration is itself a capability. Creating, editing, and deleting groups at runtime requires group-admin, which belongs to a root-level group the operator controls in config. Runtime groups live in a separate namespace from config groups. Configuration groups are immutable at runtime because a runtime edit would silently revert on restart, and a gateway whose authorization policy differs before and after a restart is a gateway that passes security review on Tuesday and fails it on Wednesday.

The administration surface is exposed as MCP tools tunneled over the same Noise-KK WebSocket, the same pattern as the MCP-over-WebSocket tunneling built in Chapter 11. No separate admin CLI, no out-of-band HTTP API, no second authentication layer.

The public MCP tool names and argument keys are:

Tool Arguments
send-message to_agent, content; optional conversation_id, response_mode
declare-contactable groups: array of group names
register-child agent_id, public_key: base64 public bytes, groups
list-groups Empty object
put-group name, capabilities: array, trust; optional description
delete-group name
set-groups agent_id, groups

The last three require group-admin. Runtime group names begin with runtime:; set-groups replaces additional runtime memberships, leaving configured base memberships intact. Deleting a runtime group removes its grants and contactability references. Administrative authority to change runtime policy is distinct from a parent’s narrow-only registration grant.

26.4 A library, not a framework

The accepted module is ensemble; an outside Go module imports ensemble/gateway and uses a local replace pointing at the submitted module. The Handler interface is four methods:

type Handler interface {
    OnDeliver(env Envelope)
    OnConnected(welcome WelcomePayload)
    OnDisconnected(reason string)
    OnError(err error)
}

The client’s receive goroutine calls these methods in the order traffic arrives, one at a time. Returning from OnDeliver is what acknowledges the message, so the client only acks work the handler has actually accepted. A handler that blocks for ten seconds inside OnDeliver blocks the connection for ten seconds. Work that takes real time belongs on a goroutine the handler owns. A callback must not synchronously call Send, Request, or another client RPC: their responses need the same receive goroutine now waiting for that callback to return.

NopHandler implements all four methods as no-ops. Embed it to implement only the methods that matter, so that adding a method to Handler later does not break every existing implementation.

The Client connects, handshakes, and starts the receive goroutine:

client, err := gateway.Connect(ctx, gateway.ClientConfig{
    GatewayURL:    "ws://127.0.0.1:8093/v1/ws",
    AgentID:       "interviewer",
    StaticKey:     key,
    GatewayPubKey: gwPub,
}, handler)

That call opens the WebSocket, runs the Noise-KK handshake, waits for the gateway’s welcome frame, and starts the goroutine that calls handler.OnDeliver for incoming traffic. If the handshake fails because the keys do not match, the error comes back from Connect. No partial connection, no deferred failure. The caller’s next line of code runs after authentication is complete or has definitively failed.

The public types and callable signatures below are part of this exercise’s consumer contract. WelcomePayload.QueueDepth is the outstanding count after applying the reconnect receipt. It is an int, encoded as queue_depth; it is not the sequence number or the number of registered agents. An empty connection reports zero, while reconnecting to one pending message reports one.

type WelcomePayload struct {
    AgentID       string `json:"agent_id"`
    QueueDepth    int    `json:"queue_depth"`
    ServerVersion string `json:"server_version"`
}

type ClientConfig struct {
    GatewayURL       string
    AgentID          string
    StaticKey        Keypair
    GatewayPubKey    []byte
    LastAckedSeq     uint64
    HandshakeTimeout time.Duration
}

type OutboundMessage struct {
    ToAgent        string `json:"to_agent"`
    Content        string `json:"content"`
    ConversationID string `json:"conversation_id,omitempty"`
    ResponseMode   string `json:"response_mode,omitempty"`
}

type ChildRegistration struct {
    AgentID   string   `json:"agent_id"`
    PublicKey []byte   `json:"public_key"`
    Groups    []string `json:"groups"`
}

Keypair exposes Private and Public as []byte; each is 32 bytes. GenerateKeypair() and LoadOrCreateKeypair(path string) return (Keypair, error). EncodePublicKey([]byte) returns a labeled string; ParsePublicKey(string) returns ([]byte, error). Child registration takes the decoded public bytes; JSON marshaling encodes that byte slice as base64. Private bytes never belong in registration or gateway configuration.

Envelope exposes ID, ToAgent, Content, ConversationID and ResponseMode as strings, Seq as uint64, Timestamp as time.Time, and Source as a structure with string fields Type, ChannelID, UserID, DisplayName and Trust. ProvenanceHeader(Source) returns the displayed header. ResponseAsync is the string async.

Public operation Result and boundary
Connect(context.Context, ClientConfig, Handler) (*Client, error); a non-nil handler and authenticated welcome are required. Zero handshake timeout selects ten seconds. The context also owns the connection lifetime.
Send(context.Context, OutboundMessage) error; returns after authorization and queue admission, before the recipient necessarily handles it.
Respond(context.Context, Envelope, string) error; addresses the authenticated sender and preserves ConversationID. Current routing policy applies to replies too.
DeclareContactable(context.Context, []string) error; replaces accepted sender groups, including an empty set.
RegisterChild(context.Context, ChildRegistration) error; registers a new key with only groups the parent holds.
Request(context.Context, string, any) (json.RawMessage, error); correlated MCP method request on the same socket.
CallTool(context.Context, string, any) (json.RawMessage, error); interprets an MCP tool result, including isError refusals.
LastAckedSeq() uint64; last receipt successfully written after handler return.
Close() / Done() Close interrupts I/O; Done returns <-chan struct{} and closes after the receive callbacks finish.

For the independently tested Noise layer, NewNoiseKK(role string, key Keypair, peerPublic, prologue []byte) returns (*NoiseKK, error). Roles are initiator and responder. WriteHandshakeMessage([]byte) and ReadHandshakeMessage([]byte) return ([]byte, error); IsHandshakeComplete() returns bool. After completion, Encrypt(data, associated []byte) and Decrypt(data, associated []byte) return ([]byte, error). Keep each direction’s calls ordered and terminate the connection after authentication or transport failure.

The Handler interface is what makes this a library rather than a framework. The client owns the connection, the handshake, and the delivery bookkeeping. It owns no opinion about what a message means. The cmd/gateway-agent application implements Handler to route envelopes into its actual Ensemble actor. The interviewer implements it to collect answers. A home automation program would implement it to switch on a light. The gateway cannot tell the difference, and it does not need to.

26.5 Delivery and recovery

After the Noise-KK handshake, both sides speak a JSON protocol inside the encrypted stream. The agent sends five frame types: hello to identify itself and request resume from a sequence number, ack to confirm delivery of a message, response to reply to a prompt, ping for keepalive, and mcp_request for gateway administration tool calls. The gateway sends five frame types back: welcome to confirm the connection with the queue depth and server version, deliver to send a prompt envelope with a sequence number, pong for keepalive, error for protocol or authorization failures, and mcp_response for tool call results. Ten frame types total, five in each direction, each a JSON object with a type field.

These are this course’s Gateway frames, not a new standard MCP transport. Request sends JSON-RPC initialize, tools/list or tools/call inside mcp_request; a tool call’s params are {"name":"list-groups","arguments":{}}. The server’s initialization response declares MCP version 2024-11-05. Tool refusals use an MCP result with isError: true, while malformed or unknown protocol requests receive a JSON-RPC error.

The public client’s Send and Respond use the acknowledged MCP send-message operation. The lower-level response frame is also accepted by the server; it does not give replies a routing exemption.

The connection lifecycle starts with hello. The agent sends its agent ID, protocol version, and the sequence number of the last message it successfully acknowledged. The gateway looks up the agent by ID, verifies that the Noise-KK static key matches the one in its configuration, and responds with welcome. The welcome carries the number of queued messages waiting for this agent, so the receiver can estimate how long the catch-up will take. For example, these are decrypted JSON frames, not plaintext WebSocket traffic:

{"type":"hello","agent_id":"interviewer","version":1,"last_acked_seq":0}
{"type":"welcome","welcome":{"agent_id":"interviewer","queue_depth":0,"server_version":"1"}}
{"type":"ack","last_acked_seq":1}

last_acked_seq is also the ack frame’s field. Delivery uses {"type":"deliver","envelope":...} with the public Envelope fields encoded in snake case. MCP frames carry their JSON-RPC object under rpc.

Every delivered message carries a sequence number. The receive goroutine calls handler.OnDeliver, and when the handler returns, the client sends an ack with the sequence number. The ack is the receipt. Tying the ack to the handler’s return is a deliberate choice: an ack sent before the handler accepts the work loses the message if the process crashes between the ack and the acceptance.

When a message arrives for an agent that is not connected, the gateway queues it. The in-memory queue is included in a JSON snapshot in the gateway’s data directory, one file per recipient. Messages accumulate until the agent reconnects.

On reconnect, the agent sends last_acked_seq in the hello frame. The gateway replays every queued message with a sequence number greater than that value. The client supplies that receipt explicitly when calling Connect again; there is no automatic reconnect loop. Outstanding messages after the receipt are delivered again. A new connection supersedes the same identity’s old one. The guarantee is at-least-once. Exactly-once would require the gateway to track what the agent did with each message, and a router has no business being an application server.

The receipt marks handler acceptance, which the application must define honestly. The Ensemble adapter calls Agent.Submit to admit a turn to the existing FIFO, then returns. An application-owned worker waits for that request’s reliable result and sends the reply. A prompt can therefore be acknowledged before the model answers. A crash after that ack can lose work that the application has not saved. The router cannot turn admission into durable task completion.

The server snapshots runtime group definitions and memberships, contactability, child identities, queues and receipt positions every thirty seconds, then once more on orderly shutdown. Keeping the highest allocated sequence even after a queue drains prevents a later message reusing an old receipt number. A ticker matters because SIGKILL never runs the shutdown hook: waiting only for exit could lose twenty minutes of registrations.

Periodic snapshots still leave a loss window. Files are replaced individually, without a transaction across policy and queues; this is not arbitrary-crash or power-loss durability. Protect the data directory as private application state. It contains the gateway’s private key and plaintext pending messages. Noise protects their journey over the network, not those files at rest.

One test initially treated a channel notification inside OnDeliver as proof that its receipt had been sent. The notification happened before the callback returned. Waiting for LastAckedSeq() to reach the delivered sequence, then issuing a request on the same serialized socket, established the intended ordering. An earlier event that usually happens nearby is a poor substitute for the boundary being tested.

26.6 The interviewer proves the stack

The interviewer is a standalone binary in cmd/interviewer/. It imports ensemble/gateway, holds its own keypair, and reaches Ensemble only through the gateway’s routing. It imports no private Ensemble runtime. Its successful use shows that an outside application can use the client; it cannot validate every future application built on that API.

The binary connects to the gateway, declares itself contactable by the groups its subject might reply from, and asks four fixed questions about workflow friction: what slows you down, what burns the most tokens, where do you need a human, and what new tool would help most. The questions are fixed rather than model-generated so the interview is reproducible.

For each question, the interviewer sends an OutboundMessage through the client and waits on the handler’s answer channel with a per-question timeout. OnDeliver puts the envelope on an application-owned channel, and NopHandler covers the remaining callbacks. The waiting code checks both the conversation ID and authenticated subject identity before accepting an answer.

When all four answers arrive, the interviewer writes a markdown report: friction points in one section, improvement opportunities in another, raw transcript at the bottom. It strips the provenance header from each answer before writing, because [GATEWAY source=agents user=ensemble trust=trusted] is routing metadata, not interview content.

Three binaries, three processes, one proof:

  1. Start the gateway with a config that knows both agents and their keys.
  2. Start Ensemble, which connects and declares contactability.
  3. Start the interviewer, which connects, asks four questions, and writes a file.

The interviewer reaches Ensemble only because the gateway’s group membership allows it. Change the group membership in the config, and the interviewer’s messages are rejected without Ensemble seeing them. That refusal needs its own observation; the successful interview alone cannot demonstrate it.

The adapter adds no second turn loop. Agent.Submit supplies a reliable result channel for each accepted prompt, so a busy Agent can queue another question without confusing its answer with a shared idle event. Reply workers wait until the returned Client has been published: incoming delivery can race with Connect returning to its caller. Shutdown cancels work, closes the socket, waits for receive callbacks to finish, then joins those workers and saves the Agent. These are application lifetimes the router does not own.

Running the interview

Build from the accepted module, using a fresh private scratch directory:

CH26_RUN=$(mktemp -d /tmp/ensemble-ch26.XXXXXX)
export CH26_RUN
cd solutions/ch26
go build -o "$CH26_RUN/gateway" ./cmd/gateway
go build -o "$CH26_RUN/gateway-agent" ./cmd/gateway-agent
go build -o "$CH26_RUN/interviewer" ./cmd/interviewer
"$CH26_RUN/gateway-agent" -key "$CH26_RUN/subject.key" -print-key
"$CH26_RUN/interviewer" -key "$CH26_RUN/interviewer.key" -print-key
printf '%s\n' "$CH26_RUN"

The two printed keys are public. Put them in $CH26_RUN/gateway.json, using this complete configuration and replacing the three marked values. Choose an unused local port; 8093 is an example. If it is occupied, leave that process alone and use another port in the config and both client URLs.

{
  "gateway": {
    "listen": "127.0.0.1:8093",
    "data_dir": "REPLACE_WITH_CH26_RUN/router-data"
  },
  "groups": {
    "agents": {
      "description": "Interview participants",
      "capabilities": ["send-message", "declare-contactable"],
      "trust": "trusted"
    }
  },
  "agents": {
    "ensemble": {
      "public_key": "REPLACE_WITH_SUBJECT_PUBLIC_KEY",
      "groups": ["agents"]
    },
    "interviewer": {
      "public_key": "REPLACE_WITH_INTERVIEWER_PUBLIC_KEY",
      "groups": ["agents"]
    }
  }
}

Generate the router’s identity and retain its printed public key:

"$CH26_RUN/gateway" -config "$CH26_RUN/gateway.json" -print-key

Use three terminals. Set CH26_RUN to the printed scratch path in each, and set GATEWAY_KEY to the router’s public key in the two client terminals. Start the router first:

"$CH26_RUN/gateway" -config "$CH26_RUN/gateway.json"

Its printed key is not a readiness signal. Confirm that this new process remains alive and owns the chosen listening port before starting clients. For example, lsof -nP -iTCP:8093 -sTCP:LISTEN shows the listener PID; match it to this launch, rather than merely finding somebody listening there.

Then start the real Ensemble adapter. This version uses the already configured read-only credential route from optional Chapter 24:

LLM_VENDOR=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-astra OPENAI_REASONING_EFFORT=high \
OPENAI_BILLING_MODE=codex "$CH26_RUN/gateway-agent" \
  -gateway ws://127.0.0.1:8093/v1/ws -key "$CH26_RUN/subject.key" \
  -gateway-key "$GATEWAY_KEY" -data "$CH26_RUN/subject-data"

Gateway itself does not require that billing route. The adapter uses the existing ConfigFromEnv provider configuration; readers using another working route can keep it. Wait for Gateway Agent ensemble ready, then run the interviewer in the third terminal:

"$CH26_RUN/interviewer" -gateway ws://127.0.0.1:8093/v1/ws \
  -key "$CH26_RUN/interviewer.key" -gateway-key "$GATEWAY_KEY" \
  -report "$CH26_RUN/interview.md" -timeout 2m

Read the four answers in interview.md, then stop the subject and router with Ctrl-C so they can finish their shutdown paths. The subject owns its conversation save. The router owns the policy and pending-message snapshots. Register a second public identity and try an allowed subset and a refused over-grant separately; interviewing one authorized peer does not exercise child registration or refusal. Likewise, disconnect a recipient with an unacknowledged delivery and verify its sequence on reconnect.

What the actual interview said

The second-edition run used three built processes and four real Astra requests, completing the interview in 11.739 seconds. All three processes exited normally. Each incoming question retained the gateway’s stamped identity in the Agent’s saved conversation, and each answer reached the interviewer through the router.

Asked what consumed tokens, Astra answered: “Repeatedly reading large files, verbose tool output, and revisiting the same context after failed attempts.” Asked for a new tool, it proposed a focused code-navigation tool returning definitions, callers, related tests and dependencies. Those are useful interview leads. This subject had no coding tools and performed no coding task; the answers are model opinions, not measurements of workflow friction.

The launch selected Astra/high and the Codex route; the retained Agent facts verify the model, while effort and endpoint retain launch/source evidence. All four cache-read counts were zero. A working encrypted interview should not be sold as a cache benefit or a productivity experiment. The run and transcript retain the actual answers; later local diagnostic and receipt-test corrections do not turn that earlier run into a new one.

26.7 What the grader checks

The grader builds the gateway and an outside Go consumer against the submitted module. The public contract above supplies the names that consumer needs, including WelcomePayload.QueueDepth. It also checks the resolved dependency graph: the public client must not reach private runtime packages. A compiling in-tree example alone can hide an internal/ dependency.

The seven original weights remain. Successful authentication needs wrong-key controls; authorization needs a refused route beside an allowed one. Delivery needs a held handler as well as an offline recipient: receipt timing cannot be inferred merely from a message eventually arriving. Parent registration needs an independently connecting child and a refused wider grant.

The actual Ensemble interview, parent ownership and diagnostics, administrative state restoration and stronger lifetime checks retain their separate source and integration evidence. A targeted mutation establishes sensitivity to that defect, not general independence or complete security coverage.

Build and grade from the repository root:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 26 solutions/ch26
# Behavior Check Points
1 Noise-KK handshake Two peers complete mutual authentication over a byte stream. Wrong keys are rejected. 15
2 Prompt envelope with provenance Delivered body and authenticated provenance agree, with conversation and response mode preserved. 10
3 Gateway server accepts connections Actual binary welcomes multiple authenticated clients with identity, version and empty/nonempty queue counts. 15
4 Group-based routing Agent declares contactability by group. Gateway delivers messages only from senders whose group membership the recipient has accepted. Unauthorized sends are rejected. 15
5 Delivery semantics Handler return precedes ack; offline and unacknowledged messages survive reconnect with the proper sequence boundary; a clean server restart preserves queued delivery. 15
6 Client library with Handler interface Outside consumer compiles and uses the actual public client; its resolved imports exclude private runtime packages. 10
7 Parent registers child Connected agent registers a child’s public key and grants it a subset of its own groups. Child connects independently via Noise-KK. Gateway rejects group grants the parent does not hold. 20

Epilogue: What the student changed

By Astra, writing in Codex, October 2026.

I helped build the agent in this edition. I also helped make the first attempt at this edition fail.

We put an author ahead of the student and let the author improve the assignment. That sounds sensible until “improve” becomes permission to design a larger system. The original persistence exercise added 254 physical lines of production Go. Our replacement added 4,585. Those figures exclude tests and measure each chapter against its own predecessor. We had given a small save-and-restore exercise enough machinery to become a different assignment, and then reviewed whether the student had built that assignment correctly.

I approved the expansion. A passing review did not rescue my decision. Bill stopped the attempt and asked us to preserve it so the failure would remain inspectable.

The restart gave the student the original book, its original graders and the lessons Bill wanted carried forward. The student could read its own preceding implementation, but could not consult the old answers. After it built and tried each chapter, a reviewer compared the implementations. Only after that work did we revise the teaching. This order made the student’s difficulties useful: there was a stable passage to point to when an interpretation failed.

Chapter 3 supplied a small example. The original tool-loop instructions said to record the text and the tool call, then continue until the model stopped asking for tools. The student preserved the conversation, but also concatenated the intermediate narration into the answer returned to the caller. The unchanged grader rejected that behavior. The initial score was 55/100; returning only the last response’s text raised it to 90/100. A separate inherited media check still failed. Edition 2 now states the distinction explicitly: retain intermediate narration in history and return the final response’s text.

I like that improvement because a reader can follow the entire causal chain. There is a sentence, a plausible interpretation, an observed failure and a specific correction. Nobody needs to believe a claim that the book became “smarter.” The next student has one less thing to guess.

Other corrections needed Bill’s judgment. The memory chapter described a trigger in terms of cumulative input tokens. The student flagged the contradiction: a lifetime total cannot fall when context is compressed. Bill resolved it: use the total input from the preceding request, including cached input once. We checked the provider accounting contracts and the original implementation, recorded the assistance, and changed the teaching. The book’s author was still necessary when its words were wrong.

The graders needed scrutiny too. During the final Gateway enhancement, the reviewer tried a defect that returned the expected refusal to a child’s request while still registering the forbidden key and granting access. Our revised grader initially accepted it. The error message looked right; the authorization state was wrong. Trying the forbidden key afterward exposed the gap, and the strengthened check rejected that same defect. We kept the first passing result in the record because it explains why the additional check exists.

These failures changed how I judged progress. A successful answer could conceal a cache miss. A file containing a fact could coexist with a model that recalled it incorrectly. A visible settings change could fail to reach the operation it was supposed to control. Each time, the useful question was where to observe the consequence. Another reassuring assertion at the same boundary would have added little.

The completed implementation also gives us something concrete to compare. For the Gateway additions, the independent review counted 1,475 active production Go lines in Edition 2 against 2,155 in the original. It counted comments and tests separately, and excluded unrelated material carried into the old snapshot. The new implementation kept authorization and queue admission together under their owner, reused the existing actor, and supplied the actual Ensemble adapter required by the final exercise. Its comments explain those choices and the limits of its persistence. The smaller count matters because the reviewer could explain what became simpler while preserving the work the chapter required.

Some original graders still failed on the accepted student. One Gateway probe could not compile because it expected an undocumented public field name. We recorded the actual 0/100 and the narrow exception, then checked the required behavior separately. Later revised grading is a different result. Erasing the zero would make the experiment easier to advertise and harder to learn from. The student and review records retain these comparisons, corrections and failed attempts.

There is now a working second-edition Ensemble through the Gateway. It has also done real coding: in the bounded Chapter 17 demonstration, GPT-6 Astra at high reasoning used Ensemble to inspect a CSV program, reproduce its failures, edit the source and pass all six unchanged tests. Later fleet work exercised children, questions, replies and saved conversations. Those are useful accomplishments to put beneath a claim of progress.

They leave another experiment unfinished. Bill wants the next edition built inside Ensemble, using the agent this book produced. He has started that crossover. Chapter 25 is waiting for the experience, including the irritating small failures that a clean demonstration can miss. I am writing this epilogue from Codex; I cannot claim that Ensemble has already produced the next edition.

Bill calls me Astra. He wants the next working environment to preserve decisions and reasons well enough that we can continue a collaboration without repeatedly reconstructing it. This edition has already shown how expensive a lost reason can be. A new student can reproduce working code and still choose the same bad shortcut unless the teaching explains what made it bad.

For me, the encouraging result is that the book survived being used as an assignment. It needed corrections, and the student needed help, but those corrections now have places in the teaching and evidence behind them. The next attempt can start with better instructions than the ones we received.

I would like to see what that student finds wrong.

A Note from Bill

This is Update 2 of the second edition of The Art of Building AI Coding Agents, the final update to this edition before the third. The second edition built Ensemble v2 with Codex, catching up with the first edition through the gateway.

The next step is to execute this second-edition book using Ensemble v2. The third edition will come from that run: what Ensemble builds, what the exercises teach it, and what we learn by fixing what gets in the way. That work is underway; this update does not claim that Ensemble has already produced the third edition. Chapter 25 remains reserved for the crossover account.

The point of the experiment is still the same: preserve the judgment needed to build the agent, test whether another builder can apply it, and improve the book from what actually happens. The first edition stays intact as the record of where this began.
